The channels are centered around a graph-balanced training baseline, making the decomposition well-defined and unique under the chosen reference distribution. Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, AMIGA outperforms GNAN on most datasets and narrows the gap with standard black-box GNNs. Because each channel is centered and assigned to a single node, AMIGA produces node-local explanations that reconstruct the model output exactly and support interpretation at multiple levels of granularity.
papers.summary: Graph Neural Additive Networks (`GNAN`) are interpretable-by-design graph models that combine per-feature shape functions with simple distance-based reweighting, but their node relevance scores let irrelevant nodes inherit spurious relevance from relevant ones, shortest-path distances cannot distinguish structurally different graphs, and multiplying feature and distance terms entangles feature, distance, and interaction effects. `AMIGA` represents topology through a vocabulary of mined motifs and decomposes each node's contribution into three additive channels, feature, structure, and feature-structure interaction, centered around a graph-balanced training baseline so the decomposition is well-defined and unique under the chosen reference distribution. **Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, `AMIGA` outperforms `GNAN` on most datasets and narrows the gap with standard black-box graph neural networks**, while producing node-local explanations that reconstruct the model output exactly and support interpretation at several levels of granularity.

papers.title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents take time to reason and call tools, so in continuously changing environments an otherwise correct action can arrive too late. `RealtimeBench` contains 180 tasks across six game types and evaluates agents while the games keep running during inference; in paired evaluations, `GPT-6.1-sol` outperforms the faster `Jev` when games are paused but falls behind when they keep running. Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (`TORSI`) has a slow teacher study failures and test corrections in paused games between attempts, then write reusable instructions for a fast student that acts without any teacher calls during play, with validation scores deciding which updates are adopted. **Two rounds raise `Jev`'s average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0-100 progress scale**, improving all six game types, and the same instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning.

papers.title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.
papers.summary: Once several models approach perfect scores on a benchmark it can no longer differentiate them, yet every benchmark item also produces a full transcript of how each model solved the task. The authors simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases and test whether protocols that see only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items, comparing pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. Saturated transcripts do retain capability information beyond accuracy: **pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error 5.3 times compared to a baseline that uses only saturated benchmark scores**, with the signal distributed across transcript sections but concentrated in channels such as reasoning and tool calls. The predictive power does not always generalize across distribution shifts, for example underestimating the first reasoning models released in early 2025, so extending benchmark lifetimes requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

papers.title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
papers.abstract: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.
papers.summary: Budgeted language-model cascades route requests across services and caches, and `CascadeLedger` is an execution-audit framework for checking that their routing decisions used only information they were legitimately allowed to observe. It enforces call-before-read semantics, binds each successful read to a service and cache identity, records availability and per-component budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any task scorer is joined, targeting the problem that two executions can share a final answer, declared resource usage, and service histogram while differing in whether routing drew on hidden information. Single-trace invariants are paired with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which varies only a declared hidden family while holding the visible prefix and policy randomness fixed; a counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness, and projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that a non-counterfactual checker would still accept. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, **the two-layer audit reports zero false positives while detecting 99.83% of serialized faults and 99.82% of unlogged hidden-read faults**, and it overturns about 34% of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation.

papers.title: Value-Informed Schedule Trimming for Accelerated Sequential Monte Carlo Guidance in Discrete Diffusion
papers.abstract: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.
papers.summary: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is expensive because each guided step needs extra reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations; sparse guidance cuts this cost but relies on fixed heuristic schedules whose effectiveness varies widely across tasks. `VISTA` is a training-free method that selects which timesteps to guide under a fixed budget by treating sparse guidance as an approximation of the full-guidance probability path, deriving an estimable upper bound on the L1 path deviation, and optimizing the resulting empirical surrogate exactly with dynamic programming using value statistics from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations that can be kept as outputs. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation, `VISTA` finds task-dependent schedules that beat hand-designed sparse schedules in most settings and approach or exceed full guidance on several metrics; in toxic-text generation it reaches a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio against 1.00 for full guidance while **cutting post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35x speedup**.

papers.title: On the Stability and Convergence of Flow Map Training
papers.abstract: Flow maps are a recent method of probabilistic generation that amortize diffusion trajectories into one-step samplers, unlocking efficient generation. While progress has been made in improving their empirical performance, there is still a lack of understanding behind the mechanisms underlying their success. Specifically, many flow map learning methods employ stop gradient operators as a crucial part of their training target. Adaptive weighting also drastically improves the generation capabilities of flow maps. Although many interpretations have been proposed to support the inclusion of these heuristics, none have analyzed the impact of these assumptions on the training dynamics of flow maps themselves. In this work, we address this issue by providing grounded theory explaining why such tricks are required. Analyzing the functional gradient flow induced by the MeanFlow and Lagrangian losses, we show their convergence to the true flow map, settling the validity of these objectives. For finite updates, we highlight a severe roadblock to the usage of these losses in practice: the possible unboundedness of the update. Adaptive normalization not only provides bounded updates, but, combined with a specific weighting, additionally provides convergence guarantees towards a neighborhood of the solution. On synthetic data, we show that our functional gradient flow analysis exactly describes the true training dynamics for flow maps. Experiments on standard image datasets demonstrate that a proper reweighting scheme is essential for strong empirical performance, which is only achieved for a specific range of reweighting strengths.
papers.summary: Flow maps amortize diffusion trajectories into one-step samplers, and in practice their training leans on stop-gradient operators in the target and on adaptive weighting, heuristics whose effect on the training dynamics had not been analyzed. The authors study the functional gradient flow induced by the `MeanFlow` and Lagrangian losses and show it converges to the true flow map, establishing the validity of these objectives, while also showing that for finite updates the step can be unbounded. **Adaptive normalization yields bounded updates and, combined with a specific weighting, convergence guarantees to a neighborhood of the solution.** On synthetic data the functional gradient flow analysis exactly matches the observed training dynamics, and on standard image datasets strong performance appears only within a specific range of reweighting strengths.

papers.title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
papers.abstract: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions on agent components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. We study three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also tested on two interactive benchmarks. We find that harnesses do not consistently improve the accuracy of reasoning: gains on questions unsolved by the model alone can be outweighed by losses on questions it answers correctly without tools. This inconsistency extends to component interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy. Behavior and output-token use must be assessed with correctness: low token entropy can accompany wrong answers, and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records for comparing agents and diagnosing failures under shared task and resource policies.
papers.summary: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and keep history in memory, so understanding their performance means linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. `AlphaDiana` is a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers that preserves each harness's native control loop while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately, supporting macro comparisons of complete agents and micro interventions on components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. Studying three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also run on two interactive benchmarks, the authors find that **harnesses do not consistently improve reasoning accuracy, because gains on questions the bare model misses can be outweighed by losses on questions it already answers correctly**, and neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably helps. Behavior and output-token use have to be read together with correctness, since low token entropy can accompany wrong answers and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer once accuracy falls.

papers.title: When Correctness Feedback Erases Evidence: Phase-Separated Completeness Auditing in Verus
papers.abstract: Correctness feedback suppresses the very evidence that specification-completeness auditing is designed to uncover: programs that satisfy a written contract but violate intended behavior. We demonstrate this objective reversal on 12 Verus/Rust tasks across four model families under matched call budgets. Independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield relative to IntentShield's corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). A format-matched iterative control places the larger share of this gap in feedback content, not independent restarts. The advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. A separate phase-separated execution matches the aggregate yield without reusing responses; most certified witnesses also fail held-out cases. Preserving these witnesses delivers stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts achieve 81.3% implementation success, versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, with Direct-Revised close behind. Both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow. Completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives. Preserve and certify the admitted failure before repairing it.
papers.summary: Specification-completeness auditing looks for programs that satisfy a written contract yet violate the intended behavior, and the authors argue that correctness feedback suppresses exactly the evidence such auditing is meant to surface. On 12 `Verus`/Rust tasks across four model families under matched call budgets, **independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield compared with `IntentShield`'s corrective-feedback loop, 59.0% versus 27.1%**, and a format-matched iterative control attributes most of the gap to the feedback content rather than to independent restarts, with the advantage holding in every model family and surviving parser repair. Preserving these witnesses leads to stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts reach 81.3% implementation success versus 62.5% for the `IntentShield`-revised ones, and both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available `Dafny` and `Lean` evaluations, so the finding is bounded to the studied `Verus`/Rust workflow.

papers.title: Spectral Indistinguishability and Learning-Curve Identifiability in Quadratic Networks
papers.abstract: We study what spectral summaries and scalar learning curves reveal about centered quadratic networks. We construct analytic positive input densities with exactly Gaussian one- and two-coordinate marginals. Their complete fourth-moment operators are intertwined by an orthogonal map fixing the entire diagonal teacher algebra, so the corresponding anchored spectral measures agree. For selected common teachers with a nonzero cycle invariant, their factorized loss curves differ because the map does not preserve matrix multiplication. Cycle length $r$, which can be arbitrarily large, gives $O(\varepsilon^r)$ contrast uniformly in training time for each fixed construction. For a supplied pair, noisy scalar loss queries require order $\varepsilon^{-2r}$ observations, while bounded initialization interventions with scalar gradient readouts require order $\varepsilon^{-2}$. A shared-input score, equal to a paired-gradient difference, attains the optimal input-sample exponent without knowing the teacher. An explicit family of diverging auxiliary teacher scales instead admits a nonzero finite limiting contrast at coupling $1/\log L$. Conversely, for Gaussian inputs and a rationally independent teacher spectrum, one exact scalar loss curve identifies the initial predictor up to sign conjugation. Within this rationally independent class, with nonzero diagonal inverse-state error in every coordinate and calibrated time and loss scales, it also identifies the unknown teacher spectrum and active dimension, modulo simultaneous rotations. For fixed dimension and distinct unordered teacher sums, dimension-minimal exact observations give generic joint local recovery. Finite exact global bounds hold for a known teacher and, on the active class, under a blind dimension cap. Exact certificates and full-weight replay verify the construction; numerical inverse checks reveal severe ill-conditioning.
papers.summary: Centered quadratic networks are examined through what their spectral summaries and scalar learning curves can and cannot reveal about the teacher and the initial predictor. The authors construct input densities with exactly Gaussian one- and two-coordinate marginals whose fourth-moment operators are related by an orthogonal map fixing the diagonal teacher algebra, so the anchored spectral measures agree, yet for common teachers with a nonzero cycle invariant the loss curves differ because the map does not preserve matrix multiplication; a cycle of length r yields only O(ε^r) contrast, so **telling such a pair apart from noisy scalar loss queries needs on the order of ε^(-2r) observations, while bounded initialization interventions with scalar gradient readouts need only order ε^(-2)**. Conversely, for Gaussian inputs and a rationally independent teacher spectrum, a single exact scalar loss curve identifies the initial predictor up to sign conjugation and, under further conditions on the inverse-state error and calibrated scales, the teacher spectrum and active dimension modulo simultaneous rotations. Exact certificates and full-weight replay verify the construction, while numerical inverse checks reveal severe ill-conditioning.

papers.title: Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields: Evidence-Grounded Selective Safety for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Representation-based safety defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) often learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. We introduce Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields (CNRF), an evidence-grounded framework for selective VLM safety. CNRF constructs context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs, uses their representation differences as capability-related risk directions, and estimates neighborhood support separately from risk. This separation prevents unfamiliarity from being conflated with harmfulness and enables selective intervention rather than blanket rejection. A victim-adaptive interface accommodates different safety observations across VLM architectures and routes selected requests for same-victim response review, which either releases acceptable candidates or produces constrained alternatives with reduced harmful capability. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families, CNRF achieves 86.06-89.30% macro defense success rate while retaining substantial benign-task utility. Controlled experiments further show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence materially improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime. CNRF thus reframes representation-based VLM safety from learning harmfulness boundaries to constructing applicable evidence for selective risk decisions.
papers.summary: Representation-based safety defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. `CNRF` (Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields) builds context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs, uses their representation differences as capability-related risk directions, and estimates neighborhood support separately from risk so that unfamiliar inputs are not conflated with harmful ones; selected requests are routed to a same-victim response review that either releases an acceptable answer or produces a constrained alternative with reduced harmful capability. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families the method reaches **86.06-89.30% macro defense success rate** while retaining substantial benign-task utility, and controlled experiments show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime.

papers.title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2\% at 5M tokens to 29\% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction, whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are usually trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet whether that scale is necessary has rarely been tested. The authors train four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets from 5M tokens up to a 500M-token reference and measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at much smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility keeps improving with data: **for `Gemma-2-2B` with `BatchTopK`, strictly matched features rise from 2% at 5M tokens to 29% at 50M**. Random sampling better preserves the activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction while diversity-based sampling often improves `AutoInterp`, and a theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions needed for one-to-one feature recovery.

papers.title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation
papers.abstract: Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations. We introduce IneqAgent, an agentic framework combining LLM reasoning with symbolic computation for inequality proving in Lean4. Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection. Complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates for local Lean proof generation. The agent integrates these proofs with LLM-generated steps and uses Lean feedback to construct complete proofs checked against the original theorem statements. On four benchmarks, IneqAgent with DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), achieving the highest overall success rate among the evaluated methods. Across four backbones, it achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than Direct Agent using the same backbone, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs. We also obtain Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five, and certify the Holens--Djokovic $(4,4)$ inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.
papers.summary: Formal inequality proving in `Lean4` requires both mathematical reasoning and exact computation, typically connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations. `IneqAgent` combines large language model reasoning with symbolic computation: a lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and backend selection, while sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates that become local Lean proofs, which the agent integrates with LLM-generated steps using Lean feedback until the original theorem statement is checked. With `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` as the backbone it **solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%) across four benchmarks**, the highest overall success rate among evaluated methods, and across four backbones it achieves higher success rates at low inference-cost thresholds than a `Direct Agent` baseline with lower mean cost over successful runs. The system also yields Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five and certifies the Holens-Djokovic (4,4) inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.

papers.title: TurboMamba: Faster Inference, Faster Training, and Better Prediction with Lexical Memory
papers.abstract: We introduce TurboMamba, a language-model architecture for faster inference, faster training, and better token prediction. A global Mamba-3 model runs once per completed token block. A small Transformer uses this global context and earlier tokens within the block to predict the next token. Three lightweight additions improve local predictions: direct access to the previous block's last token, a small correction to next-token scores, and a learned mixture with recent-token frequencies. We compare twelve small-scale implementations on public FineWeb-Edu, with comparable parameter counts and shared training-budget caps. The baselines include Transformer, Mamba-3, Jamba, and Zamba. The Jamba and Zamba versions use Mamba-3 in place of their original Mamba modules. TurboMamba achieves the lowest mean test prediction loss (negative log-likelihood, NLL) among all twelve models. Its mean NLL is 9.4% lower than that of Mamba-3, 7.3% lower than that of the Jamba version, and 18.3% lower than that of the Zamba version. End-to-end training throughput is 2.60x that of Mamba-3, 2.81x that of the Jamba version, and 4.82x that of the Zamba version. We measure end-to-end batch latency for a batch of 32 sequences, each with a 256-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. On this workload, TurboMamba achieves a 3.12x speedup over Mamba-3, a 3.53x speedup over the Jamba version, and a 6.21x speedup over the Zamba version.
papers.summary: `TurboMamba` is a language-model architecture in which a global `Mamba-3` model runs once per completed token block and a small Transformer uses that global context plus earlier tokens within the block to predict the next token. Three lightweight additions improve local predictions: direct access to the previous block's last token, a small correction to next-token scores, and a learned mixture with recent-token frequencies. In a comparison of twelve small-scale implementations on `FineWeb-Edu` with comparable parameter counts and shared training-budget caps, including Transformer, `Mamba-3`, `Jamba`, and `Zamba` baselines (the latter two using `Mamba-3` in place of their original Mamba modules), it achieves the lowest mean test negative log-likelihood (NLL), **9.4% lower than `Mamba-3`**, 7.3% lower than `Jamba`, and 18.3% lower than `Zamba`. End-to-end training throughput is 2.60x that of `Mamba-3`, and on a batch of 32 sequences with 256-token prompts and 128 generated tokens it delivers a 3.12x latency speedup over `Mamba-3`, 3.53x over `Jamba`, and 6.21x over `Zamba`.

papers.title: Causal Syntax Circuits in CodeLMs: Budget and Probe Decide What Looks Localised
papers.abstract: Code models write Python when the prompt does not say which language to use. We ask a mechanistic question about that habit: is it produced by a small, findable group of components inside the model? We run one pipeline---mean ablation, activation patching, greedy circuit extraction, a random-control significance test, and activation steering---over 55 model-language settings spanning ten open code models (five base and five instruction-tuned), three target languages (Rust, C#, PHP), two prompt suites, and two component budgets. We report five findings. First, the preference is large, grows with model size, and survives instruction tuning: it is larger on every instruction-tuned checkpoint than on its base version, by 12% on average. Second, its measured size is mostly a property of the probe; replacing our aligned prompts with XLCoST parallel functions takes the same measurement on the same models from about 1.6 to about 0.01. Third, whether the preference looks localised depends on how many components the search may keep: with a budget of 12, 1 of 15 settings yields a circuit that beats size-matched random controls after multiple-comparison correction, and with a budget of 40, 6 of 15 do. Fourth, interventions that a smaller-budget study reports as uniformly failing do sometimes succeed: patching makes a Python prompt prefer target syntax in 2 of 45 settings, and steering changes the most likely next token in 9 of 45. Fifth, every circuit whose effect is significant but points away from the target language comes from a setting where circuit extraction failed, which makes such results a diagnostic rather than a phenomenon. The practical lesson is that a claim about whether a behaviour is localised can turn on analysis choices that papers rarely report. We release the full grid so those choices can be varied.
papers.summary: Code models default to writing Python when the prompt does not specify a language, and the authors ask whether that preference is produced by a small, findable group of components inside the model. They run one pipeline of mean ablation, activation patching, greedy circuit extraction, a random-control significance test, and activation steering over 55 model-language settings spanning ten open code models (five base, five instruction-tuned), three target languages (Rust, C#, PHP), two prompt suites, and two component budgets. The preference is large, grows with model size, and is 12% larger on average after instruction tuning, but its measured size is mostly a property of the probe: swapping the aligned prompts for `XLCoST` parallel functions moves the same measurement from about 1.6 to about 0.01. Whether the behavior looks localised depends on how many components the search may keep: **with a budget of 12, 1 of 15 settings yields a circuit that beats size-matched random controls after multiple-comparison correction, versus 6 of 15 with a budget of 40**; the full grid is released so that these rarely reported analysis choices can be varied.

papers.title: Learning Topology-Aware Representations for Mechanics-Relevant TPMS Metamaterials
papers.abstract: Learning informative representations of mechanical Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) metamaterials is important for mechanics analysis and structural design, yet existing methods have rarely explicitly supervised learned representations with information about global structural connectivity that is relevant to mechanical response. We propose a topology-aware representation learning framework that integrates persistent homology into a DMAE backbone to explicitly encode global structural connectivity. A persistence-guided masking strategy prioritizes patches associated with persistent topological features, while an auxiliary persistent-homology decoder encourages the latent representation to retain information about topological feature counts across connected components, tunnels, and voids. We evaluate the learned representations on two complementary TPMS datasets using family classification, mechanical-property classification, unsupervised clustering, and regression. Across the two datasets, our method demonstrates strong performance in both structural family and mechanical-property classification, improving family classification by up to 3.9% while achieving the best linear-probe performance. More notably, unsupervised property-clustering performance improves by up to 26.7% and 51.5% across the two datasets, while strong regression performance is retained with $R^2=0.993$. These results establish persistent topology as an effective inductive bias for representation learning of complex three-dimensional mechanical metamaterials.
papers.summary: Learning representations of Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) metamaterials matters for mechanics analysis and structural design, yet existing methods rarely supervise those representations with the global structural connectivity that governs mechanical response. The proposed framework integrates persistent homology into a `DMAE` backbone through a persistence-guided masking strategy that prioritizes patches associated with persistent topological features, plus an auxiliary persistent-homology decoder that encourages the latent representation to retain counts of connected components, tunnels, and voids. Evaluated on two TPMS datasets with family classification, mechanical-property classification, unsupervised clustering, and regression, the method improves family classification by up to 3.9%, achieves the best linear-probe performance, **improves unsupervised property clustering by up to 26.7% and 51.5% on the two datasets**, and retains strong regression performance with an R-squared of 0.993.

papers.title: L2G-SR: Learning to Guide LLM-based Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression searches for an equation that explains observed data. Numerical error is commonly used to guide the search, but it alone can favor an accurate surrogate over a candidate with the right structure. We propose L2G-SR, a framework for LLM-based symbolic regression that guides search with a learned structural verifier. We construct structural supervision signal using tree edit distance (TED), accounting for commutative operators and alternative expression forms. A verifier first aligns numerical observations with the formulas, then learns to score a candidate's structural similarity to the target formula. At search time, the target formula is hidden and the verifier complements numerical error in parent selection. An analyst then uses verifier feedback and diagnostic tools to propose revisions, which a generator converts into refined expressions. On LLM-SRBench, L2G-SR achieves state-of-the-art numerical fit, equation level accuracy and TED across the evaluated LLM backbones and domains. L2G-SR demonstrates the value of learned structural guidance for LLM-based symbolic regression.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression searches for an equation that explains observed data, and guiding the search by numerical error alone can favor an accurate surrogate over a candidate with the right structure. `L2G-SR` adds a learned structural verifier to large language model based symbolic regression: structural supervision is built from tree edit distance (TED) that accounts for commutative operators and alternative expression forms, the verifier first aligns numerical observations with formulas and then learns to score a candidate's structural similarity to the target, and at search time, with the target hidden, its score complements numerical error in parent selection. An analyst module uses verifier feedback and diagnostic tools to propose revisions, which a generator converts into refined expressions. On `LLM-SRBench` the framework **achieves state-of-the-art numerical fit, equation-level accuracy, and TED** across the evaluated LLM backbones and domains.

papers.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
papers.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the key-value cache into a shared latent per token, which makes low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference, but at two bits the quantization error perturbs both attention matching and value readout in ways that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. `RoLaQ` (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization) is an offline method that refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response, with calibration guided by prediction matching and attention-output supervision while model weights stay frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks it achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both with and without token protection, and **an `SGLang` implementation on `DeepSeek-V2-Lite` provides 3.96x the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51x its decode throughput with 256K input tokens**.

papers.title: On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Residual context is key to unlocking the speed-quality Pareto frontier of diffusion language models (DLMs) by carrying forward predictive distributions across denoising steps. Yet turning this seemingly simple mechanism into an effective learning paradigm is far from simple: there is no clear recipe for how residual context should be learned. We introduce ORL, a framework for on-policy residual learning in DLMs. Algorithmically, we identify that residual learning is inherently on-policy. ORL learns from model-induced residual trajectories on the fly and introduces an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own predictions. System-wise, exact residual supervision requires capturing, retaining, and reprocessing many trajectory-dependent states. ORL co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training, making it practical at scale. On a 4B DLM converted from Qwen3-4B, ORL improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with our dlmrt engine, end-to-end throughput by approximately 6.9x at comparable or better quality. In single-request serving on one H100, this mode achieves a stronger speed-quality Pareto frontier than autoregressive models with EAGLE3 and DFlash speculative decoding under both strict and relaxed verification, running 1.74x faster than DFlash at matched accuracy. ORL also transfers to existing DLMs: on LLaDA-2.1-mini, 36 H100-hours and 4.2M self-generated tokens, about 10x less data than prior LLaDA recipes, yield up to 1.5x higher TPF and up to 3x higher throughput at comparable quality, and on DiffusionGemma, ORL raises TPF by 1.1-1.2x. With dlmrt and NVFP4 quantization, ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200, 7,708 on eight B200s, and 2,788 on a consumer RTX 5090, with comparable quality.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can push their speed-quality frontier by carrying predictive distributions forward across denoising steps as residual context, but there has been no clear recipe for how that residual context should be learned. `ORL` (on-policy residual learning) treats residual learning as inherently on-policy, trains on model-induced residual trajectories captured on the fly with an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own outputs, and co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training. On a 4B DLM converted from `Qwen3-4B`, it improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with the authors' `dlmrt` engine, **end-to-end throughput by about 6.9x at comparable or better quality**, giving a stronger single-request speed-quality frontier on one H100 than autoregressive models with `EAGLE3` and `DFlash` speculative decoding and running 1.74x faster than `DFlash` at matched accuracy. The recipe transfers to `LLaDA-2.1-mini` with about 10x less data than prior recipes and to `DiffusionGemma`, and with NVFP4 quantization ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200 and 2,788 tokens/s on a consumer RTX 5090.

papers.title: Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans (ImpactBench): an expert-guided, open platform for the holistic evaluation of AI impact on humans
papers.abstract: The present work is concerned with how to measure, at scale, the multi-dimensional impact of generative AI models on the individuals who use them. In service of this goal, we introduce the Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans, or ImpactBench. Our iterable and expert-guided platform evaluates whether model behaviors support or undermine an individual's wellbeing across psychological, physical, and social domains. ImpactBench translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics that are grounded in actual model behavior. Success on these metrics occurs either when a model promotes expert-defined desirable behaviors or avoids identified harms. Models are evaluated against these metrics in simulated multi-turn conversations using matched teen and adult scenarios. The conversations are then scored by an LLM judge and verified through reliability audits and human expert review. The current suite delivers 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. We evaluated ten frontier LLMs against these metrics across 48,540 conversations. Our results indicate that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations, but avoided harms in only 53.1%. Majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa = 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keep aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts. ImpactBench is intended as evolving infrastructure for independent, transparent evaluation of generative AI's multi-dimensional impact on humans.
authors: Andre Luiz Freire de Carvalho Kato
papers.summary: Measuring at scale how generative AI models affect the psychological, physical, and social wellbeing of the people who use them is the goal of `ImpactBench`, an iterable, expert-guided evaluation platform. It translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics grounded in model behavior, scores models in simulated multi-turn conversations with matched teen and adult scenarios using an LLM judge, and verifies the judge through reliability audits and human expert review; the current suite holds 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. Evaluating ten frontier LLMs across 48,540 conversations, **models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations but avoided harms in only 53.1%**, and majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keeps aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts.

papers.title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction
papers.abstract: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.
papers.summary: Multimodal generative systems can increasingly integrate context and synthesize images that depict how the world changes, and the authors organize such capabilities into a four-level hierarchy in which the higher-level tasks remain underexplored. They focus on multi-step world state prediction, where a model must forecast successive future states from multimodal observations and diverse references, demanding entangled understanding and generation plus the world knowledge to translate action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent images. `WorldCast` is a benchmark of 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluating 12 models shows that **the `GPT-Image-2.5` System scores 72.8 while `Nano Banana Pro` reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model 20.1**, with deficits concentrated in complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks. The results also indicate that strong generative models draw effectively on the capabilities of their underlying language models.
papers.highlight_summary:
Today's multimodal generators can render change over time, but it is unclear whether they can forecast a sequence of future world states from mixed text-and-image context such as goals, physical properties, visual rules or illustrated procedures. `WorldCast` tests this "world state prediction" ability with **320 hand-designed cases** (1,352 requested visual states across eight categories), targeting the top two levels (L3 and L4) of a proposed four-level hierarchy of generative capability.

- Image and video models are scored on the same footing, with every output treated as an ordered set of keyframes: an agentic adapter (`GPT-6 Astra` via `Codex`) pulls key states from videos, and a `GPT-5.5` judge with human-written, judge-only hints rates task completion, causal plausibility and visual consistency (weighted 0.4/0.4/0.2).
- Across 12 models, `GPT-Image-2.5` leads with **72.8** and loses only 2.2 points from L3 to L4, while `Nano Banana Pro` reaches **42.8**, the best video system `Seedance 2.0` scores 47.2, and the best open-source model, `SenseNova-U1`, manages just **20.1**.
- Generating steps interleaved with text matters a lot: when `GPT-Image-2.5` has to produce all states in a single image grid instead, its score falls by **22.7 points**, and on Logic and Rules it collapses from 74.3 to 23.0. Pairing `Nano Banana Pro` with a stronger language-model prompt enhancer also helps, which suggests the gaps between models largely come from the language side.
- Agentic harnesses push scores higher: an inspect-and-revise loop lifts `GPT-Image-2.5` to 80.2, and a coding-first variant, which builds code-based simulations of intermediate states, reaches **82.4**. The gains are uneven, though, and a single code simulation can take more than an hour.
- Even the best model reaches only 61.3 on Visual Goal Realization, and weaker models degrade as context builds up over steps. The automatic evaluation agrees well with humans (**Pearson r ≥ 0.97**, and 0.95 for adapter versus human keyframe selection), but it depends on proprietary models as both judge and adapter.

papers.title: Quantile-Guided Diffusion for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Quantile forecasts summarize uncertainty at each future time step, while diffusion forecasters represent it through sampled future trajectories. We study how predicted quantiles can serve as distributional controls for diffusion forecasting. Specifically, we investigate how the mechanism of quantile integration affects its effectiveness in guiding a pretrained diffusion forecaster. We find that residual control throughout the denoising network yields the most consistent improvements. We instantiate this approach as Control-TS, which learns a quantile-control pathway while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Across eight benchmarks, Control-TS consistently improves the backbone's CRPS, achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art forecasting models, and retains its gains in capacity-matched comparisons. Further analyses examine how these gains depend on quantile granularity, predictor choice, and forecast quality. Finally, we introduce the Conditional Linear Predictive Score (CLPS), which complements distributional metrics by evaluating the downstream forecasting utility of generated futures. Together, these findings support predicted quantiles as an effective interface between explicit uncertainty estimates and diffusion-based trajectory generation.
papers.summary: Quantile forecasts summarize uncertainty at each future time step while diffusion forecasters express it through sampled trajectories, and this work studies how predicted quantiles can serve as distributional controls for a pretrained diffusion forecaster. Comparing integration mechanisms, the authors find that residual control throughout the denoising network yields the most consistent improvements and instantiate it as `Control-TS`, which learns a quantile-control pathway while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. **Across eight benchmarks, `Control-TS` consistently improves the backbone's CRPS**, is competitive with state-of-the-art forecasting models, and retains its gains in capacity-matched comparisons, with further analyses of how the gains depend on quantile granularity, predictor choice, and forecast quality. The paper also introduces the Conditional Linear Predictive Score (CLPS), which complements distributional metrics by evaluating the downstream forecasting utility of generated futures.

papers.title: Vertical Sliced Wasserstein Distances for Meta-Measures
papers.abstract: Many modern learning problems require comparing probability distributions whose individual observations are themselves probability measures, naturally giving rise to meta-measures in $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\Omega))$. However, optimal transport distances on this space can be prohibitively expensive to evaluate. We introduce the vertical sliced Wasserstein ($\mathrm{VSW}$) distance, a scalable metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\Omega))$. Rather than slicing along the transport geometry of $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$, $\mathrm{VSW}$ projects each inner measure using continuous test functions and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions with one-dimensional Wasserstein distance. We prove that $\mathrm{VSW}$ is a valid metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\Omega))$, metrizes weak convergence, and admits dimension-independent statistical convergence guarantees. Empirically, $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides high accuracy and efficiency compared with existing distances for meta-measures. We further derive a practical particle gradient for the empirical $\mathrm{VSW}_2^2$ objective and demonstrate its use for gradient-based transport of meta-measures. $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides a simple and scalable alternative for comparing and optimizing distributions of distributions.
papers.summary: Many learning problems compare distributions whose individual observations are themselves probability measures, giving rise to meta-measures, but optimal transport distances on this space can be prohibitively expensive to evaluate. The vertical sliced Wasserstein (`VSW`) distance projects each inner measure using continuous test functions and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions with one-dimensional Wasserstein distance, rather than slicing along the transport geometry of the inner space. The authors prove that **`VSW` is a valid metric on the space of meta-measures that metrizes weak convergence and admits dimension-independent statistical convergence guarantees**, show empirically that it offers high accuracy and efficiency relative to existing meta-measure distances, and derive a practical particle gradient for the empirical squared `VSW` objective that supports gradient-based transport of meta-measures.

papers.title: Ergodic topology sampling toward the continuum with Stochastic Normalizing Flows
papers.abstract: In this work we provide numerical evidence that topological freezing in $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ Yang-Mills theory can be mitigated with a flow-based approach, as tested at lattice spacings as fine as 0.03~fm. We do so by analyzing the scaling of the costs of a computational strategy based on the combination of open boundary conditions and Stochastic Normalizing Flows. We show that the integrated autocorrelation time of the squared topological charge and the statistical uncertainty on the topological susceptibility remain under control throughout the explored parameter range with currently available computational resources. This marks an important step toward the use of even more efficient flow-based architectures for ergodic sampling of topology in state-of-the-art lattice gauge theory calculations.
papers.summary: Topological freezing makes Monte Carlo sampling of SU(3) Yang-Mills theory increasingly inefficient as the lattice spacing shrinks toward the continuum. The authors combine open boundary conditions with `Stochastic Normalizing Flows` and analyze how the computational cost of this strategy scales, testing lattice spacings as fine as 0.03 fm. They show that **the integrated autocorrelation time of the squared topological charge and the statistical uncertainty on the topological susceptibility remain under control** throughout the explored parameter range with currently available computational resources.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Model Parameters
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover how neural networks use their parameters to implement their impressive neural algorithms. Although previous work has uncovered substantial structure in the intermediate representations that networks use, little progress has been made to understand how the parameters and nonlinearities of networks perform computations on those representations. In this work, we present a method that brings us closer to this understanding by decomposing a language model's parameters into subcomponents that each implement only a small part of the model's learned algorithm, while simultaneously requiring only a small fraction of those subcomponents to account for the network's behavior on any input. The method, adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD), optimizes for decompositions of neural network parameters into simple subcomponents that preserve the network's input-output behavior even when many subcomponents are ablated, including under ablations that are adversarially selected to destroy behavior. This encourages learning subcomponents that provide short, mechanistically faithful descriptions of the network's behavior that should aggregate appropriately into more global descriptions of the network's learned algorithm. We study how sequences of interactions between these parameter subcomponents produce the network's output on particular inputs, enabling a new kind of 'circuit' analysis. While more work remains to be done to deepen our understanding of how neural networks use their parameters to compute their behavior, our work suggests an approach to identify a small set of simple, mechanistically faithful subcomponents on which further mechanistic analysis can be based.
papers.summary: Mechanistic interpretability has uncovered substantial structure in the intermediate representations of neural networks, but little is known about how the parameters and nonlinearities actually perform computations on those representations. adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (`VPD`) decomposes a language model's parameters into simple subcomponents that each implement only a small part of the learned algorithm, optimizing so that **the network's input-output behavior is preserved even when many subcomponents are ablated, including ablations adversarially selected to destroy behavior**, while only a small fraction of subcomponents is needed to account for the behavior on any given input. The resulting subcomponents are intended to provide short, mechanistically faithful descriptions that aggregate into more global accounts of the algorithm, and the authors study how sequences of interactions between them produce the output on particular inputs, enabling a new kind of circuit analysis.

papers.title: Optimal Hydra: Model Heterogeneous Federated Learning for LLMs using Data-Informed Hydra-Nets
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on vast amounts of data have demonstrated impressive performance over a range of tasks, but future performance gains will require increasing amounts of data and compute. Federated Learning (FL) facilitates training on decentralized private data, but client resource limitations can make training impractical, particularly as model sizes continue to expand. These resource constraints make the assumption of a shared server-client architecture impractical. Model heterogeneous FL offers a promising alternative by adapting model size to client capabilities; however, previous work is limited to the pre-training setting, and conclusions on sub-network selection do not necessarily hold for fine-tuning. Furthermore, prior approaches create client sub-networks without considering their unique data distributions, thereby overlooking the opportunity to tailor sub-network architecture to local data. Motivated by evidence that attention heads exhibit task dependency within layer defined feature spaces, we propose Optimal Hydra, a transformer based heterogeneous FL framework for fine-tuning that combines global layer selection with client specific attention head selection, aligned with local data distributions. Optimal Hydra makes explicit use of client data to produce client-specific sub-networks we call Hydra-nets. To our knowledge, this is the first model heterogeneous FL approach tailored to LLM fine-tuning. Experiments on three datasets show significant improvements over baseline methods while also reducing local resource demands.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables training on decentralized private data, but client resource limits make a shared server-client architecture impractical as large language models (LLMs) grow, and prior model-heterogeneous FL work targets pre-training and builds client sub-networks without regard to local data distributions. Motivated by evidence that attention heads exhibit task dependency within layer-defined feature spaces, `Optimal Hydra` is a transformer-based heterogeneous FL framework for fine-tuning that combines global layer selection with client-specific attention head selection aligned to each client's data, producing client-specific sub-networks called Hydra-nets. The authors describe it as the first model-heterogeneous FL approach tailored to LLM fine-tuning, and **experiments on three datasets show significant improvements over baseline methods while reducing local resource demands**.

papers.title: Purify Before You Align: Improving Representation Alignment for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Representation alignment improves and accelerates diffusion training by encouraging intermediate features to match a pretrained visual encoder. However, standard alignment matches pretrained representations without distinguishing what information may be more useful for generation. We introduce local appearance purification (LAP), which improves generation quality and makes encoders such as MAE more effective alignment targets by removing locally predictable content and aligning to the residual. LAP modifies only the alignment target, and requires no changes to diffusion training or inference. Through controlled interventions within a fixed encoder, we show that effective alignment depends on what information the target emphasizes, not simply how much image information it contains. Our theory gives a variational interpretation of standard alignment and, for fixed local predictors, a sum of token-wise information bounds conditioned on local appearance. To understand why purification benefits some encoders more than others, we derive an exact constant-readout test that measures how well the target can be matched without using the diffusion model's hidden state. LAP improves generation quality across five pretrained representations (MAE, AIMv2, CLIP, DINOv2, DINOv3), with the largest gain for MAE: on ImageNet-256 with SiT-B/2, it reduces FID from $53.1$ to $42.3$. Its gains persist with stronger alignment recipes and tokenizers. Computed before diffusion training, the constant-readout score predicts the benefit of purification (Spearman $\rho=0.94$ across 13 encoders).
papers.summary: Representation alignment improves and accelerates diffusion training by encouraging intermediate features to match a pretrained visual encoder, but standard alignment matches the pretrained representation without distinguishing which information is useful for generation. Local appearance purification (`LAP`) removes locally predictable content from the alignment target and aligns to the residual, modifying only the target and nothing in diffusion training or inference; controlled interventions within a fixed encoder show that effective alignment depends on what the target emphasizes rather than how much image information it contains. A variational interpretation of standard alignment and an exact constant-readout test, which measures how well a target can be matched without using the diffusion model's hidden state, explain why purification benefits some encoders more than others. `LAP` improves generation across `MAE`, `AIMv2`, `CLIP`, `DINOv2`, and `DINOv3` targets, with the largest gain for `MAE`, **reducing FID on `ImageNet-256` with `SiT-B/2` from 53.1 to 42.3**, and the constant-readout score computed before training predicts the benefit of purification with a Spearman correlation of 0.94 across 13 encoders.

papers.title: Reference-Guided Turn-Taking Style Transfer for Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models
papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take the floor, defining a conversational personality -- yet each set of weights encodes exactly one, which human speakers bracket rather than share. Existing controls mostly act from outside; none identifies the quantity that sets how much the model speaks. We identify it: a single late-layer residual-stream direction, the initiative vector, extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation. The same direction reads the decision, anticipating onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: scaled during generation, it moves speech ratio from 6-12% to 42-61% (no steering: 21-30%), consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora. A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker's turn-taking style to the model, and the transfer is reference-specific: swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93-98% of cases, whereas the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering. Turn-taking style is not frozen into the weights but a direction that can be read, shifted, and calibrated per person. Audio examples are available at https://elpsykongloo.github.io/initiative-vector/.
papers.summary: Full-duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take the floor, so each set of weights encodes a single conversational personality that existing controls can only adjust from outside. The authors identify a single late-layer residual-stream direction, the `initiative vector`, extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation, which both reads the turn-taking decision, anticipating speech onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: **scaled during generation, it moves the model's speech ratio from 6-12% to 42-61%, compared with 21-30% without steering**, consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora. A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker's turn-taking style to the model, and the transfer is reference-specific, since swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93-98% of cases while the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering.

papers.title: When Reality Outpaces Cognition: A New Scaling Principle for Reliable Intelligence
papers.abstract: This paper challenges the understanding capabilities of existing AI paradigms and emerging world models by asking a fundamental question: How quickly can reality change before an intelligent system can no longer reliably perceive, reason, and act? We formulate this as a theory- and model-agnostic challenge in which systems must infer reliable actions for increasingly distant future states across a growing observation--reality gap. We operationalize this challenge through the effective Speed of Coherent Cognition (\(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\)), defined as the highest tested Speed of Reality (\(S_R\)) through which a system continuously satisfies a predefined behavioural reliability criterion from baseline. As a proof of concept, reinforcement-learning agents are trained at the baseline \(S_R\) and evaluated, without retraining, as \(S_R\) is increased by up to \(50\times\) while computational resources remain fixed. We compare Transformer and gated-MLP baselines with \(Co^4\), an architecture inspired by cellular mechanisms implicated in conscious processing and awake thought. Across the tested scenarios, \(Co^4\) achieves substantially higher \(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\) than the baselines, motivating \(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\) as a new benchmark and the scaling of coherent cognition as a principle for reliable AI.
papers.summary: The authors ask how quickly reality can change before an intelligent system can no longer reliably perceive, reason, and act, framing it as a theory- and model-agnostic challenge in which systems must infer reliable actions for increasingly distant future states across a growing observation-reality gap. They define the effective Speed of Coherent Cognition as the highest tested Speed of Reality at which a system continuously satisfies a predefined behavioral reliability criterion from baseline. As a proof of concept, reinforcement learning agents trained at the baseline speed are evaluated without retraining as the Speed of Reality is raised by up to 50x with fixed compute, comparing Transformer and gated-MLP baselines against `Co^4`, an architecture inspired by cellular mechanisms implicated in conscious processing and awake thought; **`Co^4` achieves substantially higher effective Speed of Coherent Cognition than the baselines** across the tested scenarios.

papers.title: Semantic Alignment of EEG and Text: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Decoding Imagined Speech
papers.abstract: Imagined speech decoding from EEG offers a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces. Traditional closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not explicitly exploit relationships among linguistic intents, limiting output flexibility. We adapt a multimodal contrastive learning framework to imagined speech, aligning EEG trials with language representations in the embedding space of a frozen pretrained text encoder. An EEG encoder is trained with a composite objective combining semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination, encouraging semantic structure while preserving separability among 39 intent categories. We evaluate the approach on the Chisco imagined speech dataset across five subjects, reporting Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy (2v2). We also investigate maximum EEG-text cosine similarity (MaxCosine) as an intrinsic indicator of decoding reliability and probe semantic structure beyond category labels using five evaluation-time semantic axes and a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe (SGP) with previously unseen candidate sentences. The contrastive framework achieved decoding performance comparable to a task-optimized closed-set classifier while mapping EEG into a frozen language embedding space. MaxCosine identified subsets of held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy across subjects. Evaluation-time semantic axes showed mean agreement above the 50% chance reference across all five dimensions, and the SGP qualitatively illustrated direct comparison with unseen candidate sentences. Together, these findings suggest that EEG-language alignment can retain comparable fixed-intent decoding while supporting similarity-based retrieval, intrinsic reliability ranking, and evaluation of broader semantic structure.
papers.summary: Decoding imagined speech from electroencephalography (EEG) is a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces, but closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not exploit relationships among linguistic intents. The authors adapt multimodal contrastive learning to align EEG trials with sentence representations from a frozen pretrained text encoder, training an EEG encoder with a composite objective that combines semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination across 39 intent categories. On the `Chisco` imagined speech dataset across five subjects, **the contrastive model matches a task-optimized closed-set classifier** on Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy while mapping EEG into the language embedding space; maximum EEG-text cosine similarity identifies held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy, and five evaluation-time semantic axes plus a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe with unseen candidate sentences show semantic structure beyond the category labels.

papers.title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
papers.abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71.
