On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.
papers.summary: Early-exit networks let an input leave at a shallow layer, but calibrating a separate conformal prediction set at each exit stops guaranteeing coverage once the exit is chosen based on the data. The proposed fix builds a single terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrates one split-conformal quantile, and returns nested prefix sets that stay valid for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy, with no alpha/L correction, while the efficiency cost of the path maximum is bounded by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. **Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection reaches macro coverage of 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection**, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71, and on `CIFAR-100` with a 24-exit `ViT-L/16` the set size barely moves as exits grow from 4 to 24 while a `Bonferroni` correction degenerates to the full label space at 12 or more exits. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative result, with sets of 7,162 to 9,620 tokens.

papers.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.
papers.summary: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) hides adversarial instructions in external content that an agent reads mid-task, and existing evaluations mostly test isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrow agent setups. `INFUSE` is an end-to-end benchmark of 40 realistic long-horizon tasks and a taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios across five threat categories, with attacks injected through the interaction surfaces an agent actually touches during execution, such as shell output, code, dependencies, and remote services. Evaluating 19 models from the `GPT`, `Claude`, `Gemini`, `Llama`, `Gemma`, and `Qwen` families over 41,824 adversarial trajectories, **mean attack success is 19.6% under LLM-based judging and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model rates ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%**. Existing guard models give limited protection, and in the defense comparison prompt-level instructional hardening lowers mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3% at a model-dependent cost to utility.

papers.title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
papers.abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.
papers.summary: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state, such as whether an email needs a reply, how urgent it is, and who owns it, and a standard cross-encoder re-reads the input once per question. `Verdict-MQ` is an open 395M-parameter encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions in a single pass, using a structured attention mask that makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. **On the typed-decisions benchmark it matches the soft gold labels better than the released 421M `Laya` specialist on all five seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061)**, an advantage that survives temperature scaling, though against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on `MultiRC` and loses on `RACE` and `BoolQ`. A controlled comparison shows that giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9 to 3.5 points on `RACE` and `MultiRC` at 1.4 to 2.5 times the per-case latency, with nothing measurable on typed decisions.

papers.title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: In LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task. Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re-executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress. We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi-agent executions. Our key intuition is to turn execution-verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives. First, we collect over 24{,}000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models. From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs. It contains 3{,}953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue. Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS-agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run. The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections. Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post-hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models. Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.
papers.summary: In LLM-based multi-agent systems a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, and diagnosing finished runs or re-executing them to search for corrections yields no policy for intervening while a run is still in progress. Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (`ARIA`) turns execution-verified repairs into training supervision: the authors collect over 24,000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models, then distill **3,953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue**. A compact model trained on these pairs learns to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run, and the framework is designed to integrate with any multi-agent system that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. The trained model repairs failures in both post-hoc and runtime settings and generalizes to unseen frameworks and host models.

papers.title: ReasonUni: Reasoning-Augmented Reconstruction Advances Unified Multimodal Models
papers.abstract: Image-to-text (I2T) understanding and text-to-image (T2I) generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs). Reconstructive post-training couples these tasks, but existing reconstruction-based methods remain perception-centric and provide limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. We propose ReasonUni, a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework that extends this coupling beyond perception. Given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the corresponding target image conditioned on this understanding output. To jointly optimize both modules, we introduce TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in both understanding and generation, showing that reasoning-augmented reconstruction yields genuine mutual gains for UMMs.
papers.summary: Image-to-text understanding and text-to-image generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs), but existing reconstruction-based post-training stays perception-centric and gives little supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. `ReasonUni` extends reconstructive post-training with reasoning: given an original image and an editing instruction, the model first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the target image conditioned on that description. Both modules are optimized jointly with `TreeGRPO`, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and several candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards under one unified objective. **Experiments across multiple benchmarks show consistent gains in both understanding and generation**, supporting the claim that reasoning-augmented reconstruction produces mutual benefits for UMMs.

papers.title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
papers.abstract: The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility --- taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer --- and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference-time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a *rich representation*, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairs this.
papers.summary: Closed-world AI asks for specialized competence on a fixed criterion and can manufacture the independent and identically distributed data its theory assumes, whereas the open world asks for versatility on tasks the machine was not built for, from few examples and with data that arrives grouped rather than shuffled. Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, the authors derive three requirements: inference-time learning, a rich representation that retains more than iid generalization needs, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups, and the analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. Tests on language models up to 8B parameters ask qualitatively whether a model has each property rather than how much it wins, and **models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates while the rest degrade, with neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairing the gap**.

papers.title: APRiL: An Open-ended Benchmark for Chinese Social Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in social interactions, where appropriate responses require recognizing implicit cues, inferring mental states, identifying conflicts, and considering potential consequences. However, existing benchmarks often focus on specific social abilities, constrained task formats, or particular interaction settings, offering limited coverage of social awareness across diverse contexts. To address this gap, we introduce APRiL, an open-ended benchmark for Chinese social awareness with instance-specific rubrics. APRiL contains 2,196 Social Awareness Evaluation Instances across six categories and two complementary tasks: Social Scenario Analysis evaluates models' understanding of social cues, mental states, and conflict structures, while Socially Aware Response assesses whether they can translate this understanding into appropriate, natural responses. Experiments on 12 models from six families reveal a consistent understanding-to-response gap. Higher-quality scenario analyses improve responses, while weak analyses may reduce response quality. APRiL provides a systematic resource for advancing socially aware language models in Chinese contexts. Our data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/APRiL-05DE/.
papers.summary: Appropriate responses in social interaction require recognizing implicit cues, inferring mental states, identifying conflicts, and weighing consequences, yet existing benchmarks cover specific social abilities in constrained task formats or particular settings. `APRiL` is an open-ended benchmark for Chinese social awareness with 2,196 evaluation instances across six categories, each scored against instance-specific rubrics, split into a Social Scenario Analysis task that probes understanding of cues, mental states, and conflict structure and a Socially Aware Response task that checks whether that understanding becomes an appropriate, natural reply. **Experiments on 12 models from six families reveal a consistent understanding-to-response gap**, with higher-quality scenario analyses improving responses and weak analyses sometimes degrading them.

papers.title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
papers.abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.
papers.summary: Multimodal agents in open worlds still struggle to self-evolve: supervised fine-tuning imitates without actively organizing experience, and outcome-based reinforcement learning explores but underuses intermediate trajectory information. `EvolvingBrain` uses an adaptive skill system as the agent's brain, extracting Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from the agent's own trajectories and summarizing them into a Stratified Skill Architecture of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap skills that grows through repeated interaction with the environment. At execution time, long-horizon interactions are compressed into a Structured Abstractive Memory that drives a State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, so the agent applies knowledge matched to its current state. **On `VAB-Minecraft` and `DiscoveryWorld` the system improves open-world task success rates** and shows generalization across tasks.

papers.title: Sliced Wasserstein Sketches with Error Certificates
papers.abstract: Compact representations that support geometrically meaningful comparisons are valuable for learning from probability distributions. We study optimal, free-weight $M$-atom quantization of one-dimensional probability measures in quadratic Wasserstein distance and extend it to higher dimensions via slicing. Using $L$ shared projections yields a sketch with $O(LM)$ comparison time. Our main result is an exact decomposition of squared distance error into residual and partition-mismatch terms, yielding computable certificates for arbitrary centroid sketches. For optimal sketches, a finite $(2+\delta)$ moment for some $\delta>0$ guarantees $O(M^{-1})$ error in the finite-direction sliced distance, while equal-mass sketches can converge more slowly. Each slice preserves its mean, while storing residual energies enables covariance recovery from sufficiently many generic directions. Experiments on document, point-cloud, and flow-cytometry benchmarks show that optimal sketches substantially reduce storage while preserving the classification performance of uncompressed sliced distances. They also improve generalization from few labelled subjects and support end-to-end learning as compact pooling layers.
papers.summary: Compact representations that support geometrically meaningful comparisons are useful for learning from probability distributions. The authors study optimal free-weight M-atom quantization of one-dimensional measures under the quadratic Wasserstein distance and extend it to higher dimensions by slicing along L shared projections, giving a sketch with O(LM) comparison time. **The main result is an exact decomposition of squared distance error into residual and partition-mismatch terms, yielding computable error certificates for arbitrary centroid sketches**, and for optimal sketches a finite (2+δ) moment guarantees O(1/M) error in the finite-direction sliced distance where equal-mass sketches can converge more slowly. Each slice preserves its mean, stored residual energies allow covariance recovery from enough generic directions, and experiments on document, point-cloud, and flow-cytometry benchmarks show substantial storage reduction while preserving the classification performance of uncompressed sliced distances, better generalization from few labelled subjects, and use as compact pooling layers for end-to-end learning.

papers.title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
papers.abstract: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.
papers.summary: Music enjoyment is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds, and prior electroencephalography (EEG) work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. Enjoyment prediction is cast as regression on the public `MUSIN-G` dataset of 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners with song-level ratings, comparing six deep learning models under a participant-wise protocol with 15 listeners for training and validation and 5 held out for testing. **`DeepConvNet`, `CNN-LSTM`, and `GNN-CNN` reach the lowest mean absolute error of 0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale**, while the temporal convolutional network (`TCN`) has the highest Pearson correlation with ratings at r = 0.21. Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations averaged over held-out windows identify which segments of each two-second window most influence the `TCN` predictions, giving a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
papers.abstract: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.
papers.summary: Systems that detect health misinformation can expose sensitive user-submitted text, which motivates inference where queries stay encrypted while trained models and reference databases remain on organizational servers. The framework runs classification and semantic retrieval under `CKKS` homomorphic encryption, fusing `BioBERT` embeddings, PCA-reduced `MPNet` embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features for classification, and combining `MPNet` embeddings with `ISCC-SCT` semantic fingerprints through late fusion for retrieval. The hybrid classifier reaches 0.971 accuracy and 0.950 macro-F1 with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext inference, and the retrieval model achieves a 0.8691 Pearson correlation with human similarity scores on `STS-B`. **Packing multiple similarity scores with CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) operations cuts single-query retrieval latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222 seconds to 5.2 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB.**

papers.title: Optimal Explicit and Implicit Regularization Strengths in High-Dimensional Continual Linear Regression
papers.abstract: We study continual linear regression in a high-dimensional regime, where a learner observes a sequence of tasks and updates its parameters sequentially. In this setting, we derive an explicit closed-form expression for the generalization loss of a model trained with gradient descent for a fixed number of steps per task, which holds for arbitrary teachers. We prove that the optimal fixed step size decays nearly inversely with the number of tasks, specifically as $\ln T / T$, for a single teacher and, more generally, i.i.d. teachers. Under this scaling, we show that the resulting generalization loss is asymptotically equivalent to that achieved by optimally tuned L2 (isotropic) regularization. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to generalized ridge regression with diagonal regularization matrices, obtaining a closed-form characterization of the generalization loss and identifying necessary and sufficient conditions under which the optimal regularizer is isotropic. Finally, we identify a regime where the optimal step size remains finite even as the number of tasks tends to infinity, thus revealing a non-trivial tradeoff between task variability and implicit regularization, in contrast to the i.i.d. teacher scaling. Our theoretical predictions are corroborated by experiments on both linear models and neural networks, providing practical guidance for the design of continual learning systems.
papers.summary: Continual learning updates a model sequentially on a stream of tasks, and the authors analyze this in high-dimensional linear regression where gradient descent runs a fixed number of steps per task. They derive a closed-form generalization loss valid for arbitrary teachers and **prove that the optimal fixed step size decays as ln T / T in the number of tasks T for a single teacher or i.i.d. teachers, at which point the loss asymptotically matches optimally tuned isotropic L2 regularization**. Extending to generalized ridge regression with diagonal regularization matrices, they obtain a closed-form loss and necessary and sufficient conditions for the optimal regularizer to be isotropic, and they identify a regime where the optimal step size stays finite as the number of tasks grows, exposing a tradeoff between task variability and implicit regularization. Experiments on linear models and neural networks corroborate the predictions.

papers.title: When Reasoning Traces Conflict with Evidence: How Answer Configuration Shapes Evidence Following
papers.abstract: A reasoning trace retained at answer time plays two roles: it can raise accuracy, and it can compete with the current evidence when the two disagree. We disentangle these roles by crossing verified evidence versions with the traces generated from each and answering from the same traces and evidence under two configurations: continuation of the model's own thinking and a separate answer call. Across three model families (gpt-oss, Gemma4, Qwen3) on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, the separate call raises evidence-following over continuation by 29.9 to 60.6 points. On the same pairs, removing the trace lowers accuracy by similar amounts under both configurations. Yet continuation repeats the stale conclusion in most conflicts, and the separate call follows the current evidence far more often. Benefiting from a trace and deferring to it are therefore distinct properties. Further analyses show that the final line of a trace carries most of its value, gold evidence helps most before the trace is written, distractors weaken correction under a separate call, and renewed reasoning, unlike a verification instruction, follows the current evidence in most conflicts. Because trace deletion alone cannot reveal which source an answer follows, evaluations should report both properties together with the answer configuration.
papers.summary: A reasoning trace kept at answer time can raise accuracy but also compete with the evidence in context when the two disagree. The study crosses verified evidence versions with traces generated from each and answers from the same traces and evidence under two configurations, continuing the model's own thinking versus a separate answer call, across `gpt-oss`, `Gemma4`, and `Qwen3` on `HotpotQA` and `MuSiQue`. **The separate answer call raises evidence-following over continuation by 29.9 to 60.6 points**, even though removing the trace lowers accuracy by similar amounts under both configurations, so benefiting from a trace and deferring to it are distinct properties. Further analyses find that the final line of a trace carries most of its value, gold evidence helps most before the trace is written, distractors weaken correction under a separate call, and renewed reasoning follows the current evidence where a verification instruction does not, so evaluations should report both properties together with the answer configuration.

papers.title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower-resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross-lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five-language NF4-supervised directions successfully transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama-3.1-8B by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool-calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.
papers.summary: Language models can issue unsafe tool calls even while textually refusing, a vulnerability that text-only safety evaluations miss. `PRISM` is a framework for evaluating how activation interventions transfer across numerical precision, languages, and model scales, and it finds that lower-resource settings are a robust source of alignment signal: behavioral labels from an `NF4`-quantized copy give stable intervention estimates even from very few scenarios. **Five-language NF4-supervised steering directions transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in `Llama-3.1-8B` by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning**, and mapping paired benign activations lets the same interventions transfer to models up to 70B parameters. All code and artifacts are released along with an interactive explorer of recorded model responses.

papers.title: A Self-Improving Agent that Grows its Own DSL: Oracle-Free Operator Induction for Exact Question Answering
papers.abstract: A self-improving agent has to decide which new skills to keep, and in practice it keeps whatever earns a high reward, convinces a judge model, or compresses its library, even when the skill is wrong. That is fine until the answers have to be exactly right: over a table of transactions, a total is either right or wrong. We ask a harder question: can an agent grow what it can compute with no reward, no judge, and no answer key, and still be exactly right? A single frozen model runs two nested loops over a small, exact domain-specific language (DSL). The inner loop answers new questions only when two independently written expressions agree on every record. The outer loop discovers its own missing capability and authors an operator for it, admitted only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law, all without ground truth. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, and the outer loop self-extends on disjoint starting sets, inventing operators outside the starting closure; a no-induction control answers none of the new questions. The admission rule is empirically sound: it rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants under an independent reference, even one written by a different model family, where the admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals the field relies on admit most of them. Unmodified, the same mechanism self-extends on two further domains with unrelated schemas, business-ledger and clinical-encounter question answering, growing their answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold. The loop transfers across model families too: run with further proposers, the gate stays sound and independent families self-extend comparably, with only the induction yield tracking each proposer's DSL fluency.
papers.summary: Self-improving agents typically keep whatever new skill earns a high reward, convinces a judge model, or compresses their library, which fails when answers over a table of transactions must be exactly right. A single frozen model runs two nested loops over a small, exact domain-specific language (DSL): the inner loop answers a new question only when two independently written expressions agree on every record, and the outer loop discovers a missing capability and authors an operator for it, admitted only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law, with no reward, judge, or answer key. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, the outer loop invents operators outside the starting closure where a no-induction control answers none of the new questions, and **the admission rule rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants, whereas admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals admit most of them**. Unmodified, the mechanism also self-extends on business-ledger and clinical-encounter question answering, growing their answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold, and transfers across model families with only induction yield tracking each proposer's DSL fluency.

papers.title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy, and correcting the mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights adds high variance on long responses. Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (`GGPO`) instead minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt without importance weights; on policy its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is bounded below by the behavior policy's best-of-K reward minus finite-group, regularization, and finite-data terms. Reference refresh is empirically important: **fixed-reference GGPO scores 32.96 on a five-benchmark problem-weighted average versus 46.58 with the default refresh schedule**. On mathematical reasoning, GGPO outperforms `GRPO` and `AGRO` under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, and holds its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.

papers.title: O-RAN-Native Jamming Detection Under Network Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Radio-frequency jamming threatens cellular network operations in contested environments. The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture exposes per-User Equipment (UE) telemetry through the E2 interface, enabling Key Performance Indicator (KPI)-based jamming detection without proprietary hardware. However, operational deployment demands detection methods that generalize across heterogeneous networks. We propose a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) combining adaptive Median Absolute Deviation (MAD)-based baseline detection, count-based anomaly detection, and abrupt change detection through a weighted voting system. SEM operates in two modes: a cold-start mode requiring no labeled data for immediate deployment, and a supervised mode where parameters are refined offline via grid search as labeled data accumulates. We evaluate SEM against five machine learning (ML) classifiers and five deep learning (DL) sequence models using approximately 25 hours of testbed data comprising logs from eight heterogeneous 5G environments, employing both single-environment and multi-environment leave-one-out (LOO) validation. Our analysis indicates that under conditions not encountered during training (distribution shift), learning-based models tend to lose recall and miss jamming events, whereas SEM, even in cold-start mode, maintains detection capabilities at the cost of false alarms. Furthermore, SEM's parameter optimization can be mapped to O-RAN's Non-RT RIC as an rApp for continuous refinement, allowing operators to transition to learning-based alternatives once corpus coverage is sufficient.
papers.summary: Radio-frequency jamming threatens cellular networks in contested environments, and the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture exposes per-User Equipment telemetry through the E2 interface that enables Key Performance Indicator (KPI)-based detection without proprietary hardware. The proposed Statistical Ensemble Method (`SEM`) combines adaptive Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) baseline detection, count-based anomaly detection, and abrupt change detection through weighted voting, running either in a cold-start mode that needs no labels or a supervised mode whose parameters are refined by offline grid search as labels accumulate. Evaluated against five machine learning classifiers and five deep learning sequence models on roughly 25 hours of testbed logs from eight heterogeneous 5G environments with single-environment and leave-one-out validation, **learning-based models lose recall and miss jamming events under distribution shift, whereas SEM even in cold-start mode keeps detecting at the cost of false alarms**. The parameter optimization maps onto an rApp in O-RAN's Non-RT RIC, letting operators move to learning-based alternatives once corpus coverage is sufficient.

papers.title: Temporal Specification Guidance for Text-to-Video Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.
papers.summary: Text-to-video models often render the requested visual concepts but violate the intended ordering, timing, and persistence of events. Temporal Specification Guidance (`TSG`) expresses these requirements as formulas in Metric Temporal Logic and, at inference time without training, scores traces of visual-concept evidence from video-text attention with differentiable quantitative semantics, turning the score's gradients into attention biases that form a specification-guided denoising direction added to classifier-free guidance (`CFG`). The instantiation needs neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. **On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, it improves specification satisfaction over `CFG` by 9.5 to 20 percentage points across five models** with minimal memory overhead.

papers.title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception
papers.abstract: A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem - permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest-covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.
papers.summary: A mesh of interceptor drones defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object, an instance of N agents each covering a disc of radius r trying to cover a probability density. The authors derive closed forms, each validated by Monte Carlo, for the prediction uncertainty of a point extrapolated from a noisy linear track and for the coverage probability of a packed mesh, and show that **while agents stay at least 2r apart no mesh can exceed 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume**, a ceiling that belongs to the separation constraint and disappears when overlap is permitted above a crossover at p = 0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements, centroidal-Voronoi coverage control reaches only half its coverage at small budgets, the Gaussian assumption is fragile under aim-point bias, and the admissible commit-time window for a repositioning team can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised `PPO` averages 15% over three trainer seeds, which motivates the recommendation that such ceilings be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.

papers.title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
papers.abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .
papers.summary: Wolof is spoken by 23 million people, mostly in Senegal, yet open-weight language models support it weakly and API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty concerns for local deployment. The authors adapt open-weight models from 0.6B to 14B parameters to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging, and describe the pipeline and data behind them. **Across 63 public and in-house tasks the models perform well on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models competitive with substantially larger commercial systems.** The models are being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly released.

papers.title: Linear Independence of Polynomial Compositions with Bounded Input Degree
papers.abstract: We prove the weak composition-independence conjectures of Kohn, Marchetti, Massarenti and Mella. The proof uses deformations of rational curves and a single kernel of the linearized equation. Riemann-Roch gives a contradiction from tangent fields with controlled poles. By settling these conjectures, we prove that a neural network with a general polynomial activation function of sufficiently large degree is identifiable.
papers.summary: Compositions of polynomials arise in the function computed by a neural network with polynomial activations, and the weak composition-independence conjectures of Kohn, Marchetti, Massarenti and Mella concern when such compositions with bounded input degree remain linearly independent. The proof deforms rational curves and works with a single kernel of the linearized equation, with Riemann-Roch yielding a contradiction from tangent fields with controlled poles. Settling the conjectures implies that **a neural network with a general polynomial activation function of sufficiently large degree is identifiable**.

papers.title: Task-Phase-Conditioned Expert Routing Is Not a Reliable Proxy for Quantization Sensitivity in MoE FFN Tensors
papers.abstract: We investigate whether per-layer, per-task-phase (prompt/reasoning/response) expert-routing statistics in a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model can guide layer-wise mixed-precision quantization of routed-expert FFN tensors (down/gate and up). To attain layerwise routing statistics, we build a routing-capture and profiling pipeline for Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp, derive a composite sensitivity score from routing entropy/decisiveness, coefficient of variation (CV), Jaccard/phase-fragility, and top-1 expert strength, and use coordinate descent to tune a layer allocation that respects a fixed average bits-per-weight budget. Notably, the profiling pipeline is applicable to standard top-k MoE architectures. Across independent experimental conditions (about 4.0 bpw flat, about 2.7 bpw steep, and about 2.7 bpw random allocation as a control), reallocation fails to outperform the uniform baseline within each quality tier. In the flat regime, reallocation is statistically neutral (z about 0.9). For the steep tier, the random reallocation performs within 1 SE of the routing-guided reallocation at the same tier, indicating a structural loss at this quality rung caused by mandatory downgrades and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) tail injection. This aggressive-budget condition shows a decisive loss (z greater than 4 SE) replicated across three independent weight vectors. We argue that the deeper issue is that routing-behavior statistics are an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.
papers.summary: Layer-wise mixed-precision quantization of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models needs a signal for which layers tolerate fewer bits, and one candidate is how the router behaves in each layer during the prompt, reasoning, and response phases of a task. A routing-capture and profiling pipeline for `Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B` in `ik_llama.cpp` collects per-layer statistics such as routing entropy and decisiveness, coefficient of variation, Jaccard phase-fragility, and top-1 expert strength, folds them into a composite sensitivity score, and uses coordinate descent to allocate bits across routed-expert feed-forward tensors under a fixed average bits-per-weight budget. **Routing-guided reallocation fails to beat a uniform allocation in any quality tier**: at about 4.0 bits per weight it is statistically neutral, and at about 2.7 bits it loses decisively to the uniform baseline, a result replicated across three independent weight vectors, while a random reallocation control performs within one standard error of it. The authors attribute the steep-tier loss to mandatory downgrades and Kullback-Leibler divergence tail injection, and argue the deeper issue is that routing statistics are an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.

papers.title: CoTranslator: Reverse to Forward Chain-of-Thought Translator for Reasoning Distillation
papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation requires chain-of-thought (CoT) data with correct answers, but obtaining such data efficiently remains challenging. Forward CoT generation (FCG) followed by rejection sampling (RS) produces verified, question-only responses, yet may require many teacher calls for difficult problems. Reverse CoT generation (RCG) is cheaper because it conditions on the known answer, but access to this answer can lead to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with the student's answer-free inference setting. We propose CoTranslator, which learns to translate reverse CoT responses toward the distribution of verified forward responses. Trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, it supports large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models evaluated on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to $5.82$ percentage points. For two 4B students, it retains $95.0\%$ of rejection sampling's average accuracy while using $35.9\%$ of its estimated compute. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by $4.88$ and $4.31$ percentage points for 4B and 8B students, respectively. These results show that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable approach to reasoning distillation.
papers.summary: Distilling reasoning into small models requires chain-of-thought (CoT) traces with correct answers, but forward CoT generation (FCG) with rejection sampling (RS) can need many teacher calls on hard problems, while reverse CoT generation (RCG) conditioned on the known answer is cheap yet prone to post-hoc rationalization that does not match the student's answer-free inference setting. `CoTranslator` is trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses to rewrite reverse chains toward the distribution of verified forward ones, enabling large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models and six mathematics benchmarks it improves average accuracy over a semantic-suppression baseline by up to 5.82 percentage points, and **for two 4B students it retains 95.0% of rejection sampling's accuracy at 35.9% of the estimated compute**. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, raising average STEM accuracy by 4.88 and 4.31 points for 4B and 8B students.

papers.title: PEDBench: Can Speech Models Detect Phonetic Errors?
papers.abstract: Phonetic error detection (PED) aims to identify phoneme-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions and is essential for educational and clinical speech assessment and intervention. Despite recent advances in speech models for phoneme recognition, their ability to reliably detect fine-grained phonetic errors remains unclear because of a lack of high-quality evaluation data. To address this gap, we introduce PEDBench, the first PED benchmark spanning a continuum from natural to controlled speech. It comprises real-world recordings of spoken errors made by children (N=334), scripted error productions by human actors (N=1,188), and synthetic error productions generated using phone-conditioned text-to-speech (N=1,083). All phonetic annotations were transcribed and verified by two phonetically trained annotators. Our evaluation of 13 state-of-the-art speech models shows that they fail to reliably detect phonetic errors, even under controlled conditions with acted and synthetic speech, where acoustic variability is reduced. The models also exhibit low precision, frequently misclassifying correctly pronounced phonemes as errors. Our speech-language models, fine-tuned on synthetic data, outperform commercial and open-source baselines on word-level PED, although a sim-to-real domain gap remains. We plan to publicly release our code and recipes, along with our acted and synthetic datasets, to support the development of more accurate PED systems.
papers.summary: Phonetic error detection (PED) identifies phoneme-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions in speech, which matters for educational and clinical assessment, but a lack of high-quality evaluation data has left it unclear whether modern speech models can do it. `PEDBench` spans a continuum from natural to controlled speech, with 334 real recordings of children's errors, 1,188 scripted error productions by actors, and 1,083 synthetic productions from phone-conditioned text-to-speech, all transcribed and verified by two phonetically trained annotators. **Thirteen state-of-the-art speech models fail to reliably detect phonetic errors even on acted and synthetic speech**, and they show low precision by flagging correctly pronounced phonemes as errors. Speech-language models fine-tuned on the synthetic data beat commercial and open-source baselines on word-level detection, though a sim-to-real gap remains, and the code, recipes, and acted and synthetic datasets are slated for release.

papers.title: Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs
papers.abstract: Despite their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) struggle to adaptively gather information in experimental design tasks. We study how to amortize sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into an LLM by explicitly training the reasoning that guides action selection using information-gain rewards. Our approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM's own beliefs, allowing us to optimize expected information gain under a model of our choosing. We investigate the design choices for amortization, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines. On Twenty Questions, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, outperform inference- and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost, and generalize to unseen categories. We further demonstrate positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark. These results suggest that information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) carry extensive knowledge and reasoning ability yet gather information poorly when they must choose experiments adaptively. The approach amortizes sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into the model by training the reasoning that drives action selection with information-gain rewards, where the experimental generative model is specified independently of the LLM's own beliefs so expected information gain is optimized under a model of the designer's choosing. Design choices for amortization are compared, including generative-model construction, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and compute cost relative to training-time and inference-time BED baselines. On `Twenty Questions`, **the trained policies outperform both inference-time and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost** and generalize to unseen categories, and training transfers positively to `Medi-Q`, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark.

papers.title: Confidence-Calibrated Inference Expansion for Evaluator-Guided Test-Time Reasoning
papers.abstract: Evaluator-guided reasoning presents a local control problem at every step: trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference. We formulate this choice as a compute-aware three-action controller, scoring terminal actions by predicted answer success and expansion by a rollout-based continuation-success surrogate, with compute cost priced explicitly. A local action-gap analysis characterizes when score errors can change a decision, while an expected regret bound accounts for errors along the realized expansion path. Guided by this analysis, we learn and calibrate action-specific confidence estimates, with local uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. On held-out width expansion and revision tasks, the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively. Across four Qwen3-8B seeds, compute is lower than fitted Q in both settings, while utility differences are small and mixed. The results frame evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty, rather than a uniformly stronger reasoner.
papers.summary: At each step of evaluator-guided reasoning a system must decide whether to trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference, and the work casts this as a compute-aware three-action controller that scores terminal actions by predicted answer success and expansion by a rollout-based estimate of continuation success, with compute cost priced explicitly. A local action-gap analysis characterizes when scoring errors can flip a decision, and an expected-regret bound accounts for errors accumulated along the realized expansion path, motivating calibrated action-specific confidence estimates with uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. On held-out width-expansion and revision tasks the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies **while cutting normalized online compute by about 30% and 16% respectively**. Across four `Qwen3-8B` seeds it uses less compute than a fitted Q-function in both settings, with utility differences that are small and mixed.

papers.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.
papers.summary: Prior interpretability work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies shows that task-relevant variables can be read out linearly from activations, but readability only certifies that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, the authors build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts and find that **realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts**. Physical joint limits leave wrist orientation as an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, occupies two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, and steering along the geometry a concept realizes shows the findings are actionable.

papers.title: Analog RF Computing for Integrated Data and AI Flows Over Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: Many resource-constrained edge devices require artificial intelligence (AI) services but are not powerful enough to store or execute neural networks (NNs). Analog radio frequency (RF) computing addresses this limitation by letting a base station (BS) multicast a waveform encoding NN weights to different clients. Each client then multiplies the received weight-encoded waveform with its locally generated input-encoded waveform through a passive mixer in its RF frontend, thereby realizing the matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) needed for AI inference with an extremely low power and memory requirement. This can enable telecom operators to provide AI inference services to the edge devices connected to their networks. In practice, however, this multicast AI flow must share the spectrum, power, and spatial resources with other data flows. This paper considers a multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) downlink scenario and studies the resulting relative aggregate data rate reduction from integrating the multicast AI flow with the unicast data flows. We formulate a joint beamforming problem for the data and AI flows to maximize the aggregate data rate subject to computing accuracy, client energy, total power, and hardware-related constraints. We develop a weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE)-based algorithm to solve the problem. Numerical results based on 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) channels show that the relative aggregate data rate reduction from integrating an AI flow with data flows is below 5% in representative settings. This indicates that telecom operators can use analog RF computing to provide edge AI services while providing data communication services simultaneously.
papers.summary: Many edge devices need neural-network inference but cannot store or run the networks themselves. Analog radio frequency (RF) computing has a base station multicast a waveform encoding the network weights, and each client mixes it with a locally generated input-encoded waveform in a passive mixer to perform the matrix-vector multiplications of inference at very low power and memory cost, but this multicast AI flow must share spectrum, power, and spatial resources with ordinary unicast data flows. The authors formulate a joint beamforming problem for a multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) downlink that maximizes aggregate data rate subject to computing-accuracy, client-energy, total-power, and hardware constraints, and solve it with a weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) algorithm. On 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) channels, **the relative aggregate data rate reduction from adding the AI flow is below 5%** in representative settings, suggesting operators could offer edge AI inference alongside data service.

papers.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents
papers.abstract: Skill-policy co-evolution, in which an agent's policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training, is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents. Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank). After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address. In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental. The acceptance rule these methods share (cooperative acceptance) ties a policy's competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation; empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. We therefore introduce the CO-evolution Drift Audit (CODA), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5-13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52-93% of the delivered bank's gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution, from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve, and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited.
papers.summary: In skill-policy co-evolution, an agent's policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training, but evaluations score the policy only on the final bank it trained with, whereas in deployment skills get rewritten, added, or removed far more often than the policy is retrained. Theoretical and empirical analysis shows the resulting fragility is structural: the cooperative acceptance rule these methods share ties the policy's competence to the specific bank it co-evolved with, and sensitivity to skill drift grows as training proceeds. The CO-evolution Drift Audit (`CODA`) simulates skill drift and reports success under worst-case drift plus two new metrics, a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks, **worst-case success falls 5-13 points below each delivered pair's peak, erasing 52-93% of the skill bank's gain over a no-skill baseline**.

papers.title: Denoising Score Matching in Diffusion Models: The Effect of Rank Constraints on Generalization
papers.abstract: Architectural biases restrict the class of functions that a diffusion score network can represent, but their effect on generalization remains poorly understood. We study denoising score matching with score networks having a rank constrained non-linear term and a linear skip connection. Numerical experiments with trainable three-layer networks on data supported on an embedded sphere show that increasing rank lowers training error, but its effect on test error depends on sample size and data dimension. To explain this behavior, we analyze a random-feature score model under rank constraint with Gaussian data supported on a low-dimensional subspace. We characterize the optimal rank-constrained estimator through a truncated singular value decomposition and derive asymptotically precise limiting training and test errors when sample size $(n)$, feature width $(p)$, data dimension $(D)$, and rank $(r)$ scale proportionally with the ambient dimension $(d)$. The resulting spectral characterization distinguishes eigenmodes that improve the empirical fit from those that improve population accuracy. It also identifies the dimension of the orthogonal complement of the data subspace as a natural rank threshold. The theoretical learning curves qualitatively reproduce the observed rank-dependent overfitting, providing a tractable account of how bottlenecks or rank constraints can regularize score estimation and why their effectiveness depends on data dimension and sample size.
papers.summary: Architectural constraints limit which functions a diffusion score network can represent, but how they affect generalization is poorly understood. Experiments with trainable three-layer score networks that combine a rank-constrained nonlinear term with a linear skip connection, on data supported on an embedded sphere, show that higher rank lowers training error while its effect on test error depends on sample size and data dimension. To explain this, the authors analyze a rank-constrained random-feature score model with Gaussian data on a low-dimensional subspace, characterize the optimal estimator via a truncated singular value decomposition, and derive asymptotically exact training and test errors when sample size, feature width, data dimension, and rank all scale proportionally with the ambient dimension. **The spectral characterization separates eigenmodes that improve the empirical fit from those that improve population accuracy and identifies the dimension of the orthogonal complement of the data subspace as a natural rank threshold**, qualitatively reproducing the observed rank-dependent overfitting.

papers.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities
papers.abstract: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.
papers.summary: Mechanistic interpretability depends on knowing when supervised learning recovers the true latent variables behind the data, which the authors study through two data-generating processes distinguished by causal direction: a generative one where labels cause latents and a discriminative one where latents cause labels. When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space the optimal encoders are provably linear in the latents, while with too few dimensions identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. Additional constraints yield recovery of individual latents rather than linear mixtures: in the generative setting, non-negative activations plus energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, explaining grandmother-cell-like selectivity, and in the discriminative setting sparse latents with a measurement matrix satisfying the spark condition give the encoder compressed-sensing structure so that sparse dictionary learning recovers the latents, which the authors describe as **the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA)**. Predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.

papers.title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
papers.abstract: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention.
