While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention
papers.summary: Negation is basic to language understanding, yet how vision-language models (VLMs) process it is unclear. The study compares object-level model attention with human eye fixations on affirmative versus negated statements, in binary and multary settings and on both synthetic and realistic datasets. **Models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation**, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside attention: `PaliGemma2-3B` shifts object attention to the alternative object under negation, but head-wise ablations indicate this is a byproduct rather than a negation mechanism, and `LLaVA-1.5-7B` shows a spatial bias toward left-side objects. On downstream tasks every model performs worse on negated questions than on affirmative ones.

papers.title: Does Morphological Correctness Matter for Tokenization? A Scrambled Control Study in Tagalog
papers.abstract: Typology-aware tokenizers are motivated by the claim that segmentation which respects morpheme boundaries preserves information that frequency-driven segmentation destroys. Studies routinely establish that it helps while assuming the boundaries must be linguistically correct. We separate them. Tagalog marks voice with infixes (s-um-ulat 'wrote', s-in-ulat 'was written'), so the root is not contiguous and no sequence of BPE merges can recover it. We build MorphAustro-Tok, a tokenizer that emits the root as a contiguous unit followed by a positional infix token, and compare it against a corpus-matched BPE baseline and, at two of three fertility levels, against a scrambled-morpheme control that preserves morph count, invertibility and per-type consistency while randomising the pseudo-infix. Across 33 runs, MorphAustro-Tok improves Tagalog machine translation over matched BPE by 0.84, 1.49 and 3.40 mean sentence-level chrF++ points. Token count does not explain the gain, since it grows as segmentation coarsens, and neither does capacity: at the coarsest level the scrambled arm carries more parameters and scores lower. Scrambling the analysis moves the gain by less than between-seed dispersion at both controlled levels, so we detect no contribution from morphological correctness at this scale.
papers.summary: Typology-aware tokenizers rest on the claim that segmenting along morpheme boundaries preserves information that frequency-driven byte-pair encoding (BPE) destroys, but prior studies conflate the benefit of morpheme-like segmentation with the requirement that the boundaries be linguistically correct. Tagalog marks voice with infixes, so the root is non-contiguous and no sequence of BPE merges can recover it; `MorphAustro-Tok` emits the root as a contiguous unit followed by a positional infix token and is compared with a corpus-matched BPE baseline and, at two of three fertility levels, with a scrambled-morpheme control that keeps morph count, invertibility, and per-type consistency while randomizing the pseudo-infix. Across 33 runs the morphological tokenizer improves Tagalog machine translation over matched BPE by 0.84, 1.49, and 3.40 mean sentence-level chrF++ points, gains explained by neither token count nor parameter count. **Scrambling the morphological analysis moves the gain by less than between-seed dispersion**, so no contribution from morphological correctness is detected at this scale.

papers.title: Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model
papers.abstract:
We propose the Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model (TPGPMM), a Bayesian nonparametric framework for identifying persistent regimes and modelling nonstationary dependence in time series. The model combines an adaptive Pitman--Yor prior on contiguous segmentations with regime-specific Gaussian processes, without imposing Markovian within-regime dependence. Learning the Pitman--Yor discount parameter allows adaptation to homogeneous and heterogeneous regime lengths.
  A split--merge Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with exact Gibbs boundary updates jointly learns change points and model hyperparameters, quantifying uncertainty over segmentations and within-regime dynamics. With an RBF kernel and a fixed, conservative observation-noise level, TPGPMM favours sparse segmentations that distinguish persistent shifts from transient shocks. Simulations demonstrate recovery of the regime structure. Applications to the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) and the 10-year United States Treasury yield identify regimes aligned with major market and monetary-policy events.
  Variants that estimate observation noise improve predictive accuracy relative to the main specification, but can produce less sparse or less event-aligned segmentations. A variant with regime-specific means fits better than a fitted stationary Gaussian process and forecasts about as accurately. These results highlight a trade-off between interpretable regime identification and predictive accuracy.
papers.summary: Nonstationary time series often contain persistent regimes separated by change points, and modeling them means finding the segmentation and capturing within-regime dynamics at once. The Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model (`TPGPMM`) combines an adaptive Pitman-Yor prior over contiguous segmentations with regime-specific Gaussian processes, learning the Pitman-Yor discount to adapt to homogeneous or heterogeneous regime lengths, and fits change points and hyperparameters jointly with a split-merge Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with exact Gibbs boundary updates. With an RBF kernel and a fixed conservative noise level it favors sparse segmentations that separate persistent shifts from transient shocks, recovers regime structure in simulations, and **identifies regimes in the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) and the 10-year US Treasury yield that align with major market and monetary-policy events**. Variants that estimate observation noise forecast better but produce less sparse or less event-aligned segmentations, exposing a trade-off between interpretable regime identification and predictive accuracy.

papers.title: SNOAR: Self-training with Noise filtering, Observation adding, and Remixing for Speech Denoising Without Clean References
papers.abstract: Unsupervised speech denoising methods such as MixIT and noisy-target training can be trained directly on noisy recordings, avoiding the sim-to-real gap of synthetic training data, but remain well below supervised performance. Teacher--student self-training, as in RemixIT, narrows this gap by remixing a teacher's estimates into new mixtures that supervise a student; however, since the student is trained only toward the teacher's estimates, teacher errors, in particular over-suppressed speech, are never recovered and propagate as the teacher is updated from the student. We propose SNOAR, a self-training framework that corrects the teacher's estimates before use: the noise leaked into its speech estimate is removed by differential noise filtering (DNF), and part of the noisy observation is added back in to restore suppressed speech and attenuate artifacts. We show that the two corrections depend on each other, as without DNF the loop collapses to the identity mapping. Compared to RemixIT, SNOAR is more stable along training and outperforms it in signal-based, perceptual, and word error rate metrics, reaching 97\% of the SI-SDR improvement of a fully-supervised topline on WHAM!; on real CHiME-3 recordings, it improves every metric of three different teachers, while RemixIT degrades their perceptual quality.
papers.summary: Unsupervised speech denoisers such as `MixIT` and noisy-target training learn directly from noisy recordings but trail supervised systems, and teacher-student self-training like `RemixIT` only partly closes the gap because the student is trained toward the teacher's estimates, so teacher errors such as over-suppressed speech are never recovered and propagate when the teacher is updated from the student. `SNOAR` corrects the teacher's estimates before use: differential noise filtering (DNF) removes noise leaked into the speech estimate, and part of the noisy observation is added back to restore suppressed speech and attenuate artifacts. The two corrections are shown to depend on each other, since without DNF the loop collapses to an identity mapping. `SNOAR` trains more stably than `RemixIT` and beats it on signal-based, perceptual, and word-error-rate metrics, **reaching 97% of a fully supervised topline's SI-SDR improvement on `WHAM!`**, and on real `CHiME-3` recordings it improves every metric for three different teachers while `RemixIT` degrades their perceptual quality.

papers.title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification by the target model, but at ultra-long context a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup erodes and then reverses. Rather than training a long-context drafter or relying on a multi-token-prediction head, the authors observe that existing drafters are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the whole prefix, so they freeze released short-context drafters and run them far beyond their training length with two inference-time mechanisms: bounding the attention cache the drafter sees, which fixes its cost, and re-basing its rotary position indices into the trained range. No weights change, the single tunable saturates early, and one `vLLM` configuration spans 4k to two million tokens at a cost of at most 0.16x of speedup at short lengths, with a proof of when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged and a decomposition of acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. **Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens** across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora, provided the speculative cost per emitted token stays below the matched target-only cost.

papers.title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
papers.summary: Traffic simulation and autonomous planning need models of how vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists interact, and existing approaches learn this from large-scale human driving demonstrations. `SHRED` instead trains all three road-user types jointly through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, combining type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, with no demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. On the `Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge` (WOSAC) it controls all three agent types at once and **outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies**, while policies trained only on `nuPlan` map geometry keep comparable realism zero-shot on Waymo. For planning it beats all compared planners on the interaction-heavy `InterPlan` benchmark, and ablations show heterogeneity in self-play improves both realism and planning, with the largest gains in interaction-heavy scenarios.

papers.title: Anticipatory Commonsense with Moving Objects: An ASP-Based Framework for Predictive Reasoning with Interacting Trajectories
papers.abstract: We present a general declarative framework for anticipatory reasoning about interactive motion in complex dynamic environments. Our focus is on (explainable) anticipatory space-time mental model formation at a semantic level to heuristically guide low-level motion computation. Our method is hybrid, modular and elaboration tolerant integrating: 1) An ASP model characterising the dynamics of interactive motion trajectories; 2) Semantically-guided prediction for deriving `branching trajectory futures'; and 3) An energy-based {optimisation} model to evaluate, rank and filter anticipations. We evaluate with the Argoverse 2 benchmark, where each anticipated trajectory carries an explicit, inspectable event-level hypothesis, unlike end-to-end stochastic prediction.
papers.summary: Predicting how moving objects will interact in complex dynamic environments is usually handled by end-to-end stochastic trajectory prediction, which offers little explanation of why a future was anticipated. The framework is a hybrid, modular, and elaboration-tolerant pipeline for anticipatory reasoning: an Answer Set Programming (ASP) model characterizes the dynamics of interacting motion trajectories, semantically guided prediction derives branching trajectory futures, and an energy-based optimization model evaluates, ranks, and filters the anticipations, all at a semantic level meant to heuristically guide low-level motion computation. Evaluated on the `Argoverse 2` benchmark, **each anticipated trajectory carries an explicit, inspectable event-level hypothesis**, unlike end-to-end stochastic prediction.

papers.title: Clinically Interpretable Biological Age Estimation Using CatBoost and SHAP with Continuous and Categorical Features from NHANES
papers.abstract: Biological age (BA) captures inter-individual variation in physiological aging beyond chronological age (CA). Although machine-learning models have advanced BA estimation, many rely primarily on continuous laboratory biomarkers, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) dependence plots are typically interpreted visually. We developed a clinically interpretable machine-learning framework for BA estimation using heterogeneous clinical data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-March 2020, N = 24,983 adults aged >= 18). A CatBoost regression model incorporated 44 demographic, laboratory, physical examination, and lifestyle predictors to estimate CA, defining model-estimated age as BA. SHAP provided multi-level interpretability. Crucially, building on standard visual inspection, we implemented a prespecified automated procedure directly on SHAP dependence plots to quantify feature-value ranges associated with lowest and highest BA contributions, corresponding adjustment magnitudes, and zero-crossing thresholds. Model-estimated BA strongly correlated with CA in held-out testing data (Pearson r = 0.798, P < 0.001). Population-level SHAP identified blood urea nitrogen, serum glucose, vigorous recreational activity, red cell distribution width, and alanine aminotransferase among the leading predictors, with three categorical variables ranking among the top 25. Automated quantitative SHAP analysis mapped predictor-specific ranges, effect sizes, and inflection points, while waterfall plots enabled individual explanations. By extending qualitative visual interpretation to reproducible quantitative metrics across heterogeneous clinical data, this framework enhances transparency and provides a scalable methodological foundation for biological aging research and precision health.
papers.summary: Biological age (BA) captures how an individual's physiology diverges from chronological age (CA), but most machine-learning estimators rely on continuous laboratory biomarkers and interpret SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) dependence plots only by eye. Using 24,983 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (`NHANES` 2011 to March 2020), a `CatBoost` regression on 44 demographic, laboratory, physical-examination, and lifestyle predictors estimates CA, with the model's estimate taken as BA, and a prespecified automated procedure on SHAP dependence plots quantifies the feature-value ranges tied to the lowest and highest BA contributions, their adjustment magnitudes, and zero-crossing thresholds. Estimated BA correlates with CA on held-out data at **Pearson r = 0.798**, with blood urea nitrogen, serum glucose, vigorous recreational activity, red cell distribution width, and alanine aminotransferase among the leading predictors and three categorical variables in the top 25. Waterfall plots give individual-level explanations, and the quantitative SHAP metrics are offered as a reproducible alternative to visual interpretation.

papers.title: Machine-learning-based neutrino-event generation constrained by experimental measurements
papers.abstract: We present a generative surrogate for charged-current \(\nu_\mu\)-nucleus scattering that can be calibrated to measured differential cross sections without event-level experimental samples. Starting from a theoretical interaction model, we fine-tune the surrogate to a MicroBooNE measurement and show that this also improves the description of observables not used in the fit. The calibrated model can also be applied to measurements from different neutrino fluxes without retuning, while retaining event-level predictions of outgoing-muon kinematics. Our results show that experimental cross sections can directly constrain generative event models while preserving their applicability across different observables and beam configurations.
papers.summary: Neutrino event generators are built from theory, and calibrating them to experiment is hard because experiments publish differential cross sections rather than event-level samples. The authors build a generative surrogate for charged-current muon-neutrino scattering on nuclei, start it from a theoretical interaction model, and fine-tune it to a `MicroBooNE` cross-section measurement without any event-level experimental data. **Fitting to one measurement also improves the description of observables not used in the fit**, and the calibrated model applies to measurements under different neutrino fluxes without retuning while still producing event-level predictions of outgoing-muon kinematics.

papers.title: CogDrift-4D: Hierarchical Multimodal Modeling of Temporal Behavioral Decay for MCI Detection
papers.abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment remains a critical bottleneck in dementia care, demanding scalable tools capable of capturing subtle behavioral decay. To capture the subtle temporal changes of cognitive decline, we introduce a behavioral dataset collected across seven unscripted multimodal interactions over an 18-month horizon. This dataset formalizes continuous, multi-session interactions into a dense 4D tensor (Batch * Session * Time * Feature) that explicitly preserves concurrent local dynamics alongside long-term changes. To effectively process these complex behavioral patterns, we propose CogDrift-4D: a novel, hierarchical 4D Transformer framework. To capture the complex trajectory of cognitive decline, CogDrift-4D implements a dual-level behavioral fatigue and drift modeling architecture. At the intra-session level, the model computes localized least-squares regression slopes to quantify the acute ``fading'' of frame-level facial action units and acoustic energy. At the inter-session level, a recursive cross-attention feedback encoder acts as a cumulative fatigue accumulator, mapping the patient's continuous behavioral drift across successive sessions. To mitigate environmental noise and track failures across sessions, a localized Quality Gate dynamically filters low-integrity features before final fusion, also an early fusion that integrates semantic insights with raw physical dynamics. Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.
papers.summary: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) requires tools that can pick up subtle behavioral decline over time rather than from a single visit. The authors collect a dataset of seven unscripted multimodal interactions per participant spanning 18 months, arrange it as a dense four-dimensional tensor over batch, session, time, and feature, and train `CogDrift-4D`, a hierarchical Transformer that measures within-session fading of facial action units and acoustic energy through local regression slopes while a recursive cross-attention encoder accumulates drift across sessions. A quality gate filters low-integrity features before fusion with semantic signals, and on structured verbal interactions the model **detects MCI with 0.733 accuracy and 0.716 F1-score**, ahead of the compared baselines.

papers.title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning), the first pixel-level AL framework built around ViT representations. TEAL uses a frozen ViT backbone and performs diversity-based selection directly on its native token lattice, avoiding the artifacts introduced by interpolating token embeddings to dense pixel resolutions. Our framework applies a two-level MaxHerding strategy over multi-layer token descriptors to select representative candidates, followed by margin-based uncertainty refinement on a finer decoder grid. Across CamVid, Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Pascal Context, TEAL consistently outperforms previous baselines under extreme label scarcity, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +24.36 mIoU with a single labeled pixel (px) per image, and reaching up to 97% of fully supervised performance with just 10 px. To rigorously establish the source of the gains, we further show that the improvements persist when all baselines are equipped with the same DINOv3 backbone, demonstrating that coupling token-space selection with uncertainty refinement on the decoder grid makes ViT token geometry an effective foundation for extremely low-budget active segmentation.
papers.summary: Active learning (AL) for semantic segmentation with vision transformer (ViT) backbones has mostly queried patches or regions, which still demands heavy pixel labeling, and pushing it to a budget of about one labeled pixel per image means choosing informative locations while training a decoder from very sparse supervision. `TEAL` (Token-space Efficient Active Learning) keeps a frozen ViT, runs diversity-based selection directly on the native token lattice with a two-level `MaxHerding` procedure over multi-layer token descriptors, and then refines candidates with margin-based uncertainty on a finer decoder grid. Across `CamVid`, `Cityscapes`, `ADE20K`, and `Pascal Context` it **beats the strongest baseline by up to 24.36 mIoU with a single labeled pixel per image** and reaches up to 97% of fully supervised performance with ten pixels, and the gains persist when every baseline is given the same `DINOv3` backbone.

papers.title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined harmful tasks can induce emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. While prior work has identified shared misalignment-associated representations across independently fine-tuned models, it remains unclear whether these models rely on common computational components. We investigate this question using three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. Using direction-based activation tracing, we identify three attention-head locations shared among the five highest-ranked heads of all three organisms. Replacing each organism's five selected head contributions with Base contributions reduces free-generation EM from 38.9% to 22.9% for medical, 50.7% to 12.5% for finance, and 41.7% to 11.1% for sports, outperforming layer-matched random interventions without reducing judged coherence. Cross-organism activation transfer further shows that the shared heads exhibit partially interchangeable effects on fixed-response preference. These findings provide evidence that representational convergence in EM extends to shared, causally relevant attention-head components within a common model architecture.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a language model on one narrow harmful task can cause emergent misalignment (EM) in unrelated domains, and earlier work found shared misalignment representations across separately fine-tuned models without showing whether they rely on the same computational components. The authors train three LoRA fine-tunes of `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` on harmful medical, risky financial, and extreme-sports advice, then use direction-based activation tracing to rank attention heads and find three head locations that appear among the top five for all three models. **Replacing the five selected heads' contributions with those of the base model cuts free-generation misalignment from 38.9% to 22.9%, 50.7% to 12.5%, and 41.7% to 11.1%** across the three fine-tunes without lowering judged coherence, beating layer-matched random interventions, and transferring activations between models shows the shared heads have partially interchangeable effects on fixed-response preference.

papers.title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost
papers.abstract: Learned warm starts for the simplex method build starting bases using predictions of which variables will be basic at optimality. Prior work has shown that starting bases predicted by graph neural networks can sharply reduce iteration counts, but the time saved may fall well short of the iterations saved. On 25 classes of linear programs (LPs), we find that a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of the dual simplex's iterations but only a third of its time. Two effects explain the gap: the iterations removed by a good start tend to be cheap, and closeness to an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost. We prove that two starts with equal overlap with an optimal basis and equal pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor that grows with the square root of the number of rows. Empirically, across the starts of one LP, the pivot count explains 71% of the variance of log solve time, while the CPU instruction count explains 98.5%. We introduce CostStart, which uses supervised prediction for the basis and trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose, per LP, how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all. On unseen LPs of the training classes, including LPs four times the training size, CostStart roughly halves the solve time relative to the solver's default start and is 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data.
papers.summary: Learned warm starts for the simplex method predict which variables will be basic at the optimum, and graph neural network predictors cut iteration counts sharply, but on 25 classes of linear programs (LPs) the authors find a strong supervised predictor removes two thirds of dual simplex iterations yet only a third of the time. The gap arises because the iterations a good start skips tend to be cheap and because overlap with an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost; they prove two starts with equal overlap and pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor growing with the square root of the row count, and measure that pivot count explains 71% of the variance in log solve time versus 98.5% for CPU instruction count. `CostStart` keeps the supervised basis prediction but trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose per LP how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all, and **it roughly halves solve time relative to the solver's default start** while running 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data, including on LPs four times the training size.

papers.title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes
papers.abstract: Estimating causal effects on right-censored time-to-event outcomes is challenging under unmeasured confounding. Proximal causal inference addresses unmeasured confounding through proxy variables, but existing proximal survival methods rely largely on restrictive parametric bridge models. We introduce Proximal Survival Bridge learning (PSB), a flexible doubly robust proximal framework for censored outcomes. Building on existing proximal identification of treatment-specific survival curves, the framework yields outcome-bridge (OB), treatment-bridge (TB), and doubly robust (DR) estimators, with two flexible bridge learners: PSB-K, a kernel estimator with a low-rank time decomposition, and PSB-N, a neural estimator trained by a projected maximum-moment-restriction loss. Unlike existing flexible proximal learners for scalar outcomes, PSB directly handles censoring and survival-curve targets. On a standard SEM benchmark, a proximal semi-synthetic ACTG study, and the real-world Framingham study, PSB-K performs strongest on SEM and ACTG, whereas PSB-N is the most stable on Framingham. Additional results with modern causal survival baselines, weakened or invalid proxies, and heavier censoring assess robustness across challenging settings.
papers.summary: Estimating causal effects on right-censored time-to-event outcomes is hard when confounders are unmeasured, and existing proximal causal inference methods for survival data, which use proxy variables to stand in for hidden confounders, mostly rely on restrictive parametric bridge functions. Proximal Survival Bridge learning (`PSB`) builds on proximal identification of treatment-specific survival curves to derive outcome-bridge, treatment-bridge, and doubly robust estimators, paired with two flexible learners: `PSB-K`, a kernel estimator with a low-rank time decomposition, and `PSB-N`, a neural estimator trained with a projected maximum-moment-restriction loss. On a structural equation model benchmark, a semi-synthetic `ACTG` trial, and the real `Framingham` study, **the kernel variant performs best on the first two while the neural variant is most stable on `Framingham`**, and further experiments cover modern causal survival baselines, weak or invalid proxies, and heavier censoring.

papers.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent: A Nonlinear Time Series Perspective
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the statistical behavior of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with constant step size under the framework of iterated random functions. Compared to previous studies establishing the convergence of SGD in probability measure, e.g., Wasserstein distance, our approach directly provides the convergence in Euclidean distance by showing the Geometric Moment Contraction (GMC) of SGD. This new convergence can address the non-stationarity of SGD due to fixed initial points and can provide a more refined asymptotic analysis of SGD. Specifically, we prove quenched central limit theorem, invariance principle and $\alpha$-stable convergence for averaged SGD (ASGD) regardless of initialization. Furthermore, we provide a novel perspective to understand the impact of step sizes in SGD by studying its derivative with respect to the step size. The existence of stationary solutions for the derivative processes is shown, enabling the use of interpolation to recover the full-trajectory of SGD. Subsequently, we utilize multiple step sizes and show an enhanced Richardson-Romberg extrapolation with improved bias representation, which brings ASGD estimates closer to the global optimum. Finally, we propose a new online inference method and a bias-reduced variant for the extrapolated ASGD. Empirical confidence intervals are constructed and the coverage probabilities approach the nominal level as $n$ grows.
papers.summary: Constant-step-size Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is analyzed as an iterated random function, and instead of convergence in a probability metric such as Wasserstein distance the authors establish Geometric Moment Contraction (GMC), which gives convergence in Euclidean distance and handles the non-stationarity caused by a fixed starting point. From this they prove a quenched central limit theorem, an invariance principle, and alpha-stable convergence for averaged SGD (ASGD) regardless of initialization, and they study the derivative of the iterates with respect to the step size, showing stationary solutions exist so the full trajectory can be recovered by interpolation. Combining runs at multiple step sizes yields **an enhanced Richardson-Romberg extrapolation with an improved bias representation that moves ASGD estimates closer to the global optimum**, and a new online inference method with a bias-reduced variant produces confidence intervals whose coverage approaches the nominal level as the sample size grows.

papers.title: Wrong Votes, Right Gradients: Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with self-generated labels, such as majority vote over a model's own samples, often recovers most of the gain of training with verifiable rewards. This is puzzling from the usual prompt-level view, in which majority vote only returns a model's modal answer and cannot add information about correctness. We argue that the relevant unit is the batch-level update. Because parameters are shared, a prompt's own gradient accounts for less than 1\% of the change in that prompt's output at practical batch sizes, so a wrong label matters only to the extent that label errors share a direction across prompts. We decompose the majority-vote update into shrinkage and misdirection relative to the gold update, and show that misdirection vanishes with batch size whenever errors are incoherent across prompts, however often the labels are wrong. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, we find that majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, that the majority-vote update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and that its noise-corrected cosine with the gold update is 1 within error. Randomly flipping up to 30\% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact, while the same fraction flipped by a shared rule destroys it, and rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt, such as a learned reward model, fall measurably short. The equivalence holds at every checkpoint we examine but is local: gold-reward training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy. Error coherence, not error rate, determines when self-generated labels can stand in for verification.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning on self-generated labels such as the majority vote over a model's own samples often recovers most of the gain from verifiable rewards, which is puzzling at the prompt level, since the majority vote merely returns the modal answer and adds no information about correctness. The authors argue the right unit is the batch-level update: because parameters are shared, a prompt's own gradient accounts for under 1% of the change in its output at practical batch sizes, so wrong labels matter only when their errors point in a shared direction across prompts, and decomposing the majority-vote update into shrinkage and misdirection shows misdirection vanishes with batch size whenever errors are incoherent, however often the labels are wrong. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, they find majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null and **the majority-vote update's noise-corrected cosine with the gold update is 1 within error**; randomly flipping up to 30% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact while flipping the same fraction by a shared rule destroys it, and rewards with a consistent bias such as a learned reward model fall measurably short. The equivalence holds at every checkpoint examined but is local, since gold-reward training still finishes ahead on held-out majority accuracy.

papers.title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
papers.abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects
papers.summary: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) requires a robot to pick a grasp that suits the intended use, such as holding a knife by the handle to slice bread but leaving the handle clear when handing it over, and existing methods are limited to planar grasps, task-agnostic grasp generators, or finite hand-annotated task-grasp datasets. `TGrasp6D` is a zero-shot vision-language approach that, from a task description and a single RGB-D image, reasons about the relevant semantic affordance and object geometry to produce a task-informed grasp prior, then refines it through 6DoF pose optimization that avoids collisions while preserving task consistency. It reaches **a 94% success rate on the `TaskGrasp` dataset against 74% for the best baseline** and is deployed on a Franka Research 3 arm to show zero-shot generalization to real objects.

papers.title: Sign Betting for Misspecified Regression: Variance Adaptivity and Optimal Approximation
papers.abstract: We study bounded regression under model misspecification, evaluating a function $f$ by its $L_1(P_X)$ distance to the conditional mean $\eta(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$, rather than the standard $L_2(P_X)$. This $L_1$ metric is natural for downstream decision problems such as bandits and reinforcement learning. We analyze the min--max estimator of Baraud & Maillard (2025), which we call \emph{sign-betting regression}. Our main results show that sign-betting regression achieves high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequalities under misspecification. Under realizability, our bound adapts to the average conditional variance and recovers the variance-adaptive rate of Li et al. (2026). We further characterize the optimal universal approximation factor for proper learning by showing that sign betting achieves factor 3, while no proper learner can satisfy a distribution-free, high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequality with a universal approximation factor strictly below 3. We extend the upper-bound analysis beyond finite classes and complement the theory with experiments in synthetic and real-world model-selection tasks.
papers.summary: Bounded regression under model misspecification is evaluated by the L1 distance between a learned function and the conditional mean of the outcome rather than the usual L2 distance, a metric that matches downstream decision problems such as bandits and reinforcement learning. The authors analyze the min-max estimator of Baraud and Maillard, which they call sign-betting regression, and prove it achieves high-probability L1 oracle inequalities under misspecification, with a bound that under realizability adapts to the average conditional variance and recovers a known variance-adaptive rate. They further show **sign betting attains a universal approximation factor of 3 and that no proper learner can achieve a distribution-free high-probability L1 oracle inequality with a factor strictly below 3**, extend the upper bounds beyond finite classes, and test the method on synthetic and real model-selection tasks.

papers.title: Task-Centric Multimodal Learning for Cognitive Impairment Detection
papers.abstract: Dementia affects millions of older adults worldwide, yet early detection remains difficult outside clinical settings. Traditional models primarily rely on text or voice-based responses, capturing only a limited view of human cognition despite the inherently multimodal nature of human expression. This work proposes a contactless, multimodal screening framework that leverages video, audio, and text signals collected during structured voice-based interactions with Amazon Alexa. By incorporating these modalities, our approach captures a more holistic representation of human behavior encompassing speech patterns, vocal characteristics, facial expressions, and linguistic structure, which may enable more accurate detection of cognitive decline. Different participants completed three conversational tasks designed to probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall. We pursued three objectives: (1) evaluate which of the three Alexa tasks provides the most informative cognitive signals, (2) compare the effectiveness of unimodal models, and (3) assess the benefits of multimodal fusion models. Task-level analysis shows that the video model achieves its best performance on Command-Reading, with an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69), while the audio model performs best on Question-Answering, reaching an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73). In contrast, the multimodal model demonstrates consistently stable performance across tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.76 (AUC 0.75) on Command-Reading and 0.76 (AUC 0.73) on Question-Answering. These findings demonstrate that multimodal behavioral cues captured through naturalistic interactions can reliably distinguish MCI from healthy aging, highlighting the limitations of traditional diagnostic paradigms and supporting the shift toward multimodal, real-world cognitive assessment frameworks.
papers.summary: Dementia screening outside clinics usually leans on text or voice alone, even though cognition shows up across speech, voice, face, and language at once. The authors build a contactless screening pipeline from video, audio, and text captured during three structured conversational tasks on Amazon Alexa that probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall, then compare which task is most informative, how unimodal models fare, and whether multimodal fusion helps. The video model peaks on the command-reading task and the audio model on question answering, each at roughly 0.65 to 0.67 accuracy, while **the multimodal model reaches 0.76 accuracy on both tasks** with more stable performance, supporting multimodal cues from naturalistic interactions as a way to distinguish mild cognitive impairment from healthy aging.

papers.title: Replicable Dueling Bandits
papers.abstract: Dueling bandits choose each comparison based on earlier noisy outcomes, so two runs on the same preferences can compare different pairs. We study replicable dueling bandits, where two executions with shared internal randomness and independent comparison outcomes must select the same ordered pair in every round with probability at least $1-\rho$. Building on Beat-the-Mean, whose scores change as arms are eliminated and need not rank the best arm highest, we design the first such algorithms with sublinear regret. Under relaxed stochastic transitivity with parameter $\gamma\ge 1$ and the stochastic triangle inequality, we design an algorithm that achieves expected regret $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^8 K^4 H_{\mathrm{p}}/\rho^2)$, where $H_{\mathrm{p}}=\sum_{i=2}^{K}(P_{1i}-1/2)^{-1}$. Under strong stochastic transitivity, we design an algorithm based on simultaneous elimination that improves the dependence on $K$ and achieves $\widetilde{O}(K^2 H_{\mathrm{p}}/\rho^2)$ regret. For linear dueling bandits, we design an algorithm that achieves regret $\widetilde{O}(d^3\sqrt{T}/(c_\mu\rho))$. Experiments on synthetic and language-model preferences show replicability, with sublinear regret.
papers.summary: Dueling bandits adaptively choose which pair of arms to compare based on past noisy outcomes, so two runs on identical preferences can diverge in the pairs they query. The authors define replicable dueling bandits, in which two executions sharing internal randomness but drawing independent comparison outcomes must select the same ordered pair in every round with probability at least 1 minus rho, and build on `Beat-the-Mean`, whose scores shift as arms are eliminated and need not rank the best arm first, to give **the first replicable dueling bandit algorithms with sublinear regret**. Under relaxed stochastic transitivity and the stochastic triangle inequality the regret scales with the eighth power of the transitivity parameter and the fourth power of the number of arms, strong stochastic transitivity permits a simultaneous-elimination variant with only quadratic dependence on the arm count, and a linear dueling bandit algorithm attains regret growing as the square root of the horizon, with experiments on synthetic and language-model preference data confirming replicability.

papers.title: Recursive Offline Distillation via Entropy Gain Sampling and Answer Mixing
papers.abstract: Distillation of reasoning chains from Large Language Models (LLMs) into their smaller siblings is a standard training approach. Frequently, researchers do not have full access to a teacher model and its internal representations, which limits the resulting performance. We propose a recursive offline distillation method combining two components: entropy-based sampling for selective distillation and answer mixing. Specifically, for three open models (3-4B), at each epoch, we sample reasoning chains weighted by entropy difference with an auxiliary medium model (70-72B) and, next, supplement thinking traces with single-token ground truth answers. Our approach consistently outperforms naive distillation with comparable data budgets ($57.15 \pm 1.01$ vs 51.61 on average) and offers a much steeper learning curve. Additionally, we present a comparative analysis of methods to generate and normalize distillation traces.
papers.summary: Distilling reasoning chains from large language models (LLMs) into smaller ones usually assumes access to the teacher's internal representations, which researchers often lack. The proposed recursive offline distillation trains three open 3-4B parameter models over multiple epochs, at each epoch sampling reasoning chains weighted by their entropy difference against an auxiliary 70-72B model and appending single-token ground-truth answers to the thinking traces. With comparable data budgets it **scores 57.15 on average versus 51.61 for naive distillation** and shows a much steeper learning curve, and the authors also compare methods for generating and normalizing distillation traces.

papers.title: Forecast lead time and the timing of crew deployment for weather-driven power outages using AI weather models
papers.abstract: Utilities request mutual aid crews to restore power after severe storms, and requesting early secures more crews but relies on less accurate forecasts. We examined how forecast lead time affects the value of outage predictions for crew deployment, using operational forecasts from two AI weather models, GraphCast and FourCastNet, to predict outage occurrence for counties across the contiguous United States 24 to 120 hours ahead. Forecasts were evaluated by the share of outage burden captured by the counties where crews would be staged. Captured burden declined with lead time: the loss between three and five days was significant in all analyses, whereas the loss within three days was significant only for outages that had not yet started. Early deployment with all requested crews outperformed late deployment with fewer, and we report the availability ratio at which the two break even. Antecedent land surface predictors computed at forecast valid time include weather from the forecast period, which inflates their skill by 42 to 53% and reverses their apparent advantage over forecast meteorology at long lead times. Computed correctly, they improved occurrence skill by 17.5% at 24 hours but did not significantly change captured burden, a gap that attribution analysis linked to their static component. Prediction intervals covered only 0.476 of tropical cyclone events against a nominal 0.90. Calibration by hazard class corrected most of this shortfall at an 11% cost in interval width, as a diagnostic only, because hazard class is known only after the event.
papers.summary: Utilities that request mutual aid crews early after a storm secure more crews but must rely on less accurate forecasts, so the authors ask how forecast lead time changes the value of outage predictions for crew staging. Using operational forecasts from the AI weather models `GraphCast` and `FourCastNet` to predict county-level outage occurrence across the contiguous United States 24 to 120 hours ahead, they score forecasts by the share of outage burden captured in the counties where crews would be placed. **Captured burden fell significantly between three and five days of lead time**, early deployment with all requested crews beat late deployment with fewer, and the authors report the crew availability ratio at which the two break even. They also show that antecedent land-surface predictors computed at forecast valid time leak weather from the forecast period and inflate skill by 42 to 53%, and that prediction intervals covered only 0.476 of tropical cyclone events against a nominal 0.90 until calibrated by hazard class, a correction usable only as a diagnostic since hazard class is known after the event.

papers.title: A Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM): Proportionate Access and Capability Limits for Comprehensive Frontier AI Safety
papers.abstract: Most debate about releasing capable AI systems treats the choice as binary: keep the model behind an API, or publish the weights. That framing runs together two separate decisions. One is how capable a system may become. The other is who may obtain a given capability, and on what terms. This paper is about the second decision. We propose a Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM) that sorts access by purpose, safety, and capability instead of by release artifact. Tier 1, AI for Learning, is broadly accessible and deliberately capability-bounded. Tier 2, AI for Exploration, serves research and development under registration, identity, and usage controls that tighten as capability rises. Tier 3, Full-Scale Frontier AI, is available only through structured, recorded, and accountable access. The principle behind the tiers is that accessibility should be proportional to capability, safety, and risk. We show why publishing frontier-class weights forfeits every safety lever a developer has after release, and, using evidence that safety fine-tuning can be stripped from open weights for a few hundred dollars, why an evaluation of the base model says little about its derivatives. We give criteria for assigning a system to a tier along capability, autonomy, domain-consequence, and usage/safety axes, and combine MAIAM with the SAFE AI Operating Point into a two-part framework: a Capability Boundary that fixes the safety limits not to be crossed, and an Accessibility Boundary that fixes who may obtain a capability below that limit. Capability limits alone do not make AI safe; a tiered access regime administered by regulating bodies is also needed.
papers.summary: Debate over releasing capable AI systems is usually framed as a binary between API access and publishing weights, which the authors argue conflates how capable a system may become with who may obtain a given capability and on what terms. Their Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (`MAIAM`) sorts access by purpose, safety, and capability: a broadly accessible but capability-bounded learning tier, a research and development tier under registration, identity, and usage controls that tighten with capability, and a frontier tier reachable only through structured, recorded, and accountable access. They argue that releasing frontier-class weights forfeits every post-release safety lever, citing evidence that **safety fine-tuning can be stripped from open weights for a few hundred dollars**, give criteria for tier assignment along capability, autonomy, domain-consequence, and usage axes, and pair the tiers with a SAFE AI Operating Point to form a two-part framework of a Capability Boundary and an Accessibility Boundary.

papers.title: Defining and Generating Compositional Structure
papers.abstract: Compositional structure is pervasive in nature and across scales: atoms combine into molecules, molecules into cells, and cells into organisms, while further compositional hierarchies appear within each level. More broadly, compositionality, the reuse and recombination of parts into novel structures, is a fundamental source of interesting complexity in both natural and artificial systems. Yet despite its importance, and despite our apparent ease in recognizing it, mathematical accounts capturing what we intuitively mean by compositional structure remain limited. Here, we fill this gap by formalizing a simple idea: compositional structure emerges when parts, considered together, reveal shared structure that is not captured when those parts are modeled separately. We express this idea using algorithmic information theory, the mathematics of information and compression, which provides a natural way to identify structure in arbitrary data without specifying in advance what that structure must look like. Applied across scales, our definition informs where and how compositional structure emerges within an object. Using tractable approximations, we then invert the framework to generate compositional objects: we specify the desired form of their compositional structure without prescribing their particular content, and optimize directly over strings and images. The resulting objects exhibit readily recognizable hierarchical reuse and part-whole organization, suggesting that the definition captures compositional structure rather than merely complexity, regularity, or shared information. Finally, we discuss implications for machine learning, including a new perspective on depth in neural architectures and principles for constructing compositional data curricula capable of supporting open-ended learning.
papers.summary: Compositional structure, the reuse and recombination of parts into new wholes, is easy to recognize but has lacked a mathematical definition that matches intuition. The authors formalize it with algorithmic information theory: compositional structure is present when parts modeled together reveal shared structure that modeling them separately misses, a criterion that applies across scales and locates where within an object such structure arises. Using tractable approximations they invert the definition to generate objects, specifying the desired form of compositional structure without fixing content and optimizing directly over strings and images, and **the resulting objects show recognizable hierarchical reuse and part-whole organization**, which they take as evidence the definition captures compositionality rather than mere complexity, regularity, or shared information. They close with implications for depth in neural architectures and for compositional data curricula aimed at open-ended learning.

papers.title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
papers.abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
papers.summary: Robust adaptive control keeps robots safe while they reduce uncertainty in unfamiliar settings, but traditional methods are conservative because they ignore the parameter learning guaranteed to happen during the plan and scale poorly to high-dimensional systems. `A-SLS` is a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework built on system-level synthesis that forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations among process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to build tight reachable sets that credit future information gain, with a GPU-accelerated solver for real-time use. Across nonlinear robotic systems it shrinks reachable-tube conservativeness while staying real-time, **scales to whole-body control of a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs**, and runs on a physical Crazyflie drone that learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online while stabilizing.

papers.title: SkillNEO: Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization of Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Agent skills turn procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts, allowing LLM agents to accumulate and refine expertise through experience. Building on this, skill evolution iteratively improves skills using execution feedback. However, improvement may require several interdependent edits, so low-reward versions can still be worth developing. Requiring immediate reward gains can discard useful partial repairs before their benefits emerge. Non-elitist evolution allows new versions to receive further edits despite scoring below earlier ones. For agent skills, this calls for evidence of what to preserve and repair next. We introduce SkillNEO (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills), which separately selects a version to use and versions to keep improving. Comparing how related versions perform the same task reveals working steps to preserve and remaining failures to fix. It can also revisit and revise earlier versions using later evidence. Across 86 SkillsBench tasks in eight domains, including software engineering and office work, SkillNEO raises GPT-5.4 Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%, within GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna's original-skill range. Mini executes tasks, proposes revisions, and edits skills; final evaluation uses the same task instances. Gains span all eight domains. The same skills improve stronger models without further editing. On the 41 tasks with modified skills, reuse improves Luna by 10.5 percentage points and places GPT-5.5 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Execution records show these skills can benefit stronger models even when Mini still fails some task requirements. Search histories also show lower-scoring versions leading to skills ultimately selected for use. Together, these findings show that skill evolution can turn a weaker model's partial progress into reusable procedural knowledge for improving more capable agents.
papers.summary: Agent skills package procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts that LLM agents can refine from execution feedback, but improvements often need several interdependent edits, so evolution schemes that demand an immediate reward gain can discard useful partial repairs. `SkillNEO` (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills) separates the choice of which skill version to deploy from which versions to keep editing, compares how related versions perform the same task to identify working steps to preserve and failures to fix, and can revisit earlier versions in light of later evidence. Across 86 `SkillsBench` tasks in eight domains including software engineering and office work, with `GPT-5.4 Mini` executing tasks, proposing revisions, and editing skills, **the method raises Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%**, and the evolved skills transfer without further editing, lifting `GPT-5.6 Luna` by 10.5 percentage points on the 41 tasks with modified skills and placing `GPT-5.5` 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Search histories show lower-scoring versions leading to the skills ultimately selected, though final evaluation uses the same task instances as the search.

papers.title: Prune the Summary, Not the History: Source-Judged Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction: when the interaction history outgrows the context window, a compressor replaces it with a natural-language summary. We show that these summaries contain more than a record of what happened. Compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, so each summary mixes facts established by the environment with reasoning written by the compressor, and the agent cannot tell the two apart afterwards. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, 83% of failed runs trace back to an action that carries out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports. We propose Source-Judged Compaction (SJC), a training-free post-processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it has a source in the environment outputs or the previous summary, and removes the entries that do not. It changes neither the agent nor the compressor and adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction. The judge is Jev, a non-generative decision model that answers the source question with a calibrated probability instead of text. On AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1%-8.9% without increasing the agent's token usage.
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents compact their history into a natural-language summary once it outgrows the context window, and because compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, each summary mixes facts established by the environment with the compressor's own reasoning in a way the agent cannot later separate. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, **83% of failed runs trace back to an action carrying out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports**. Source-Judged Compaction (`SJC`) is a training-free post-processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it is grounded in environment outputs or the prior summary and drops the ungrounded ones, using `Jev`, a non-generative decision model that returns a calibrated probability rather than text, at the cost of one inexpensive judge call per compaction and without changing the agent or the compressor. On `AppWorld` and `OfficeBench` with two agent models it improves cross-run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1% to 8.9% without raising the agent's token usage.

papers.title: RAC: A Relational Agent Contract for Constraint-Governed Engineering Tasks
papers.abstract: Engineering agents must produce artifacts that satisfy exact, coupled constraints. Existing solutions often require agents to make semantic decisions and also derive consequences such as precise geometry or timing from those decisions, leading to failures in constraint-governed engineering tasks. In this paper, we introduce RAC, a harness-agnostic contract for the action and feedback layer of engineering agents. It specifies authoritative observations, semantic actions, tool-based realization, independent verification, and repair evidence. The agent decides which relations an artifact should satisfy; specialized tools derive their concrete consequences. On PCB placement, routing, and repair tasks, RAC achieves the highest clean-pass rate for all nine evaluated models, averaging 90.9%, compared with 74.0% for the strongest baseline, requirements-only delegation. In job-shop scheduling, direct relational actions achieve 96.3% quality pass versus 59.6% for code-mediated delivery with access to the same scheduling backend. Our evaluations on 141 embedded-code tasks across four microcontroller identify the action contract as a source of agent capability: preserving semantic control while delegating mechanically derivable outputs improves the reliability of constrained artifacts.
papers.summary: Engineering agents must produce artifacts that satisfy exact, coupled constraints, and current setups fail when the agent both makes semantic decisions and derives their consequences, such as precise geometry or timing. `RAC` is a harness-agnostic contract for the action and feedback layer that specifies authoritative observations, semantic actions, tool-based realization, independent verification, and repair evidence, so the agent decides which relations an artifact should satisfy while specialized tools compute the concrete consequences. On PCB placement, routing, and repair tasks **it achieves the highest clean-pass rate for all nine evaluated models, averaging 90.9% against 74.0% for requirements-only delegation**, in job-shop scheduling direct relational actions reach a 96.3% quality pass versus 59.6% for code-mediated delivery to the same backend, and evaluations on 141 embedded-code tasks across four microcontrollers point to the action contract itself as a source of agent capability.

papers.title: MAI-Gym: An Open All-in-One Platform for GUI Agent Evaluation and RL Training across Mobile and Computer Environments
papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has driven rapid progress in mathematics, coding, and tool use, but scaling this success to GUI agents remains challenging due to the high cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks. We introduce MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments. Through a shared rollout pipeline, MAI-Gym ensures consistent agent behavior across evaluation and training, supports ten established benchmarks, and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances. Beyond scalable infrastructure, MAI-Gym enables automated synthesis of diverse GUI applications and challenging tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. Using MAI-Gym, we train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open GUI agents under 10B parameters: 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified. Importantly, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a phys- ical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. We release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint to support repro- ducible research and further advances in scalable GUI agent training.
papers.summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has advanced math, coding, and tool use, but GUI agents lag because interactive environments are costly and realistic training tasks are scarce. `MAI-Gym` is an open platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments through a shared rollout pipeline, supports ten established benchmarks, scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances, and automatically synthesizes resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. The resulting `MAI-Gym-9B`, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, **scores 78.4% on `MobileWorld` and 76.2% on `OSWorld-Verified`, the best among open GUI agents under 10B parameters**, and RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to the real app, raising task success on a physical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. The authors release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint.
papers.highlight_summary:
Online RL for GUI agents is held back by two costs: every attempt needs its own phone, desktop or browser in a known starting state, and realistic tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. `MAI-Gym` addresses both with one open platform. Evaluation, data collection and online RL share a single agent harness and rollout path across mobile, computer and web, and the platform automatically builds mocked apps, multi-app task environments and code-based verifiers that are tested by running them.

- Because the harness is shared, the agent that gets evaluated is the agent that was trained; the platform supports ten benchmarks, has run **20,000 parallel environments**, and groups screenshot history into overlapping windows, which doubles KV prefix-cache hits (42.5% to **85.9%**) and cuts training update time by **62.6%**, at the cost of about 19% lower rollout throughput.
- The synthesis pipeline uses coding agents to build 7 resettable clones of real apps and 42 entirely new apps, fills multiple apps with linked files and records generated from a persona and scenario, and writes golden-solution code and verifier code in separate calls, accepting a verifier only if it scores 0, 1 and 0 on the initial, completed and reset states.
- `MAI-Gym-9B` starts from `Qwen3.5-9B`, gets supervised warm-up training, then one joint mobile-and-computer `GRPO` run on 5,000 synthesized tasks (512 GPUs, about 96 hours); it reaches **78.4% on `MobileWorld`** and **76.2% on `OSWorld-Verified`**, ahead of `UI-Venus-2-9B` (75.2 / 70.8) and better on both than any merge of separately trained mobile and computer models (best merges: 76.4 / 74.8).
- Skills learned in synthetic apps carry over: RL only in a clone of the 12306 train-ticketing app raises success in the real app on a physical phone from **28.8% to 48.1%**, and RL with reward alone on the new apps raises held-out success from 25.8% to 45.2%.
- Most of the gain comes from the supervised warm-up rather than RL, results on computer environments never seen in training stay low (**3.7%** binary on `OSWorld 2.0`, 15.2% on `MyPCBench`), the gap between clone and real-app success widens from 7.7 to 25.0 points after RL, and repeated rounds of the diagnose-then-synthesize loop are not evaluated.

papers.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
papers.abstract: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.
papers.summary: Action-only monitors that watch what a coding agent does can miss harmful behavior, and red-teaming them has usually required access to the developer's infrastructure. `Screwtape` has an LLM attacker edit real agent transcripts so the agent appears to cause a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent, while an LLM verifier rejects edits that are inconsistent with the original transcript or fall below a severity bar, and the attacker revises until the target monitor stops flagging the edit. Applied to 94 `Claude Code` and `Codex` transcripts from Redwood Research staff, 252 runs produced 35 verifier-passing attacks that evaded the authors' own monitors, and **six human-confirmed attacks also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer**. The authors expect more attacks when the pipeline runs inside developer infrastructure with attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor.

papers.title: Ranked Right, Sized Wrong: Ensemble Spread Fails Silently at Streamflow Extremes
papers.abstract: Deep learning models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory networks, are increasingly used for operational streamflow forecasting, with ensemble spread providing a signal of predictive uncertainty. As climate change increases the frequency of hydroclimatic extremes, these models will increasingly operate under flow conditions that are rare in their historical records. We therefore evaluate whether ensemble spread remains informative under increasing flows, examining both its magnitude relative to error and its ability to rank errors. Prediction error is approximately $2\times$ the corrected spread at ordinary flows and up to $4\times$ at the highest flows, with the discrepancy increasing with flow (log-log slope $1.30$, 95% CI: $[1.20,1.41]$). Under-dispersion is strongest in observed extreme flows beyond the training record, reaching an $18\times$ discrepancy. This is pervasive and not explainable by conditional mean bias. Area Under the Sparsification Error, a standard distribution-free metric of uncertainty ranking, describing how well a model knows when it is uncertain, indicates near-oracle ranking for ensemble spread ($0.071$), yet ordering by predicted discharge alone nearly matches it. Informative uncertainty ranking can coexist with severe under-dispersion. In deployment, error ranking cannot be verified, yet the spread is available, and it is relied on as the uncertainty signal under increasingly extreme conditions, while systematically understating risk, most severely for the extreme events that matter most.
papers.summary: Long Short-Term Memory ensembles used for operational streamflow forecasting rely on ensemble spread as their uncertainty signal, yet climate change increasingly pushes them into flow conditions rare in their training records.
