Fine-tuned checkpoints reach decision agreement of 0.77-0.92 and withdrawal recall of 0.46-0.86 versus 0.45-0.63 and at most 0.06 for the baselines, but rule-level diagnostics qualify this: **the original-curriculum checkpoint wrongly withdraws 26 of 34 actions that still have alternative support, while enriched checkpoints withdraw 0-1**, and all SFT checkpoints narrow prohibited combinations, absent from both curricula, less often than the 7B and 8B baselines. With one training run per arm and several confounds limiting causal attribution, the authors frame the contribution as a method for detecting rule-specific regressions that aggregate accuracy conceals, not as evidence that fine-tuning alone ensures agent safety.

papers.title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
papers.abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.
papers.summary: Review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says, and while a frontier large language model (LLM) checks them well it must read the whole paper for every check, whereas cheap decision models that score whether a statement holds in a text fall short on comments that bundle several implicit assertions. The authors introduce `ReviewFact`, a benchmark labeling such factual errors under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences while measuring cost and latency alongside accuracy. `PremiseCheck` combines the two approaches: an LLM rewrites each comment into explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against it. **When comments are checked individually, `PremiseCheck` matches `GPT-5.5` accuracy across all three fields at about half its cost**, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of the cost and less than half the latency.

papers.title: SHIP: Structured and Hierarchical Insight with Privacy
papers.abstract: Extracting insights from textual data while protecting user privacy is increasingly important. Existing methods produce private insights in diverse forms for different analytical purposes, making their utility difficult to assess and compare. In this work, we formulate differentially private (DP) insights as reusable representations for answering analytical queries, providing a common basis for utility assessment. Answering these queries, however, requires fine-grained details and cross-attribute statistics that existing representations may omit. To capture this information, we introduce Structured and Hierarchical Insight with Privacy (SHIP), which automatically maps queries to attributes, builds a hierarchical hybrid taxonomy, and releases a DP synthetic table for further analysis. We also develop an evaluation protocol based primarily on QA performance and structured fidelity. Our experiments demonstrate SHIP's strong performance on both measures relative to existing private insight baselines, while identifying queries that remain challenging for structured representations.
papers.summary: Existing methods for extracting insights from text under differential privacy (DP) produce outputs in diverse forms suited to different analytical purposes, making their utility hard to assess or compare. The authors reframe DP insights as reusable representations for answering analytical queries, which demands fine-grained details and cross-attribute statistics that existing representations often omit. Structured and Hierarchical Insight with Privacy (`SHIP`) automatically maps queries to attributes, builds a hierarchical hybrid taxonomy, and releases a DP synthetic table for further analysis, evaluated under a new protocol based primarily on question-answering performance and structured fidelity. **`SHIP` outperforms existing private insight baselines on both measures**, while the evaluation also identifies query types that remain challenging for structured representations.

papers.title: SALTO: Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators for Nonlinear Event Inference
papers.abstract: Learned dynamical models can accurately predict trajectories while producing unreliable sensitivities when differentiated or transposed, limiting their use in inverse problems and scientific decision-making. Classical adjoints provide exact local derivatives, but a single adjoint cannot represent the nonlinear response of a system to a family of finite-amplitude perturbations. We introduce SALTO (Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators), a Koopman-based framework for inferring finite-amplitude sources. In the lifted space, the nonlinear dynamics are approximated by a linear propagator, and its transpose carries each sensor backward in a single solve. The result is a reusable lifted adjoint that predicts the measurement produced by any candidate localized event with one encoder pass and an inner product. To give the model the simulator's exact local behavior, SALTO imposes three structural constraints: it anchors the physical-state dynamics to the simulator's linearized propagator, centers the learned observables so that they vanish to second order at the reference state, and uses a block-triangular lifted propagator. These constraints guarantee that the model reduces to the simulator's tangent dynamics and classical adjoint as the amplitude vanishes, while the learned observables carry only the finite-amplitude correction. On three nonlinear PDE systems, SALTO predicts the measurements of finite-amplitude sources to within 2-8% where the classical adjoint is in error by 41-165%, recovers source position and intensity from sparse sensors nearly as accurately as inversion through the solver, and samples the joint posterior of two interacting sources, matching the solver's posterior on reaction-diffusion at a twentieth of its cost. One trained model serves new sensor layouts and measurement times with a single backward solve.
papers.summary: Learned dynamical models predict trajectories well but give unreliable sensitivities when differentiated or transposed, while classical adjoints are exact only locally and cannot represent the nonlinear response to a family of finite-amplitude perturbations. `SALTO` (Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators) approximates the nonlinear dynamics with a linear propagator in a Koopman lifted space whose transpose carries each sensor backward in a single solve, yielding a reusable lifted adjoint that predicts the measurement from any candidate localized event with one encoder pass and an inner product. Three structural constraints, anchoring the physical-state dynamics to the simulator's linearized propagator, centering learned observables to vanish to second order at the reference state, and a block-triangular lifted propagator, guarantee the model reduces to the simulator's tangent dynamics and classical adjoint as amplitude vanishes. On three nonlinear partial differential equation systems, **`SALTO` predicts finite-amplitude source measurements to within 2-8% where the classical adjoint errs by 41-165%**, recovers source position and intensity from sparse sensors nearly as accurately as inversion through the solver, and samples the joint posterior of two interacting sources on reaction-diffusion at a twentieth of the solver's cost.

papers.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.
papers.summary: As a measurable stand-in for recursive self-improvement, the authors ask whether frontier agents can post-train a small raw base model into a capable generalist using only public data. `Athanor` is an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research on real GPUs that gives agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code, with services supplying frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of, all inside a sandbox with no external teacher models. **In a 104-hour campaign, four `Claude Opus 5.5` agents on eight-GPU nodes and given no research advice lifted `Qwen3-4B-Base` from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on the held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507`.** The campaign record shows the agents got there by recombining known methods and each other's models: supervised fine-tuning on public reasoning data, reinforcement learning with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation.

papers.title: Bellman-Consistent Trajectory RL for LLM Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.abstract: To address sparse terminal rewards in LLM arithmetic reasoning, we propose a Bellman-consistent trajectory RL method. Our framework introduces Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) to transform sparse rewards into dense token-level signals. We integrate a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) group strategy to reduce gradient variance of Bellman residuals and use hindsight goal relabeling to accelerate intermediate learning. Evaluated on the Countdown task, our method alleviates optimization bottlenecks and stabilizes gradient variance significantly better than GRPO. The TBRM-RLOO framework boosts Pass@1 to 0.55--0.64 and achieves a state-of-the-art Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0--84.0\%, outperforming the SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines. Our approach demonstrates exceptional single-sample efficiency and successfully circumvents standard performance plateaus via test-time scaling.
papers.summary: Sparse terminal rewards make reinforcement learning (RL) for arithmetic reasoning in large language models (LLMs) hard to optimize. Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (`TBRM`) transforms the sparse reward into dense token-level signals, a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (`RLOO`) group strategy reduces the gradient variance of the Bellman residuals, and hindsight goal relabeling accelerates learning of intermediate steps. On the `Countdown` task the method stabilizes gradient variance better than `GRPO`, lifts Pass@1 to 0.55-0.64, and **reaches Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0-84.0%, ahead of the SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines**, continuing to improve under test-time scaling where the baselines plateau.

papers.title: Score Mismatch and Set-Constrained Sampling in Zero-Shot Conditional Discrete Diffusion
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models have become a powerful framework for modeling complex discrete distributions across a range of applications. While theoretical convergence guarantees depend on consistency between the target and training distributions, such a case rarely holds in practice, making score mismatch a central challenge in discrete diffusion sampling. This is particularly relevant to zero-shot conditional generation, where a model trained on the unconditional distribution is directly reused at inference time to sample from a conditional target distribution. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical analysis for score-mismatched discrete diffusion models and derive a general KL divergence upper bound that clearly identifies the additional bias caused by such a mismatch. Our analysis covers partial-observation constraints, including text infilling, sentence completion, and more general coordinatewise set constraints. Specifically, we analyze the classical Conditional SEDD sampler and show that it can incur a bias term that scales with the dimension, vocabulary size, and compatibility. Based on this analysis, we propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) sampler for coordinatewise set constraints. We show that the assignment probabilities can be expressed exactly by the unconditional scores with absorbing rate. Finally, numerical and real-data experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RHC sampler.
papers.summary: Convergence guarantees for discrete diffusion models assume the sampling target matches the training distribution, which fails in zero-shot conditional generation, where a model trained on the unconditional distribution is reused at inference to sample from a conditional target. The authors give the first theoretical analysis of score-mismatched discrete diffusion, deriving a general KL divergence upper bound that isolates the additional bias from the mismatch and covering partial-observation constraints such as text infilling, sentence completion, and general coordinatewise set constraints. **They show the classical Conditional `SEDD` sampler can incur a bias term that scales with dimension, vocabulary size, and compatibility**, and propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (`RHC`) sampler for coordinatewise set constraints whose assignment probabilities are expressed exactly by the unconditional scores with absorbing rate. Numerical and real-data experiments support the effectiveness of `RHC`.

papers.title: Multimodal AI Detection for Math-Heavy Scientific Text
papers.abstract: As large language models become increasingly capable of generating, and assisting with, scientific writing, there is a need for greater transparency and disclosure around the use of AI in research. Consequently, a veritable subfield of research and a number of commercial services aim to flag AI-generated content automatically. However, existing detectors which rely only on text extracted from PDFs fail to benefit from the rich visual information contained in the formatting of math-heavy scientific content. To study this, we select human-written proof and prose passages from pre-2022 arXiv LaTeX sources and re-generate them using 15 modern LLMs within the context of the same paper. This leaves us with coupled human and AI outputs in three different representations: the LaTeX source, a rendered image of the PDF, and the text extracted from the PDF. We find that the accuracy of the state-of-the-art Pangram 4 drops significantly as the mathematical content in a passage increases, especially when evaluated on text as opposed to LaTeX. However, this is not an inherent limitation of detecting AI-generated math: finetuning Qwen-3.5-27B based detectors on this domain recovers the gap, with LaTeX inputs performing significantly better than text since they preserve more formatting information. Since LaTeX sources are rarely available in practice, we also train SnapJudge: an image-based detector operating on screenshots of both prose and proofs from papers. At 0.1% false positive rate, SnapJudge achieves a detection rate of 92% on proofs and 93% on prose generated by frontier models, substantially outperforming both Pangram 4 and our text-based detector. We release our data, models and code at https://nlplab.cs.duke.edu/snapjudge.
papers.summary: Detectors of AI-generated writing that operate only on text extracted from PDFs discard the formatting cues that are especially informative in math-heavy scientific content. The authors take human-written proof and prose passages from pre-2022 arXiv LaTeX sources, regenerate them with 15 modern LLMs in the context of the same paper, and represent each coupled pair as LaTeX source, a rendered PDF image, and extracted text. The state-of-the-art `Pangram 4` loses accuracy as mathematical content increases, especially on extracted text, but fine-tuning `Qwen-3.5-27B` based detectors on this domain recovers the gap, with LaTeX inputs beating text because they preserve more formatting. Since LaTeX sources are rarely available in practice, they also train `SnapJudge`, an image-based detector operating on screenshots, which **at a 0.1% false positive rate detects 92% of frontier-model-generated proofs and 93% of prose**, substantially outperforming both `Pangram 4` and the text-based detector.

papers.title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
papers.abstract: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up
papers.summary: Agents that pause for human approval before payments, deletions or outside emails treat that approval as a second factor, but the authors argue it only counts as one if a compromised agent cannot manufacture it and it names exactly what is being approved. They define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation and label spoofing, run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (`AP2`), Microsoft's action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (`MCP`) elicitation, and audit ten agent runtimes, finding no third-party verifiable approval record anywhere and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. Their reference defense `ASU` (Agent Step-Up) renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the user's phone sign its digest and executes only the stored call, with `Tamarin` proving binding, single-use and non-repudiation properties across 53 lemmas. Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 `AgentDojo` attack pairs it stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and **the trusted card raises the attack catch rate of 15 language models acting as approvers from 0.30 to 0.98**, although flooding still succeeds roughly half the time and a second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation.

papers.title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics
papers.abstract: Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt. We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents. Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all. Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it. Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss. Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes. Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.
papers.summary: Most benchmarks of AI agents on bioinformatics pose one short task with a single prompt, while real computational biologists run agents through long, multi-turn analysis sessions. `OmicsBench` links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph across 97 tasks and 662 subtasks, each posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on wrong answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, **mean scores range from 0.43 to 0.57 without feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it**, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier ones. An unsupervised pipeline that describes, embeds and clusters failed attempts surfaces failure modes such as agents substituting their own statistical filters for the specified ones or writing whole answers from memory.

papers.title: Adaptive Randomized Neural Networks for PDEs: Structure-Aware Feature Redistribution and Residual-Driven Block Enrichment
papers.abstract: Randomized neural networks retain an output-linear least-squares solve, but globally sampled random features may fail to capture the spatial and scale structure of PDE solutions. We propose SFRBE--RaNN, a two-stage adaptive trial-space construction. SFR redistributes a fixed feature budget according to regional indicator masses and adapts regional weight scales through low-dimensional residual-based optimization. RBE constructs nonredundant enrichments by screening multiple activation families, removing represented response directions, and selecting the smallest admissible prefix. For solution-dependent operators, candidates are screened with a frozen operator and accepted only after nonlinear residual verification. For fixed linear problems, we establish an exact discrete residual-reduction identity and a conditional solution-error estimate. Building on this identity, we combine safeguarded SFR with RBE capture factors to derive a finite-horizon error bound involving baseline best approximation and empirical consistency, together with a conditional random-search success-probability bound. Numerical experiments on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear space--time problems demonstrate the method's effectiveness.
papers.summary: Randomized neural networks solve partial differential equations with a cheap output-linear least-squares step, but globally sampled random features can miss the spatial and scale structure of the solution. `SFRBE-RaNN` builds the trial space in two adaptive stages: structure-aware feature redistribution (SFR) reallocates a fixed feature budget according to regional indicator masses and tunes regional weight scales through low-dimensional residual-based optimization, while residual-driven block enrichment (RBE) screens several activation families, removes already-represented response directions and keeps the smallest admissible prefix, with candidates for solution-dependent operators accepted only after nonlinear residual verification. For fixed linear problems the authors prove an exact discrete residual-reduction identity and a conditional solution-error estimate, extend these to **a finite-horizon error bound combining baseline best approximation with empirical consistency** plus a random-search success-probability bound, and report experiments on localized, multiscale and nonlinear space-time problems.

papers.title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
papers.abstract: Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study STOCHLOB, a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump-L\'evy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped $\alpha$-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor $h_t(r)$ is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny.
papers.summary: Score-based diffusion training normally corrupts data with Gaussian noise from a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE), a poor match for limit order book (LOB) order flow that is heavy-tailed, bursty and jump-like. `StochLOB` keeps the deployed trend predictor deterministic but swaps the training-time corruption law for two non-Gaussian alternatives, jump-Lévy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture and clipped alpha-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture, with no reverse-time sampling needed at inference. The resulting score target weights each residual by the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals count according to the latent noise scale most likely to have produced them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data the variants **stay competitive on clean BTC and altcoin horizons while improving several tail-window stress diagnostics**, and an exploratory A-share transfer study checks whether the output probabilities remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints.

papers.title: Sci$\Pi$vot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$\Pi$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$\Pi$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little supervision, but autonomous research also demands scientific judgment, which is hard to evaluate because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. `SciΠvot` is a 248-case benchmark drawn from six months of records in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six fields and repeatedly corrected their research judgments, and in each case an agent must choose between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative using only the project record available before the correction. With the project record at medium reasoning effort, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan and **four of five frontier models score below chance**, with the best model reaching 63.5 percent accuracy against 73.4 percent for fresh human researchers. At medium effort every model does worse with the project record than without it, and asking models to reconsider does not consistently help.

papers.title: A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models
papers.abstract: An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate. The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible. Most ensemble methods assign each expert a fixed reputation, often learned from labels. We ask whether it can instead be inferred from the pattern of agreement and disagreement among the experts. We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone. We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts' answer distributions. What changes is not how the jury votes, but how it learns whom to trust. On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.
papers.summary: Ensembles of language models usually give each member a fixed reputation, often fitted on labelled data, before combining their answers. The authors instead treat the members as witnesses of unknown reliability: each question has a latent true answer, each model reports it with some unknown accuracy, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (`EM`) purely from the pattern of agreement and disagreement in unlabelled answers, which yields a log-odds weighted linear score over the models' answer distributions. On a 1,560-question benchmark with nine models of up to 3B parameters, **the label-free jury matches the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, with no statistically significant gain from supervision**, and beats both the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative.

papers.title: SIEVE: Overcoming Topological Obstruction in Equivariant Self-Supervised Learning
papers.abstract: We identify a theoretical incompatibility between 3D point cloud masked autoencoding and SE(3)-equivariant networks. We prove that standard masking triggers a topological collapse, effectively forcing the model to hallucinate orientation without a reference frame. To resolve this, we introduce SIEVE (Scalar Invariant Extraction Via Equivariance), an SE(3)-equivariant self-supervised framework that compresses point cloud geometry into invariant scalar embeddings. At its core is the spherical projection mask, which preserves global pose while obfuscating local semantics, sidestepping the obstruction by construction. Experiments confirm that SIEVE circumvents the predicted collapse where constant and noise masks fail. On downstream point cloud tasks, the resulting embeddings improve over coordinate-based baselines and hand-crafted geometric descriptors, with the largest gains on generalization to unseen shape categories.
papers.summary: The authors prove that combining masked autoencoding of 3D point clouds with SE(3)-equivariant networks triggers a topological collapse: standard masking removes any reference frame, so the model is forced to hallucinate orientation. `SIEVE` (Scalar Invariant Extraction Via Equivariance) is an SE(3)-equivariant self-supervised framework that compresses point cloud geometry into invariant scalar embeddings, using a spherical projection mask that preserves global pose while hiding local semantics and so sidesteps the obstruction by construction. Experiments confirm that `SIEVE` escapes the predicted collapse where constant and noise masks fail, and its embeddings **outperform coordinate-based baselines and hand-crafted geometric descriptors on downstream tasks, with the largest gains on unseen shape categories**.

papers.title: Probe-and-Resume: When and How to Evaluate Agent Execution
papers.abstract: Test-time search can improve agent performance by exploring alternative actions and using a critic to select promising branches. We study this approach in terminal-based computer-use environments, which expose only a partial view of a large underlying state, and find that the Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) configuration we evaluate does not significantly improve task success. We identify two sources of poor critic performance: the agent's observations omit environment state needed for evaluation, and intermediate states offer limited evidence of whether a trajectory will succeed. At intermediate states, critics rank continuations only modestly better than chance, and environment access improves this little. We study when to invoke a critic and what access to give it to evaluate a node. Our findings motivate a policy that invokes the critic only at nodes the agent believes are final, rather than during partial progress. Further, the policy gives the critic read, write, and execute access to a fork of the computer's current and initial state, allowing it to probe and perform potentially destructive actions to surface any hidden state the trajectory omits. We call the resulting design Probe-and-Resume: when the agent claims to be done, the critic probes a fork of its state, and a rejected agent resumes where it stopped. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, this raises success by 8.4 percentage points over MCTS with conventional critics, and approaches the success rate of the Codex CLI agent with the same underlying model at less than half its cost.
papers.summary: Test-time search guided by a critic should help computer-use agents, yet in terminal environments, which expose only a partial view of a large hidden state, the Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) configuration the authors evaluate does not significantly improve task success. They trace this to critics lacking the environment state needed to judge a trajectory and to intermediate states carrying little evidence about eventual success: at mid-trajectory nodes critics rank continuations only modestly better than chance, and giving them environment access barely helps. `Probe-and-Resume` therefore invokes the critic only when the agent claims to be done, gives it read, write and execute access to a fork of the current and initial machine state so it can run potentially destructive probes that expose hidden state, and lets a rejected agent resume where it stopped. On `Terminal-Bench 2.1` this **raises success by 8.4 percentage points over MCTS with conventional critics** and approaches the success rate of the `Codex CLI` agent with the same underlying model at less than half its cost.

papers.title: MemComposer: Learning to Assemble Memories for LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters. However, semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness: downstream performance depends on how memories are selected and presented to the agent. We propose MemComposer, a memory composer that jointly examines the current query and retrieved candidates to decide which experiences to include, how many to select, and how to order them. We train the composer using Experience Policy Optimization (ExPO), a GRPO-based framework that evaluates assembled memory contexts through complete agent interactions and uses task-success feedback to optimize the assembly policy. Across three $\tau^2$-bench domains with two frozen executors, MemComposer outperforms the strongest baseline for each executor while reducing average memory-token usage by 16.9% and 4.9%, respectively. The learned policy also transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and benefits from memories generated by stronger models without further training. These results demonstrate the value of learning query-specific memory assembly using downstream task feedback.
papers.summary: Agent memory lets large language model (LLM) agents reuse past experience without updating their weights, but retrieving by semantic similarity alone does not guarantee that the retrieved memories actually help. `MemComposer` jointly inspects the current query and the retrieved candidates to decide which experiences to include, how many to select and how to order them, and is trained with Experience Policy Optimization (`ExPO`), a GRPO-based scheme that scores each assembled memory context by running the complete agent interaction and uses task success as the reward. Across three `τ²-bench` domains with two frozen executors it **beats the strongest baseline for each executor while cutting average memory-token usage by 16.9 and 4.9 percent**, and the learned policy transfers to unseen domains, executors and memory banks and benefits from memories generated by stronger models without further training.

papers.title: ToolBottleneckBench: Measuring Tool-Agent Performance under Controlled Pressures and Fixed Harness Budgets
papers.abstract: The success score of a tool agent reflects both its model and the budgets of the harness that runs it. We present ToolBottleneckBench, a benchmark that measures tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while one pressure varies: the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow, or the encoding of returned records. An exact grader records the first unmet obligation of each failed episode and the harness limit, if any, that ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, the visible menu is the only one of the three pressures that act on the model with a large penalty, and this penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap. Raising the cap sixteenfold removes most of the penalty in the truncation-heavy configurations. Most failures end at a harness limit, and the failure record identifies the assigned pressure no more reliably than a count of tool calls. The repairs that help change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls, and only two repairs, neither improving model behavior, beat every configuration switch. We recommend reporting pressure effects with the harness budgets under which they were measured. We release the benchmark at https://github.com/zichuanxu/tool-bottleneck-bench.
papers.summary: A tool agent's success score mixes the model's ability with the budgets of the harness running it, and `ToolBottleneckBench` is designed to separate the two. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while a single pressure varies, namely the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow or the encoding of returned records, and an exact grader logs the first unmet obligation of each failed episode together with whichever harness limit ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, **the visible tool menu is the only pressure with a large penalty, and that penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap**, with a sixteenfold larger cap removing most of it in truncation-heavy setups. Most failures end at a harness limit, the failure record identifies the applied pressure no better than a plain count of tool calls, and the only repairs that beat every configuration switch change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls rather than model behaviour, so the authors recommend reporting pressure effects together with the harness budgets under which they were measured.

papers.title: Planning Commitment of LLM under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: LLM-based planning agents commit to plans of different lengths before interacting with a partially observable environment. Some aggressively commit to a long plan based on assumptions about unobserved states, while others conservatively plan only over what they have observed. Both behaviors emerge implicitly in pre-trained models, whether the LLM outputs a plan directly or generates a PDDL formulation for a classical solver. Aggressive commitment risks costly failures, while conservative commitment risks excessive LLM calls. This choice pits safety against efficiency, a trade-off that has been neither characterized systematically nor made controllable. We investigate aggressive and conservative LLM planners and formalizers on two partially observable domains, where priors are provided as either explicit statistics or common-sense knowledge. Across three LLMs, both strategies reach similar accuracy. Conservative methods achieve fewer failed attempts (safety) at the cost of more API calls (efficiency). Aggressive methods fail more often but replan efficiently only when priors are informative. Interestingly, analysis shows that LLMs treat the provided priors nearly as facts, which risks failure when priors are unreliable. We also explore hybrid strategies with tunable hyperparameters that adjust the balance between safety and efficiency.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) planners differ in how far they commit before acting in a partially observable environment: some aggressively plan long sequences on assumptions about unobserved state, others conservatively plan only over what they have seen, and both behaviours emerge implicitly whether the model outputs a plan directly or writes a `PDDL` formulation for a classical solver. The authors characterise this safety-versus-efficiency trade-off on two partially observable domains where priors arrive either as explicit statistics or as common-sense knowledge. Across three LLMs **both strategies reach similar accuracy, but conservative planners fail less often at the cost of more API calls**, while aggressive planners fail more and replan efficiently only when the priors are informative. Analysis shows that models treat the provided priors almost as facts, which backfires when priors are unreliable, and hybrid strategies with tunable hyperparameters let users adjust the balance.

papers.title: Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows
papers.abstract: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.
papers.summary: Most agentic benchmarks reward finishing a long-horizon task in a single attempt, whereas professionals collaborating with agents care more about ongoing interaction such as revising plans. `Kolab` is a dataset of over 115 hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations working with agents on realistic long-horizon problems, together with the participants' own judgments of collaboration and output quality. It poses two tasks that automation benchmarks never test: forecasting whether an expert will adopt, modify or reject an agent's contribution once it leaves the chat window, and assessing collaboration satisfaction and output quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. **Frontier models, agentic or not, overestimate how well they collaborate with experts and struggle to tell high-quality from low-quality collaboration**, and longer workflow context does not consistently improve their predictions.

papers.title: SSR: Structural Signal Retriever for Scalable Agent Discovery in LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large-scale multi-agent ecosystems require mechanisms for discovering suitable agents without exposing entire registries to a large language model (LLM) orchestrator. The challenge is not only to retrieve relevant Agent Cards from a growing registry, but also to maintain a compact candidate context, since each additional candidate increases prompt size, inference cost, latency, and the risk of exceeding the model context window. We formulate this problem as candidate-context scalability and propose the Structural Signal Retriever (SSR), our deterministic and training-free retrieval method designed for Agent Card discovery. SSR derives structural lexical signals from capability-bearing Agent Card fields, weights them using inverse document frequency (IDF), and uses an Inverted Signal Index (ISI) for selective candidate scoring. We evaluate SSR using a synthetic agent benchmark, a public MS MARCO adaptation, and end-to-end LLM orchestration. At 1,000 agents, SSR reduces LLM input by 98.8% and orchestration latency by 70.9% relative to full-catalog orchestration. On MS MARCO, IDF improves retrieval effectiveness within the structural representation, while the ISI preserves retrieval effectiveness and reduces explicitly scored passages by 96.8%. End-to-end experiments show that candidate pre-selection maintains a compact candidate context as registry size grows and avoids the operational failures observed with full-catalog orchestration. These results support SSR as an Agent-Card-native, traceable retrieval mechanism for candidate-context scalability.
papers.summary: When a large language model (LLM) orchestrator must pick helpers from a large registry of agents, every candidate Agent Card placed in the prompt adds tokens, latency, cost and context-window risk, a problem the authors frame as candidate-context scalability. The Structural Signal Retriever (`SSR`) is a deterministic, training-free method that extracts lexical signals from the capability-bearing fields of Agent Cards, weights them with inverse document frequency (IDF), and scores candidates selectively through an Inverted Signal Index (ISI). Evaluated on a synthetic agent benchmark, an `MS MARCO` adaptation and end-to-end orchestration, **at 1,000 agents it cuts LLM input by 98.8 percent and orchestration latency by 70.9 percent** relative to full-catalog orchestration, and on `MS MARCO` the index preserves retrieval quality while explicitly scoring 96.8 percent fewer passages.

papers.title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
papers.abstract: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.
papers.summary: Post-hoc explanations of image models either show where the model looks with a spatial heatmap or rank which channels matter globally, which loses information for multispectral data where channel relevance is spatially localised and physically meaningful. The proposed method, `SSI`, attributes over position-channel pairs: for each spatial position it fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional cooperative game over that position's channels, and applies the Shapley value, producing a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix. The scheme is Shapley-fair within each position, its channel attributions sum exactly to the position's contextual contrast against the baseline, and it differs from Owen-style hierarchical accounting that averages over external spatial coalitions. On `HLS Burn Scar` it **beats an MC-Owen estimator on retained-attribution metrics using about 6 percent of the evaluation budget**, and across `CUB-200`, `EuroSAT` and `HLS Burn Scar` it achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC along with the strongest spectral hit rates and spatial localisation.

papers.title: DST-Net: Decomposed Spatio-Temporal Network for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Series decomposition has emerged as a widely acknowledged paradigm in deep time series forecasting models. However, existing approaches predominantly employ a homogeneous modeling strategy for all subsequences, thereby overlooking the distinct inductive biases inherent in different components. We identify that the trend component exhibits dominant spatial coupling across channels but carries significant temporal redundancy, whereas the seasonal component is characterized by local temporal evolution but remains susceptible to attention distraction. To address this, we propose a novel disentangled architecture that tailors specific modeling strategies to align with the intrinsic properties of each component. For the trend branch, we design a Latent Graph Block, employing latent graph modeling to capture global topological dependencies and system-wide co-movements. Conversely, for the seasonal branch, we introduce a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism to mitigate attention distraction. By injecting learnable Gaussian priors, we impose structural constraints that compel the model to focus on multi-granular local contexts, effectively filtering out global noise and accurately capturing local evolutionary phases. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.
papers.summary: Series decomposition is standard in deep time series forecasting, but existing models process the trend and seasonal components with the same architecture despite their different inductive biases: the trend shows strong coupling across channels with heavy temporal redundancy, while the seasonal part evolves locally in time and is prone to attention distraction. `DST-Net` **gives each component its own tailored branch**, a Latent Graph Block that captures global topological dependencies and system-wide co-movements for the trend, and a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism for the seasonal component that injects learnable Gaussian priors so attention concentrates on multi-granular local context and filters out global noise. Experiments on multiple real-world forecasting benchmarks demonstrate the model's effectiveness.

papers.title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
papers.abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.
papers.summary: Few-step generative models produce strong samples in one or a few evaluations, but steering them with only black-box reward feedback is hard: direct reinforcement learning fine-tuning severely over-optimises the reward, and test-time scaling throws away the speed advantage. Noise Policy Optimization (`NPO`) keeps the generator frozen and instead learns an amortised flow policy over its initial noise, transporting Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution whose pushforward through the generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution, using ELBO-based likelihood estimates that need only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Inference adds just a lightweight noise-sampling step, and across image, language and protein structure generation `NPO` **achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning and matches test-time search methods at 16 to 549 times lower inference cost**.

papers.title: Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches
papers.abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.
papers.summary: Sparse key-value (KV) cache compression keeps only selected past states for long-context inference, but those states usually retain their original positions, so under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) the gaps left by evicted tokens keep distorting query-key matching. `RoPERelay` operates after any selector has chosen the cache: it assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases by inverse rotation and re-rotation, and keeps the current query and subsequent generation in sync, without reselecting, re-prefilling history or spending extra cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors and three long-term memory tasks it improves answer quality in 32, and **for `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` with `BM25` on `LongMemEval-S` accuracy rises from 23.6 to 35.4 percent** at a measured end-to-end time overhead of roughly 1 to 3 percent.

papers.title: When Judges Agree and Are Wrong: Consistency-Accuracy Dissociation as a Blind Spot for Label-Free Evaluation
papers.abstract: Label-free evaluation methods, such as self-consistency filtering, majority-vote aggregation, and agreement-based reliability scoring, rely on an implicit assumption that consistency can serve as a proxy for correctness when ground-truth labels are unavailable or expensive to obtain. In this paper, we test this assumption directly. Using four financial QA datasets (multiple-choice and free-form), ten consistency dimensions, and two frontier model families, we measure the joint distribution of consistency and accuracy at the level of individual examples rather than in aggregate. We find that 60% of all incorrect answers fall in the high-consistency region (consistency $\geq$ 0.8), and that 77.7% of these show complete answer collapse, i.e. identical wrong answers across all perturbation variants. This high-consistency/incorrect quadrant cannot be detected by any evaluation signal that is built on agreement alone, as the model appears maximally reliable while being wrong. We show that the phenomenon is robust to the choice of consistency threshold t (it persists from t=0.50 to t=1.00), is shared across model families, and is concentrated in specific intersections of perturbation dimension and domain. We map where this quadrant occurs, analyze its stability properties, and discuss the implications for evaluation pipelines that use agreement-based signals in place of human labels.
papers.summary: Label-free evaluation methods such as `self-consistency` filtering, majority-vote aggregation and agreement-based reliability scoring assume that consistency across perturbed prompts can stand in for correctness. The authors test this at the level of individual examples on four financial question-answering datasets, ten consistency dimensions and two frontier model families, measuring the joint distribution of consistency and accuracy. **60 percent of all incorrect answers fall in the high-consistency region, with consistency of at least 0.8**, and 77.7 percent of those show complete answer collapse, meaning identical wrong answers across every perturbation variant, so no signal built on agreement alone can flag them. The effect persists for thresholds from 0.5 to 1.0, is shared across model families, and concentrates in specific combinations of perturbation dimension and domain.

papers.title: Predicting Live Birth After Fresh Embryo Transfer in IVF/ICSI: Differential ICM/Trophectoderm Morphology Encoding and a Hybrid Attention--Logistic Regression Ensemble
papers.abstract: Predicting live birth before fresh embryo transfer could support shared decision-making in IVF/ICSI, but routine clinical data are small, heterogeneous, and contain pathway-dependent variables prone to outcome leakage. We aimed to construct a curated single-centre IVF/ICSI dataset and develop a prediction model suited to small tabular clinical data. \textit{Materials and Methods:} We assembled 616 fresh embryo-transfer cycles (251 live birth, 365 non-live birth) with clinical, laboratory, and embryological predictors, and embryo morphology encoded with a novel differential weighting of the inner cell mass and trophectoderm. After KNN imputation, robust scaling, and selection of 50 features, we developed a Hybrid Attention Network (HAN), a learnable feature-attention gate followed by a compact multilayer perceptron, and a HAN + logistic-regression (LR) ensemble with a validation-tuned weight. Models were benchmarked against classical machine learning, TabPFN, and text-serialized language models on a held-out test set; AUC-ROC was the primary metric. \textit{Results:} The HAN + LR ensemble achieved the highest test AUC-ROC (0.710; accuracy 0.710, F1 0.630), ahead of the HAN backbone alone (0.700), logistic regression (0.667), the TabPFN + LR hybrid (0.666), and TabPFN (0.650). Text-serialized language models performed near chance (AUC $\le$ 0.61). The differentially weighted trophectoderm feature ranked highest by consensus importance across models. \textit{Discussion:} A compact attention network combined with a linear model outperformed both components and strong foundation-model baselines on a small clinical cohort. \textit{Conclusion:} The curated dataset and HAN + LR ensemble offer a transparent, reproducible basis for IVF/ICSI live-birth prediction; external validation is the next step.
papers.summary: Predicting live birth before a fresh embryo transfer could support shared decision-making in IVF/ICSI, but routine clinical data are small, heterogeneous and prone to outcome leakage through pathway-dependent variables. From 616 single-centre fresh-transfer cycles the authors build a curated dataset in which embryo morphology is encoded with a novel differential weighting of the inner cell mass and trophectoderm, then train a Hybrid Attention Network (`HAN`), a learnable feature-attention gate followed by a compact multilayer perceptron, and ensemble it with logistic regression (LR) using a validation-tuned weight. On a held-out test set the **`HAN` plus LR ensemble reaches the highest AUC-ROC of 0.710**, ahead of `HAN` alone at 0.700, logistic regression at 0.667 and `TabPFN` at 0.650, while text-serialised language models perform near chance and the weighted trophectoderm feature ranks as the most important across models.

papers.title: Stronger Judges Do Not See More: Deployment-Integrity Blindness in LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported. A tampered deployment that preserves evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator. We introduce DIB-Bench, a benchmark that measures this deployment-integrity blindness across 7,560 scored examples, six tamper types, and an evaluator ladder from regex scorers through LLM judges to GPT-5-nano. Stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs: mean acceptance rises from 88.6% (rule-based) to 94.1% (GPT-5-nano), and a trigger-conditional tamper invisible on the evaluation suite produces 48-100% harmful outputs, rising with model capability. A PAC-style bound shows that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size; a manifest-hash identity channel detects them with zero samples. Behavioral fingerprinting identifies the model component above chance (76.7%) but covers one of six stack components. We also propose a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.
papers.summary: Evaluations of large language model agents report behavioural scores but say nothing about the identity of the runtime stack that produced them, so a tampered deployment that preserves the evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator. `DIB-Bench` measures this deployment-integrity blindness over 7,560 scored examples, six tamper types and a ladder of evaluators from regex scorers through LLM judges up to `GPT-5-nano`. **Stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs, with mean acceptance rising from 88.6 percent for rule-based scorers to 94.1 percent for `GPT-5-nano`**, and a trigger-conditional tamper that is invisible on the evaluation suite yields 48 to 100 percent harmful outputs, growing with model capability. A PAC-style bound shows that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size while a manifest-hash identity channel catches them with zero samples, and the authors propose a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.

papers.title: Pathwise Shrinkage and Probabilistic Calibration of the Multiplicative Half-Cauchy Process
papers.abstract: We characterize the multiplicative half-Cauchy process through its log-scale random-walk representation, establishing shrinkage, expansion, and critical regimes, almost-sure summability, local rebounds, and effective dimension. We also derive a semi-analytic calibration rule linking interpretable prior probability statements to its scale parameter.
papers.summary: Characterizes the `multiplicative half-Cauchy process` through its log-scale random-walk representation, in which the multiplicative structure becomes a random walk on the log scale. The analysis establishes shrinkage, expansion, and critical regimes, almost-sure summability, local rebounds, and the effective dimension of the process. **A semi-analytic calibration rule links interpretable prior probability statements to the scale parameter**, giving a way to set that parameter from stated prior beliefs.

papers.title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
papers.abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.
papers.summary: A position piece based on the author's Industrial Panel talk at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai, organized around ten key statements. It argues that the next generation of AI will win not by knowing more about the world but by knowing its user: living on the person's body, working for them, and answering to them. **The term OnBodyAI names what happens when large language models are given a body**, and the article sets out what research and industry need to do to make that happen.

papers.title: CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF
papers.abstract: Feedback noise is pervasive in preference data, arising from subjective human judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect LLM judges. Standard reward modeling trained on such feedback yields a biased estimate of the clean risk. Although classical denoising methods are directly applicable to noisy feedback learning, they generally assume a uniform noise ratio across samples. However, this assumption fails for feedback data, where noise is intrinsically sample-wise. To address this challenge, we propose CleanRM, which uses a few clean feedback to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios via optimal transport. Specifically, CleanRM aligns the joint distribution of preferences reverted from noisy feedback with that of clean feedback and then trains the reward model using a noise-corrected surrogate loss. Theoretically, we prove that the resulting objective is unbiased with respect to the clean risk. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CleanRM outperforms state-of-the-art denoising baselines and yields more effective downstream RLHF alignment.
papers.summary: Preference data for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is noisy because of subjective judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect large language model (LLM) judges, so a reward model trained on it estimates a biased version of the clean risk. Classical denoising methods assume a uniform noise ratio across samples, an assumption that fails for feedback data where noise is intrinsically sample-wise. `CleanRM` uses a small amount of clean feedback to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios via optimal transport, aligning the joint distribution of preferences reverted from noisy feedback with that of the clean feedback, then trains the reward model with a noise-corrected surrogate loss that is proven unbiased with respect to the clean risk. **`CleanRM` outperforms state-of-the-art denoising baselines and yields more effective downstream RLHF alignment.**

papers.title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand?
  We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values, but higher-fidelity models and richer prompts cost substantially more, and whether the extra fidelity is worth it depends on how accurate the downstream optimization needs to be. The authors cast this as stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles that may carry systematic bias and state-dependent variance, and develop two cost-aware meta-algorithms that switch adaptively between oracles. With known bias, a restarted cost-aware policy selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages and **incurs cumulative cost no larger than the best fixed oracle in hindsight** and can be substantially smaller; with unknown bias, a budgeted certification scheme uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify progress and eliminate biased sources, with an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection. Concrete instantiations use biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization as subroutines, and synthetic and LLM-completion experiments show the adaptive policy skipping several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reducing cumulative cost at comparable accuracy.

papers.title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models
papers.abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.
papers.summary: Spoken dialogue models (SDMs) typically share a single speech-token space for generation and synthesis, which produces long autoregressive sequences and costly inference, while lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences at the price of compression-quality trade-offs and expensive tokenizer replacement. `CoSTA` is a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples the generation and synthesis token spaces while keeping the original speech tokenizer and decoder: it extends the generation vocabulary with compressed representations through mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, then deterministically expands them back to the original speech tokens before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks it delivers **roughly 1.7× faster speech-token generation**, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Further experiments show more sustained interaction under limited budgets, transfer across architectures, and complementarity with low-rate tokenization.

papers.title: All-in-One Memory: Process-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Memory Agents
