papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.
papers.summary: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents, but existing memory methods optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, with no shared reward space for judging search, writing, and stopping decisions. `All-in-One Memory` (`AiO-Mem`) compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, treats these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state, and has a unified memory policy actor roll out complete interaction trajectories over that state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model, trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level `DPO`, assigns process scores that are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by `Process-Aligned DAPO` (`PA-DAPO`) to optimize the policy. **Across long-context memory benchmarks, `AiO-Mem` consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.**

papers.title: From Observation to Intervention: Distilling Self-Generated In-Context Demonstrations via Executable Causal Intervention
papers.abstract: Self-generated In-Context Learning (ICL) enables LLMs to synthesize their own few-shot demonstrations, often outperforming manual prompts. However, existing methods filter demonstrations by observation, assuming a rationale is high-quality if it leads to the correct output. We show such filtering suffers from \textit{observational equivalence}, whereby both faithful causal rationales and spurious post-hoc rationales can yield same outputs and are statistically indistinguishable from observation alone. Inspired by independent causal mechanisms, we argue that faithful rationales imply \textit{transfer invariance}, in which causal rationales should remain effective across logically similar samples. We instantiate this criterion as \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{I}ntervention for \textbf{D}emonstrations \textbf{D}istillation (ECI2D), which abstracts language rationales into executable programs and applies the causal interventions ($do$-operator) on logically similar samples, retaining only those demonstrations that imply transfer invariance. Experiments on math, logical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ECI2D consistently outperforms observation-based ICL while retaining far fewer demonstrations, with gains exceeding 7 points as the test distribution shifts.
papers.summary: Self-generated in-context learning (ICL) lets large language models synthesize their own few-shot demonstrations, but existing methods filter demonstrations by observation, keeping a rationale whenever it leads to the correct output. The authors show this suffers from observational equivalence: faithful causal rationales and spurious post-hoc ones can yield identical outputs and are statistically indistinguishable from observation alone. Drawing on independent causal mechanisms, they argue faithful rationales imply transfer invariance, remaining effective across logically similar samples, and instantiate this as `Executable Causal Intervention for Demonstrations Distillation` (`ECI2D`), which abstracts language rationales into executable programs, applies do-operator interventions on logically similar samples, and keeps only demonstrations that pass. On math, logical, and commonsense reasoning benchmarks `ECI2D` consistently beats observation-based ICL while retaining far fewer demonstrations, **with gains exceeding 7 points as the test distribution shifts**.

papers.title: CARE-SD: Explainable Reasoning Architecture for Local SLM Self-Disclosure Analysis in Textual Data
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity interviews uncover critical security experiences, behaviors, and privacy concerns often not fully captured by conventional technical assessments. Consequently, identifying genuine self-disclosures is challenging because statements are context-dependent, categories overlap, and automated interpretations may introduce unsupported claims. Locally deployed Small Language Models (SLMs) protect sensitive participant data by keeping processing within controlled environments, but their limited reasoning capabilities make simple prompting insufficient for context-aware and factually reliable analysis. This study developed CARE-SD (Context-Adaptive Reasoning and Explanation for Self-Disclosure), a novel four-module architecture integrating context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation. We evaluated three local SLMs, including Llama 1B, Qwen 1.5B, and Llama 3B, using 82 independently annotated cybersecurity interviews across five organizational sectors. Comparisons included conventional classifiers, three prompting strategies, larger 8B--32B models, and architectural ablations. Two independent reviewers assessed disclosure labels, factual claims, and explanation correctness. CARE-SD improved the accuracy and evidence reliability of SLMs, increasing Llama 3B Macro-F1 from 0.80 to 0.88 while reducing unsupported claims by 60\%. Remarkably, the 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category Macro-F1, demonstrating the effectiveness of the architecture without requiring a larger model.
papers.summary: Cybersecurity interviews reveal security experiences, behaviors, and privacy concerns that technical assessments miss, but identifying genuine self-disclosures is hard because statements are context-dependent, categories overlap, and automated interpretation can introduce unsupported claims; locally deployed small language models (SLMs) keep sensitive participant data in controlled environments but reason too weakly for simple prompting to suffice. `CARE-SD` (Context-Adaptive Reasoning and Explanation for Self-Disclosure) is a four-module architecture that integrates context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation. Evaluated with `Llama 1B`, `Qwen 1.5B`, and `Llama 3B` on 82 independently annotated interviews across five organizational sectors, and compared against conventional classifiers, three prompting strategies, 8B to 32B models, and ablations, it raised `Llama 3B` macro-F1 from 0.80 to 0.88 while cutting unsupported claims by 60%. **The 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category macro-F1.**

papers.title: Stop Training Against Soft Users: Mentalized Adversarial Self-Play for Proactive Dialogue
papers.abstract: Proactive dialogue agents must guide multi-turn interactions toward task goals while adapting to users whose intentions and attitudes evolve. Existing planners improve system side action selection through search, learned policies, or user aware planning, but are often trained and evaluated against fixed or overly compliant simulators; as a result, high simulated success can reflect soft user bias rather than robust dialogue ability. We introduce MASP, a Mentalized Adversarial Self Play framework that treats proactive dialogue as a partially observable game between a system and a rationally resisting user. MASP represents the user's evolving mental state with a BDI based latent state, separates reward side teacher mentalization from policy side student mentalization, and alternates self play updates for the system and user policies. This turns robustness to rational resistance into a training objective rather than only an evaluation condition. Across diverse proactive dialogue benchmarks, compared with the widely used SFT and Planner-only approaches, MASP substantially improves success rate (SR) and rationality constrained success (RCSR), reduces average turns (AT), and performs better against hard users who make the task goal more difficult to achieve.
papers.summary: Proactive dialogue agents must guide multi-turn interactions toward task goals while adapting to users whose intentions and attitudes evolve, yet existing planners are trained and evaluated against fixed or overly compliant simulators, so high simulated success can reflect soft-user bias rather than robust dialogue ability. `MASP` (Mentalized Adversarial Self-Play) treats proactive dialogue as a partially observable game between a system and a rationally resisting user, representing the user's evolving mental state with a belief-desire-intention (BDI) latent state, separating reward-side teacher mentalization from policy-side student mentalization, and alternating self-play updates for the system and user policies. This turns robustness to rational resistance into a training objective rather than only an evaluation condition. Across diverse proactive dialogue benchmarks, **`MASP` substantially improves success rate and rationality-constrained success rate over supervised fine-tuning and planner-only approaches**, reduces average turns, and performs better against hard users who make the goal harder to reach.

papers.title: Coordination-Free Workload Regularization for Variable-Cost Distributed Training
papers.abstract: Synchronous data-parallel training usually assigns every rank the same number of records, even when record costs vary by orders of magnitude. For variable-length models, this converts input variation into idle time because each step waits for its most expensive rank-local batch. We present Batch Cost Lookahead (BCL), a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs with balanced estimated cost. BCL preserves the trainer's record-count contract and requires neither cross-rank metadata exchange nor runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions, enabling BCL reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%. Across 13 NeMo-RL SFT corpora on eight H200 GPUs, rank-local BCL runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled MFFD. Compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes. We also identify a memory-feasibility boundary: a p99 cap for high-variance or OOM-prone data bounds outliers before BCL balances the rest. These results show that substantial variable-cost imbalance can be removed at the data-loader boundary, while clarifying when data preparation or broader coordination is still necessary.
papers.summary: Synchronous data-parallel training assigns every rank the same number of records even when per-record costs vary by orders of magnitude, so for variable-length models each step idles waiting on the rank with the most expensive local batch. `Batch Cost Lookahead` (`BCL`) is a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs of balanced estimated cost, preserving the trainer's record-count contract with no cross-rank metadata exchange or runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions it reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%; across 13 `NeMo-RL` supervised fine-tuning corpora on eight H200 GPUs it runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled `MFFD`, and **compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes**. The authors also identify a memory-feasibility boundary where a p99 cost cap must bound outliers for high-variance or out-of-memory-prone data before `BCL` balances the rest.

papers.title: Automatic Sentence Completion Using Bengali Audio Speech with a Transformer-Based Early Speech Recognition System
papers.abstract: Dementia severely impairs communication abilities and turns everyday conversations into challenging experiences. Individuals affected by dementia frequently struggle to express their thoughts or complete sentences, making it difficult for family members and caregivers to understand their needs. This study proposes a novel approach to assist dementia patients by developing an integrated system that detects signs of dementia through Bangla speech and text analysis and provides sentence auto-completion support during conversations. To achieve this, recorded voices from individuals with and without dementia were analysed, and key acoustic features were extracted to capture vocal patterns associated with cognitive decline. A transformer-based model was employed to transcribe voice signals into text for linguistic analysis. In the classification task, several Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models were evaluated using both acoustic and textual representations, and the LSTM model architectures demonstrated strong capabilities for modelling contextual patterns in speech and language data. For the sentence auto-completion task, a sequential learning model based on a Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) network with an attention mechanism was developed to sequentially complete partially expressed Bangla sentences during conversation. This research bridges the gap in dementia analysis in an underrepresented language and implements a sentence auto-completion framework for cognitive disorders.
papers.summary: Dementia impairs communication, and affected individuals often cannot finish their sentences, leaving family members and caregivers struggling to understand their needs, while Bangla remains underrepresented in dementia analysis research. The system detects signs of dementia from Bangla speech and text and offers sentence auto-completion during conversation: acoustic features are extracted from recordings of people with and without dementia, a transformer-based model transcribes speech for linguistic analysis, and several machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) classifiers are compared on acoustic and textual representations. **`LSTM` architectures proved strongest at modeling contextual patterns in the speech and language data.** For auto-completion, a bidirectional LSTM (`Bi-LSTM`) with an attention mechanism sequentially completes partially expressed Bangla sentences.

papers.title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.
papers.summary: Expanding context windows does not relieve the compute, storage, and information-selection pressures that large language models (LLMs) face at inference time, and prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory are usually discussed in isolation. The survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem of allocating inference-time resources, distinguishing compute-active memory that participates directly in computation from compute-inactive memory that sits outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, with offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states. Writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting are formulated as state transitions in an information lifecycle under a single budgeted cost model that unifies short-term context compression with long-term memory management. **The central claim is that the challenge is deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form, rather than merely reducing information volume**, and the survey closes with evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and a call to move from static pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.

papers.title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty
papers.abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly deployed to retrieve precise information from large corpora, yet multi-hop, long-horizon tasks remain challenging. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a scalable solution, with existing pipelines typically expanding seed tasks to increase their apparent depth and breadth. However, this expansion does not reliably translate into necessary reasoning: newly introduced evidence may be only weakly coupled to the answer, creating a mismatch between intended and empirical difficulty. To address this problem, we introduce GRADS, a graph-guided agentic data synthesis framework with explicit difficulty control. GRADS runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question--answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required to derive each answer. At each step, it conditions generation on a relevant subgraph, preserving indispensable inference without accumulating irrelevant context. Experiments across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains show that GRADS consistently generates verified tasks with empirically separated difficulty distributions, as measured by independent solvers. Moreover, under matched training budgets, post-training on this data delivers consistent gains at every level: SFT raises the solution-termination rate to over 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and on our held-out, domain-specific benchmarks, the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet~4 on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains.
papers.summary: Deep research agents still struggle with multi-hop, long-horizon retrieval over large corpora, and synthetic-data pipelines that expand seed tasks for apparent depth and breadth often introduce evidence only weakly coupled to the answer, so intended and empirical difficulty diverge. `GRADS` runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question-answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required for each answer, conditioning every generation step on a relevant subgraph so indispensable inference is preserved without accumulating irrelevant context. Across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains it generates verified tasks whose difficulty distributions are empirically separated as measured by independent solvers. Under matched training budgets, supervised fine-tuning on this data raises the solution-termination rate above 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, reinforcement learning trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and **the resulting 4B model matches `Sonnet 4` on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains** of the held-out benchmarks.

papers.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
papers.abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.
papers.summary: Agent memory architectures are typically fixed after deployment, and self-evolving approaches that adapt them from evaluation scores or compressed summaries cannot localize failures precisely in long-horizon systems with many interacting components, so updates often become large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable architecture. `MemScope` performs evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture: its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and the architecture code to identify repair targets and applies bounded in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On `GAIA` the trace-and-memory inspection variant reaches **86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback**; on `xBench` the evolved architecture improves from 49 to 55 correct answers with `DeepSeek V3.2` and from 50 to 53 with `Kimi K2.7 Code`, and on disjoint unseen `ALFWorld` tasks success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions the median code-change ratio is 4.4%.

papers.title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect position. Two accounts could explain this: a precision account, where softmax attention cannot concentrate on the item exactly N positions back so neighbors are retrieved instead, and an interference account, where attention selects the right item but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. Across 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and minimal transformers trained from scratch, the task-carrying attention heads attend to the target on most missed matches, linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a match occurred at the target or a lure position even on false-alarm trials, and sharpening attention yields negligible gains, **whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d-prime) in nearly all model-by-load conditions**. Larger models spread the task over more heads and benefit more from removing interference, and in minimal transformers a second attention layer removes the precision limit of a single layer, placing the working-memory limit in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

papers.title: AgentEval: Evidence-Bounded Assessment of Stateful Agents
papers.abstract: Task completion alone does not determine whether a stateful agent satisfied its obligations, and a recorded judgment does not guarantee that its supporting evidence remains valid. We present AgentEval, a system that carries a contract-bound assessment record through tool execution, state and event capture, report qualification, and case maintenance. It separates what the agent did, what the evidence establishes, and whether the conclusion is supported for present use. On 32 tool-world administrations, independent checks agree on all 30 complete episodes, distinguishing satisfied, violated, and unresolved obligations; two interrupted administrations are retained. Controlled interventions on 48 evidence views expose 36 binding faults missed by hash-only checks without changing agent behavior. Scenario Studio connects reviewed cases to 12 two-turn reports with 24 independently checked answers. A separate public-benchmark study on 192 held-out executions reveals ten completed return subgoals within broader task failures and isolates the effect of missing evidence. These studies show how an executable assessment record makes scope, evidential support, and report reuse inspectable across an agent evaluation workflow.
papers.summary: Task completion alone does not establish that a stateful agent met its obligations, and a recorded judgment about an agent does not guarantee that its supporting evidence is still valid. `AgentEval` carries a contract-bound assessment record through tool execution, state and event capture, report qualification, and case maintenance, separating what the agent did, what the evidence establishes, and whether the conclusion is supported for present use. On 32 tool-world administrations, independent checks agree on all 30 complete episodes in distinguishing satisfied, violated, and unresolved obligations, and **controlled interventions on 48 evidence views expose 36 binding faults that hash-only checks miss** without changing agent behavior. A `Scenario Studio` component connects reviewed cases to 12 two-turn reports with 24 independently checked answers, and a separate public-benchmark study on 192 held-out executions reveals ten completed return subgoals inside broader task failures and isolates the effect of missing evidence.

papers.title: Judging the Judges: Confidence and Disagreement in Rubrics as Rewards
papers.abstract: Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) extends reinforcement learning to non-verifiable domains by using an LLM judge to score responses against a structured rubric. Prior work has focused on improving the rubric or strengthening the single judge, with comparatively little attention to how different single or multiple judges might be used during RaR training. We first show that judge identity alone produces a substantial spread in scores when training Qwen3-4B-Base on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science across five frontier and open-weight judges. Building on this, we propose RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel judge ensemble strategy for RaR with two mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that uses judge logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. We find that this design is critical: while a naive average of judge scores fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE outperforms every single-judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, with per-theme analysis showing that it inherits the complementary strengths of its constituent judges. Our findings establish judge ensembling as a compelling axis for improving RaR.
papers.summary: Rubrics as Rewards (`RaR`) extends reinforcement learning to non-verifiable domains by having a large language model judge score responses against a structured rubric, but prior work has focused on improving the rubric or strengthening a single judge rather than on how one or several judges should be used during training. Training `Qwen3-4B-Base` on `RaR-Medicine` and `RaR-Science` with five frontier and open-weight judges, the authors first show that judge identity alone produces a substantial spread in scores. `RaRE` (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles) adds two mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that uses judge log-probabilities to weight more confident judges more heavily, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the `GRPO` update. **A naive average of judge scores fails to beat the best single judge, but `RaRE` outperforms every single-judge variant on both `HealthBench` and `GPQA Diamond`**, and per-theme analysis shows it inherits the complementary strengths of its constituent judges.

papers.title: Does Latent Chain-of-Thought Actually Reason? A Single, Unifying Taxonomy for Latent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Latent chain-of-thought replaces written reasoning steps with continuous hidden states, giving models additional steps to compute before answering. It remains unclear what computation these steps actually perform. High task accuracy and decodable intermediate answers do not establish that a model uses its latent chain to reach an answer. We study this question across twenty-one model-task configurations covering three training recipes, three reasoning tasks, and two backbones. We combine chain deletion and content replacement with probes and trajectory analysis to test whether the chain affects the answer, what it encodes, and how its states change. On logical tasks, COCONUT often carries an answer that is already readable before the chain begins. Its states settle early, and deleting the chain leaves predictions almost unchanged. Per-step supervision produces an ordered layout of reasoning steps and can make the model depend on the chain. Yet even an ordered chain can act as a placeholder, with deletion hurting performance while content replacement leaves answers unchanged. On arithmetic tasks, all tested recipes show dependence on chain content. These results show why readable latent states alone are insufficient evidence of reasoning. We introduce a taxonomy that separates what a chain represents from how the model uses it. Seen this way, earlier reports no longer compete: placeholder tokens, collapsed superposition and step-dependent causal roles are each consistent with a different kind of chain, each obtained on a different task, training recipe or measurement. Once a study says which property it tested, whether the model uses the chain, what the chain holds, or how its state moves, claims about latent reasoning can be compared.
papers.summary: Latent chain-of-thought replaces written reasoning steps with continuous hidden states that give a model extra computation before it answers, but high task accuracy and decodable intermediate answers do not establish that the model actually uses the chain to reach its answer. Across twenty-one model-task configurations covering three training recipes, three reasoning tasks, and two backbones, the authors combine chain deletion and content replacement with probes and trajectory analysis to test whether the chain affects the answer, what it encodes, and how its states change. **On logical tasks, `COCONUT` often carries an answer that is already readable before the chain begins, its states settle early, and deleting the chain leaves predictions almost unchanged**; per-step supervision produces an ordered layout of reasoning steps and can make the model depend on the chain, yet even an ordered chain can act as a placeholder whose deletion hurts while content replacement leaves answers unchanged, whereas on arithmetic tasks every recipe depends on chain content. A taxonomy that separates what a chain represents from how the model uses it reconciles earlier reports of placeholder tokens, collapsed superposition, and step-dependent causal roles as descriptions of different kinds of chains obtained under different tasks, recipes, and measurements.

papers.title: Beyond Retrieval Failure: Understanding Why LLMs Miss Evidence in Multi-Hop RAG
papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires an agent to retrieve evidence for a sequence of dependent sub-questions. When a wrong answer lacks a required passage, the passage may be inaccessible to the retriever, or the agent may have failed to issue a query that would retrieve it. Standard retrieval evaluations conflate these two causes. We study how much apparent retrieval failure is instead caused by search drift: the search no longer tracks an unanswered sub-question. Holding the retriever, corpus, and generation model fixed, we introduce ExecutionRAG, a training-free requirement register that records open sub-questions and their supporting evidence. The register changes search guidance but not evidence access, so each gold passage it recovers certifies that the passage was reachable by the original retriever. On 1,000 MuSiQue questions, the number of wrong answers with unretrieved required evidence falls from 382 to 234 with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and from 383 to 274 with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. These counts correspond to 69% to 44% and 66% to 48% of each system's wrong answers, respectively. Crucially, evidence recovery does not produce a proportional reduction in total error: premature resolutions and abstentions increase as missing-evidence failures decrease. The central finding is therefore a shift in the remaining bottleneck, from guiding search toward required evidence to verifying that the retrieved evidence is sufficient.
papers.summary: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires an agent to retrieve evidence for a sequence of dependent sub-questions, and when a wrong answer lacks a required passage, standard evaluations cannot tell whether the retriever could not reach it or whether the agent never issued a query that would have found it. `ExecutionRAG` is a training-free requirement register that records open sub-questions and their supporting evidence; because it changes search guidance but not evidence access, each gold passage it recovers certifies that the original retriever could reach it, exposing failures caused by search drift, where the search stops tracking an unanswered sub-question. On 1,000 `MuSiQue` questions with retriever, corpus, and generation model held fixed, **wrong answers with unretrieved required evidence fall from 382 to 234 with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` and from 383 to 274 with `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`**, from 69% to 44% and 66% to 48% of each system's wrong answers. Recovering evidence does not proportionally reduce total error, since premature resolutions and abstentions increase as missing-evidence failures decrease, shifting the remaining bottleneck from guiding search toward verifying that retrieved evidence is sufficient.

papers.title: Mine, Sample, Render: Test-Time Diversity Alignment Of Generative Models
papers.abstract: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER (MSR), a test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from a corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses a generative model purely as a conditional renderer of a sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.
papers.summary: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to. `MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER` (`MSR`) is a test-time approach that externalizes diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure: it mines an interpretable categorical schema and sampling statistics from a corpus of real artifacts, samples attribute configurations from those statistics, and uses the generative model purely as a conditional renderer of each sampled configuration. Evaluated on diversity and output quality across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, **`MSR` improves alignment with corpus distributions and the diversity of generated outputs**.

papers.title: Sensor Diagnosis for Fuel and Emissions Monitoring in Heavy-Duty Diesel Vehicles
papers.abstract: Faulty sensor readings can distort estimates of fuel use and carbon dioxide emissions from diesel engines. We evaluate two procedures that use relationships learned from healthy measurements to diagnose faults and guide fuel correction. The diagnosis procedure tests whether replacing a suspected faulty reading with an estimated healthy value helps a model predict another sensor's recorded reading more accurately. It then predicts the fault type and decides whether to report the diagnosis. We evaluate five synthetic fault types on 217 steady-state operating points from a heavy-duty diesel engine, excluding all measurements at selected engine speeds from training. Across 31,500 fault-injected groups of 20 operating points, it issues diagnoses for 77.3% of groups, with 92.1% of diagnoses issued on these groups correct. The fuel correction procedure uses a different sensor-selection rule at individual operating points, testing how each replacement changes the largest prediction error across all six sensors. Fuel correction requires a fault alarm and engine speed and torque close to the training conditions. A fuel reading is replaced only when its replacement reduces the largest prediction error sufficiently more than replacements for the other sensors. Assuming faults in 1% of one-hour scenarios, equally likely sensors and fault types, and equal time at each measured condition, selected fuel corrections reduce mean absolute error in calculated combustion CO2 by 83.8%. On this engine map, learned relationships support complete sensor diagnoses and fuel corrections that improve emissions accounting while preserving unaffected readings.
papers.summary: Faulty sensor readings on diesel engines distort estimates of fuel use and carbon dioxide emissions. Two procedures are evaluated that learn relationships among healthy sensor readings, then test whether substituting an estimated healthy value for a suspect reading improves prediction of other sensors, using that test to name the fault type, decide whether to report a diagnosis, and decide whether to correct the fuel reading. On 217 steady-state operating points from a heavy-duty engine with selected engine speeds excluded from training, the diagnosis procedure issued a verdict for 77.3% of fault-injected groups and 92.1% of those verdicts were correct. Under the authors' assumed fault rate, selective fuel correction reduced mean absolute error in calculated combustion CO2 by **83.8%**.

papers.title: Resisting Harmful Instructions through Training-Free Weight Editing
papers.abstract: Instruction-following language models can comply with requests that conflict with intended behaviors and safety alignment. We introduce a training-free weight-editing approach for reducing compliance with targeted undesirable instructions. Our method needs only forward passes on a small set of prompt pairs per target behavior, and because the edit is stored in the model's weights, changing or deleting instructions in the prompt cannot undo the weight modification. We evaluate the approach on two target harmful behaviors across five instruction-tuned models: instructed falsehood and instructed sexism. On two instructed-lying benchmarks, it improves mean honest response rates by 6.2 and 4.6 percentage points over the strongest alternative, significantly on three of the five models and within noise on the other two. In a controlled study of seven prompt formats, it maintains higher honest-response rates than single-layer activation steering when orders to lie arrive in single-turn formats not used to construct the edit. For instructed sexism, it reduces the mean sexist-response rate from 57.9% to 24.3%; combining the edit with a fairness prompt reduces it further to 11.9%. These results establish our contrast-based weight editing approach as an effective training-free intervention in two distinct behavioral domains, supporting its use both independently and alongside prompt-based safeguards.
papers.summary: Instruction-tuned models will comply with prompts that tell them to lie or to answer unfairly, and prompt-level guardrails disappear whenever the prompt changes. The proposed intervention edits model weights directly, needing only forward passes over a small set of contrasting prompt pairs per target behavior, so deleting the instruction from the prompt cannot undo it. Across five instruction-tuned models it raised mean honest-response rates by 6.2 and 4.6 percentage points over the strongest alternative on two instructed-lying benchmarks, and held up better than single-layer activation steering on prompt formats not used to build the edit. For instructed sexism it cut the mean sexist-response rate from 57.9% to **24.3%**, and to 11.9% when paired with a fairness prompt.

papers.title: FedSumUp: User-Auditable Privacy-Aware Representation Sharing for Resource-Constrained Federated Intelligence
papers.abstract: Existing federated data condensation methods face privacy risks, as uploaded synthetic data may preserve sensitive information and remain vulnerable to reconstruction attacks. Moreover, their generation often incurs considerable client-side computational overhead, limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices. To address these issues, we propose FedSumUp, which employs a learnable lossy compressor on clients to generate compact and visually interpretable representations. By controlling information capacity, FedSumUp reduces privacy leakage while allowing users to directly assess the privacy-utility tradeoff. We further introduce a dual-objective optimization mechanism to preserve task-relevant semantics while suppressing reconstruction risks. The compressor is trained on the server and only performs lightweight inference on clients. Since the server cannot access raw data, we develop a data-free closed-loop optimization strategy that optimizes the compressor by minimizing the discrepancy between original and twice-compressed representations after structure-preserving upsampling. Experiments on BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10, and ChestMNIST demonstrate reconstruction PSNR as low as 8.56 dB (with synthetic PSNR as low as 5.45 dB), client runtime reductions up to 96.5% (from 778s to 27s on ChestMNIST), and competitive classification accuracy (89.72% ChestMNIST, 82.24% BloodMNIST, 65.63% CIFAR-10), while remaining inherently robust to non-IID data distributions.
papers.summary: Federated data condensation has clients upload synthetic data that can still carry sensitive information and costs them considerable compute to produce. `FedSumUp` replaces this with a learnable lossy compressor trained on the server, so clients run only lightweight inference, and its controlled information capacity bounds leakage while leaving representations visually interpretable enough for users to judge the privacy-utility tradeoff themselves. Because the server never sees raw data, the compressor is optimized data-free by minimizing the discrepancy between original and twice-compressed representations after structure-preserving upsampling. On `BloodMNIST`, `CIFAR-10` and `ChestMNIST` it pushed reconstruction quality down to 8.56 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio and cut client runtime by **up to 96.5%**, from 778 to 27 seconds on `ChestMNIST`, with competitive classification accuracy.

papers.title: Condition-Contrastive Extrapolation for On-Policy Distillation of Language Models
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves a student language model by training on its own generated trajectories with supervision from a stronger teacher. However, when conditioned on student-generated prefixes, the teacher can favor invalid continuations that violate the question's premises, causing OPD to encourage erroneous reasoning steps. As a remedy, we introduce Condition-Contrastive Extrapolated On-Policy Distillation (CCE-OPD), which makes teacher supervision sensitive to question conditions. CCE-OPD incorporates (1) a fixed-prefix comparison in which the same frozen teacher evaluates the complete question and a counterpart with a selected condition masked, and (2) a bounded log-probability contrast that reweights the teacher distribution into an auxiliary distillation target. On 200 diagnostic reasoning states, condition contrast reduces the rate of preferring invalid continuations from 27.0% to 16.0%. Extensive experiments across six mathematical benchmarks show that CCE-OPD improves avg@8 over OPD by an average of 1.60 and 1.95 percentage points when distilling Qwen3-8B into 0.6B and 1.7B students, respectively. It also achieves the strongest results on four transfer benchmarks.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation trains a student language model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, but when the teacher is conditioned on a flawed student prefix it can endorse continuations that violate the question's stated premises. `CCE-OPD` makes the supervision condition-sensitive by having the same frozen teacher also score a copy of the question with one condition masked out, then using a bounded log-probability contrast between the two to reweight the distillation target. On 200 diagnostic reasoning states this cut the rate of preferring invalid continuations from 27.0% to **16.0%**, and distilling `Qwen3-8B` into 0.6B and 1.7B students improved avg@8 across six math benchmarks by 1.60 and 1.95 percentage points over standard on-policy distillation.

papers.title: Poisoning the corpora of protein design systems during pre-training and retrieval
papers.abstract: Protein foundation models increasingly support the generation of novel biological sequences, yet their reliance on large public datasets creates opportunities for adversarial manipulation of the material they learn from and retrieve. We investigate two data-only poisoning attacks against protein design systems, targeting the pre-training corpus of autoregressive protein language models and the retrieval corpus of a text-guided protein generator. For the first, we pre-trained ProtGPT2 and ProGen2 variants of 300 million parameters, introducing poisoned protein sequences containing one of two triggers followed by one of three payloads. Across all poisoned runs, both architectures acquired highly reliable trigger-dependent generation under uniform and ramped poisoning schedules. Under ramped exposure, the earliest majority activation occurred after only 200 contaminated examples, while for the uniform schedule earliest activation occurred around 5000 poisoned samples. For the second attack, we inserted records into a retrieval corpus system without modifying its weights or decoding procedure. A single query-aware record captured a top-16 retrieval position for 58\% of templated requests and 97\% of free-text requests. Conditional on successful poisoned retrieval, 62\% of requests produced altered sequences, while 19-21% acquired the inserted domain by profile-HMM homology. A universal query-unaware attack using 1,500 records also achieved substantial retrieval capture and domain transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that adversarial protein sequence contributions can establish persistent, sequence-specific behaviour during pre-training or redirect protein generation at inference, while leaving ordinary model behaviour largely preserved. Our work establishes the integrity and biological provenance of protein sequence data as critical safeguards for generative protein design systems.
papers.summary: Protein design systems learn from and retrieve from large public sequence databases that outside parties can contribute to, which makes the provenance of that data a security property. Two data-only threat models are studied: contributed sequences present in the pre-training corpus of autoregressive protein language models at the 300-million-parameter scale, and records added to the retrieval corpus of a text-guided protein generator without touching its weights or decoding procedure. In both settings the systems' behavior on ordinary requests was largely preserved while generation could be steered toward content the contributor chose, with the retrieval route working at inference time alone. The authors conclude that **the integrity and biological provenance of sequence data are themselves critical safeguards** for generative protein design, rather than something downstream filtering can recover.

papers.title: Hard Way, The Only Way: Provable Merits of Training on Hardest Examples
papers.abstract: Despite a surge of empirical interest in the ``unreasonable effectiveness'' of drastic data pruning for AI systems, a unified theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains elusive. In this work, we provide a precise high-dimensional theory of learning under data pruning via weighted empirical risk minimization (ERM). As in previous work, we analyze a setting where pruning is performed along a one-dimensional subspace of the input space. Our analysis precisely characterizes the limiting test error curves in the regime where the input dimension N and sample size P tend to infinity with a fixed ratio N/P. The resulting theory recovers several recent results in the literature as special cases and provides a general lens to evaluate how pruning strategies interact with the loss function and label noise. Crucially, we characterize the optimal pruning strategy in the high-sample regime where P greatly exceeds N. We demonstrate that strategic pruning can accelerate the decay of classification test error from the classical sqrt(N/P) rate, typical of vanilla ERM with loss functions without exponential tail (e.g., quadratic loss), to the much faster Bayes-optimal scaling of order N/P. In this setup, we prove that, surprisingly, this optimal performance is achieved by a drastic pruning strategy: discarding almost all training data except for a small proportion, consisting strictly of the 2N hardest training examples.
papers.summary: Aggressive data pruning sometimes outperforms training on the full dataset, a phenomenon with plenty of empirical support and no unified theory. Using weighted empirical risk minimization in the high-dimensional limit where input dimension N and sample size P grow with a fixed ratio, the paper derives exact limiting test-error curves for pruning along a one-dimensional subspace, recovering several published results as special cases and showing how pruning interacts with the choice of loss and with label noise. In the regime where samples greatly outnumber dimensions, the optimal strategy turns out to be **discarding almost everything and keeping only the 2N hardest examples**, which speeds classification error decay from the usual sqrt(N/P) rate to the Bayes-optimal N/P.

papers.title: Who May Release an Agent's Promise? Standing over Commitments in Multi-Party Chat
papers.abstract: When an assistant serving a team makes a promise to Alice, who may cancel it? We call this standing: only the creditor (the person owed) or someone the creditor or operator policy authorizes may release a commitment, regardless of rank. In a controlled chat environment we vary who cancels and separate two errors: unauthorized release (obeying someone without standing) and override (executing a released promise). Across six models, smaller open ones override the creditor (Qwen3.5-9B: 69%); larger ones drop promises on a peer's direct word (Qwen3.8-27B: 89%; gpt-6.1-sol: 83%); nearly all act on a bystander's "go ahead after all". Oracles dissociate the errors: stating the rule or the creditor curbs unauthorized release but not override, which the latter even raises in three of four models; among them, only knowing whether the promise is still owed cuts override. Enabling thinking moves smaller models the way scale does. A self-kept commitment ledger stops override in four of five models; with a one-paragraph release policy it matches or beats the best oracle store, raising gpt-6-luna's strict accuracy from 49% (policy alone) to 83%. Code, prompts, outputs and labels are released.
papers.summary: When an assistant serving a team promises something to one person, the question of who may cancel that promise is a permission question the paper calls standing: only the person owed, or someone they or operator policy authorizes. A controlled chat environment varies who issues the cancellation and separates two distinct failures, obeying someone with no standing and executing a promise that was properly released. Across six models, smaller open ones overrode the creditor's wishes and larger ones dropped promises on a peer's direct word, while nearly all acted on a bystander's casual go-ahead; stating the rule or naming the creditor curbed unauthorized release but not override, and in three of four models made override worse. Having the agent **keep its own commitment ledger stopped override in four of five models**, and combined with a one-paragraph release policy it raised one model's strict accuracy from 49% to 83%.

papers.title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
papers.abstract: When a speaker says ``some students passed'', listeners infer that not all of them did. Reasoning models now let users decide how long a model thinks before it answers, but we do not know what extra thinking does to such everyday inferences. We study this directly: we keep a model's weights fixed, change only how much it thinks, and record which reading it chooses. A second tool cuts the model's own reasoning at successive points and asks for an answer, showing where the reading changes. Thinking makes models read logical words as logic: it cancels the implicatures of \emph{some} (\emph{not all}) and \emph{or} (\emph{not both}) in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve. The trace shows why: models first entertain the enriched reading and cancel it later. Answering from that early reading, an exploratory inference-time remedy, recovers these implicatures without losing literal accuracy. Evaluations of reasoning models should measure how they interpret, not only how accurate they are.
papers.summary: Saying "some students passed" normally implies not all of them did, and the paper asks what a longer thinking budget does to such everyday pragmatic inferences. Weights are held fixed while only the amount of thinking varies, and a second tool truncates the model's own reasoning at successive points to locate where its chosen reading flips. More thinking **cancels the enriched readings of "some" (not all) and "or" (not both)** in most tested open reasoning models and in `GPT-5`, pushing them toward literal logical interpretations, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve. The traces show models entertain the enriched reading first and discard it later, and answering from that early state restores the implicatures without costing literal accuracy.

papers.title: Clean Data Can Still Carry Backdoors: Support-Persistent Backdoors for Model Reuse
papers.abstract: Traditional backdoor attacks inject artificial trigger patterns into training data, causing models to misclassify triggered inputs while maintaining normal behavior on clean samples. Since these artificial triggers are absent in clean datasets, standard knowledge distillation (KD) typically eliminates them, leading to the common belief that KD serves as an effective purification defense. In this paper, we propose DAR (Discover-and-Relabel), a support-persistent backdoor method that retains its behavior even after clean-data distillation. DAR identifies naturally abundant patterns in low-dimensional feature subspaces using subspace clustering and applies label-only poisoning to samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule. At test time, the backdoor is activated by locally modifying the corresponding subspace of the target images. By instantiating spatial and frequency operators, DAR achieves attack accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art backdoor attacks in ImageNet classification and CLIP-based prompt tuning. Notably, DAR keeps attack success above 96% after clean KD and remains defense-resistant in practice. Project page: https://junhoo.me/backdoor
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation on clean data is widely treated as a purification defense, on the reasoning that artificial backdoor triggers never appear in the clean set and so cannot survive. `DAR` (Discover-and-Relabel) tests that belief by using subspace clustering to find patterns already abundant in low-dimensional feature subspaces, then poisoning only labels of samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule, so the trigger is a direction the data itself contains rather than an added artifact. On `ImageNet` classification and `CLIP`-based prompt tuning it reached attack accuracy comparable to leading backdoor methods while **keeping attack success above 96% after clean distillation**, which undercuts distillation's reputation as a safe path for model reuse.

papers.title: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess large language model (LLM) outputs by decomposing quality into multiple criteria and assigning each a binary judgment from an LLM verifier. However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria. Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity. As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL). To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration. Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal $p$-values with provable coverage guarantees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.
papers.summary: Rubric-based evaluation breaks output quality into criteria and has a language model verifier give each one a binary verdict, then aggregates them uniformly as if every verdict were equally certain. Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (`URW`) instead elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal p-values with provable coverage guarantees, requiring no training. Treating uncertain criteria as less informative **improves pairwise preference accuracy and yields stronger downstream reinforcement-learning alignment**, which the authors attribute to removing misleading reward signal rather than to better judges.

papers.title: AutoOnboarder: Autonomously Onboarding LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.
papers.summary: Agentic language models have been shown to lose reasoning capability once placed inside a harness, the software layer that mediates their observations and actions. `AutoOnboarder` treats closing that gap as an onboarding problem, putting the worker agent under a supervising coding agent that iteratively rewrites its foundation model choice, prompt, and harness source code to raise performance and lower cost, given only tens of examples and with evaluation data isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. On genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission, autonomously onboarded agents matched or exceeded a `Gemini 3.5 Flash` baseline at **up to 29 times lower cost**, but outcomes varied greatly between runs. The authors conclude the supervising agent needs a structured thought interface, controlled internet access, and a wide model search space.

papers.title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
papers.abstract: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165--228x faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.
papers.summary: Recommender systems balance conflicting objectives, and adjusting the balance at serving time usually means output reranking, which limits which trade-offs are reachable, or parameter-generating modules, which are expensive. `RecSoup` merges objective-specific models instead, first pruning parameters by both per-objective importance and cross-objective relevance to reduce interference, then learning a mapping from a preference setting to merge coefficients so the trade-off can be dialed at inference without joint retraining. The authors prove this can traverse the full Pareto front without the smoothness constraints parameter generation needs, and report better Pareto front quality with **165 to 228 times lower inference latency**.

papers.title: Learning and Forecasting Multiscale Spatiotemporal Epidemic Dynamics with Lagrangian-Eulerian Graph Neural ODEs
papers.abstract: Accurate medium- to long-range epidemic forecasting requires extrapolating high-dimensional, heterogeneous and nonstationary dynamics from partial observations. Yet hybrid models often leave implicit which observations inform which epidemic processes and how learned graph interactions modify system state. We introduce LE-EpiGNODE, which replaces generic message passing with process-specific, mechanism-guided neural operators: age-contact information drives Lagrangian infection generation, whereas mobility drives conservative Eulerian population transport within a structure-preserving universal differential equation. We evaluated LE-EpiGNODE across 14 controlled synthetic mechanisms spanning time-modulated, state-dependent, nonlinear and coupled dynamics, three complementary COVID-19 settings, 21 comparator models and five targeted ablations. Forecasting gains tended to become more pronounced at longer horizons; at the longest horizon, LE-EpiGNODE achieved the lowest WMAPE in all three real-world datasets, reducing error by 17.7-40.0% relative to the best baseline. Controlled ablations linked these gains to the Lagrangian-Eulerian decomposition and process-aligned priors, while synthetic ground truth showed that learned operators and induced state fluxes track known generating dynamics. These results support mechanism-organized graph neural dynamics as a route to reliable long-horizon extrapolation with directly testable, process-level mechanistic interpretation beyond trajectory accuracy.
papers.summary: Medium- and long-range epidemic forecasting requires extrapolating high-dimensional, nonstationary dynamics from partial observations, and hybrid mechanistic-neural models rarely make explicit which observations inform which epidemic process. `LE-EpiGNODE` swaps generic message passing for process-specific neural operators inside a structure-preserving universal differential equation, so age-contact information drives Lagrangian infection generation while mobility drives conservative Eulerian population transport. Tested across 14 controlled synthetic mechanisms, three COVID-19 settings, 21 comparator models and five ablations, it achieved the lowest weighted mean absolute percentage error on all three real datasets at the longest horizon, **reducing error 17.7 to 40.0% relative to the best baseline**, with ablations attributing the gains to the Lagrangian-Eulerian split.

papers.title: KBS: A Korean Benchmark Suite for Foundation Model Evaluation
papers.abstract: We present a Korean Benchmark Suite (KBS) comprising Ko-ARC, Ko-GSM8K, Ko-EQ-Bench, Ko-WinoGrande, Ko-LAMBADA, and Ko-IFEval, covering six capabilities across 9,396 items. The suite combines review, localization, direct Korean construction, and redesign for Korean, avoiding a translation-only approach to benchmark adaptation. We evaluate Korean-developed models, multilingual open models, and closed API models under protocols that account for model access, prompt format, and scoring differences. Results show that Korean benchmark scores depend on task construction, scoring rules, prompting, and model post-training. These findings suggest that Korean evaluation should report both final scores and the settings used to obtain them.
papers.summary: Korean evaluation of foundation models has largely meant translating English benchmarks, which imports artifacts and misses language-specific phenomena. The Korean Benchmark Suite (`KBS`) covers six capabilities across 9,396 items through `Ko-ARC`, `Ko-GSM8K`, `Ko-EQ-Bench`, `Ko-WinoGrande`, `Ko-LAMBADA` and `Ko-IFEval`, built by a mix of review, localization, direct Korean construction and redesign rather than translation alone, and evaluates Korean-developed, multilingual open and closed API models under protocols that account for differences in model access, prompt format and scoring. The authors find **scores depend on task construction, scoring rules, prompting and post-training**, and argue Korean results should always be reported together with the settings that produced them.

papers.title: What Should We Remove? Evaluating the Reliability and Costs of RLVR Data Decontamination
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) math corpora are routinely screened for benchmark overlap, but the reliability and data-loss costs of cleaning policies remain underexamined. We audit sixteen open RLVR math corpora comprising 1,673,514 corpus-specific training items against six benchmarks containing 1,949 questions. We evaluate eight policies based on exact, lexical, and semantic matching using 594 independently and blindly dual-reviewed training-benchmark pairs. Calibration and held-out sets have disjoint benchmark questions and training-example families. A separate review of all 83 candidate matches for 80 sampled training items measures item-level false removal. At cosine threshold 0.80, 52 of 59 sampled removals (88%) were confirmed false removals; this is not a demonstrated population rate. No semantic threshold in our preregistered grid (0.80-0.98) meets the 90% conservative-precision target on calibration. The existing judge-adjudicated policy achieves 98.1% resolved precision and 98.2% candidate-frame recall on held-out corpora. It has zero confirmed false removals among six sampled removals, with one unresolved case; this does not establish zero risk. Within the evaluated candidate frame, this policy offers a more favorable precision-recall balance than the semantic-threshold alternatives tested. Recall does not measure contamination outside the candidate frame. We release reviewed labels, per-policy decisions, and coverage accounting to support evaluation of cleaning reliability and cost rather than overlap counts alone.
papers.summary: Math corpora for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (`RLVR`) are routinely screened for benchmark overlap, but how reliable those screens are and how much good data they throw away has gone largely unexamined. The authors audit sixteen open corpora totaling 1,673,514 items against six benchmarks, comparing eight exact, lexical and semantic matching policies against 594 blindly dual-reviewed training-benchmark pairs, with calibration and held-out sets using disjoint benchmark questions and example families. **No semantic similarity threshold in their preregistered 0.80 to 0.98 grid met the 90% conservative-precision target**, and at cosine 0.80 the large majority of sampled removals were confirmed as false, whereas an existing judge-adjudicated policy reached 98.1% resolved precision on held-out corpora. They release the reviewed labels and per-policy decisions so cleaning cost can be weighed rather than just overlap counts.

papers.title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all three base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.
papers.summary: Unlearning is normally judged by whether removed knowledge stays removed, which is not enough for a model that keeps being fine-tuned after release: it must resist relearning the deleted content while retaining plasticity, the ability to pick up new tasks. The authors argue that measuring preservation against the pre-update model wrongly penalizes useful changes the update itself caused, and formulate a reference-timing hypothesis in response. Update-Matched Unlearning applies the same simulated relearning update to both the defended model and an undefended reference started from the same unlearned checkpoint, using new-task learning to guide selection. On `TOFU` and `FaithUn` with `Llama` and `Qwen` models it cut harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while **raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points**, whereas withholding the update from the reference kept relearning low but dropped plasticity below the base method.

papers.title: Compatibility Matters: A Framework for Token-Level Teacher Selection in On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently been introduced as a promising paradigm for continual learning, where a student policy can be supervised at the token-level. Typically, OPD is performed using a single teacher per prompt rollout (or even per training run). However, this ignores a whole other axis of flexibility that is available due to the on-policy nature - token-level teacher selection during rollouts. Building on this insight, we theoretically explore what makes a teacher and a student compatible for OPD, and leverage our findings to derive several empirical heuristics for teacher selection. In particular, our framework captures several desiderata for OPD: compatible teacher-student reasoning patterns, teacher competence, and induced student diversity. Theoretically, we categorize several types of teacher routing schemes, and we prove that under different scenarios, different routing schemes are likely to be beneficial for optimization and student diversity. We back up our findings with extensive experimental results in domains such as math, coding, kernel generation, and visual reasoning, where we find upwards of 10 percentage points of improvement on pass@$k$ when compared to vanilla OPD and the teacher experts on certain tasks, indicating both capability improvement and diversity over high-quality responses.
