papers.summary: Optical wireless communication (OWC) links are highly sensitive to line-of-sight blockage, attenuation, ambient light saturation, and misalignment, and conventional diagnostics offload channel analysis to cloud or external nodes, adding latency. The authors build a self-diagnosing receiver on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller that decodes 1000 bit/s on-off keying (OOK) payloads with majority voting while extracting bit error rate (BER), received signal voltage, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and ambient light baseline as features for an on-device TinyML classifier. A post-training INT8 quantized `TensorFlow Lite Micro` model **reaches 74.68% accuracy in only 3.32 kB of SRAM** across four fault conditions, compared with 77.22% for a `Random Forest` baseline and 78.48% for a floating-point neural network, and on-device tests confirm deterministic real-time classification.

papers.title: Beyond Invariance: Factor-wise Selective Treatment of Shifts for Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Distribution shifts pose a fundamental challenge to robust multimodal learning. Existing methods typically promote invariance by suppressing environment-dependent variations, implicitly applying a uniform treatment to shifted information. However, shifted information can have different predictive consequences: some contributes little to prediction, some remains reliably informative, and some exhibits environment-dependent predictive effects. This raises a fundamental question: which shifted information should be suppressed, preserved, or attenuated? To address this question, we propose FaShift, a factor-wise shift framework that diagnoses latent representation factors according to their distributional changes, intervention effects, and cross-environment stability. By factorizing multimodal representations and evaluating these complementary properties, FaShift distinguishes non-predictive factors, stably predictive factors, and predictively useful but unstable factors. It then selectively suppresses, preserves, or attenuates their contributions, rather than enforcing uniform invariance. Experiments on MOSI, MOSEI, and CH-SIMS show that FaShift achieves the best ID accuracy and F1 across all three datasets. Compared with the strongest competitors reporting OOD results, it improves OOD accuracy/F1 by 1.5/3.6 points on MOSI and 1.7/2.7 points on MOSEI, while achieving the best reported OOD accuracy and F1 on CH-SIMS.
papers.summary: Robust multimodal learning under distribution shift usually enforces invariance by suppressing all environment-dependent variation, even though some shifted information remains reliably predictive. `FaShift` factorizes multimodal representations and diagnoses each latent factor by its distributional change, intervention effect, and cross-environment stability, sorting factors into non-predictive, stably predictive, and predictive-but-unstable groups that are suppressed, preserved, or attenuated respectively. On the `MOSI`, `MOSEI`, and `CH-SIMS` sentiment datasets it achieves the best in-distribution accuracy and F1, and **improves out-of-distribution accuracy/F1 by 1.5/3.6 points on `MOSI`** and 1.7/2.7 points on `MOSEI` over the strongest reported competitors.

papers.title: Multi-Reward Hacking: From Aggregation-Induced Drift to Trust-Anchored Defense
papers.abstract: To improve task performance while encouraging desirable response properties, LLM post-training often combines a primary reward (e.g., correctness) with auxiliary rewards (e.g., brevity or efficiency). However, how these rewards are aggregated can critically affect training outcomes. We show that symmetric aggregation, which treats reward channels equally, can induce a failure where aggregate reward improves while primary-task performance degrades, even when individual rewards are meaningful. We investigate this aggregation-induced failure through a one-step multi-reward decision formulation, characterizing when it constitutes multi-reward hacking. We prove that, under symmetric aggregation, deterministic conditional-mean GRPO converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior when auxiliary rewards are more reliably obtained, regardless of initialization. We propose Trust-Anchored Gating (TAG), which first elects an anchor channel based on the policy drift induced by optimizing each channel alone, then gates auxiliary credit on anchor satisfaction. Unlike calibration-sensitive static reweighting, TAG structurally eliminates credit for auxiliary-only outcomes while preserving additional credit for joint success. In the same analytical setting, TAG provably reverses this selection, converging to the primary-favoring action from any initialization when the primary channel is anchored. Experiments across Qwen and Llama models on mathematics and program synthesis reveal substantial degradation under symmetric, constrained, and normalized aggregation, whereas TAG mitigates this failure. On Qwen3-4B with a brevity reward, TAG achieves 0.581 pass@4 versus 0.220 for additive aggregation, while shortening responses by 44% relative to correctness-only training.
papers.summary: Post-training large language models with a primary reward such as correctness plus auxiliary rewards such as brevity can backfire when the rewards are aggregated symmetrically: the aggregate reward rises while primary-task performance falls. Using a one-step multi-reward decision formulation, the authors prove that deterministic conditional-mean `GRPO` under symmetric aggregation converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior whenever the auxiliary reward is more reliably obtained, regardless of initialization. Their fix, Trust-Anchored Gating (`TAG`), elects an anchor channel based on the policy drift each reward induces when optimized alone and then grants auxiliary credit only when the anchor is satisfied, which provably reverses the selection in the same setting. Across `Qwen` and `Llama` models on math and program synthesis, additive, constrained, and normalized aggregation all degrade substantially, while **`TAG` reaches 0.581 pass@4 versus 0.220 for additive aggregation on `Qwen3-4B`** with a brevity reward, still shortening responses by 44% relative to correctness-only training.

papers.title: MemCut: Every Secret Leaves a Trail in the Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a crucial component of large language model (LLM) agents, with most research focusing on retrieving relevant information accurately and efficiently. However, a dependable memory system must also forget sensitive user data upon request. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MemCut, a systematic benchmark for user-requested forgetting. Its 456 hand-designed secrets in long-horizon conversations have fully annotated evidence trails to test recovery after deletion, including from messages that never state the secrets directly. We propose two recovery metrics. Native recovery measures reader success through the system's retrieval, whereas residual recovery measures the same reader's success when directly given surviving objects traced to annotated disclosures or evidence. We establish three reference deletion baselines to test how far existing retrievers and write models support forgetting across five memory designs and four LLMs. Disclosure removal reduces native recovery far more than residual recovery. LLM-guided deletion of ten additional turns from twenty retrieval candidates leaves 39-76% residual recovery. Subset sweeps (144 facts, three systems, two models) show that widening the pool at a fixed budget reduces residual recovery more than deleting all original candidates. These sweeps identify candidate coverage as a bottleneck in the reference baselines.
papers.summary: Long-term memory systems for large language model (LLM) agents are mostly evaluated on retrieval, yet they also need to forget sensitive user data on request. `MemCut` is a benchmark of 456 hand-designed secrets embedded in long-horizon conversations, each with annotated evidence trails including messages that never state the secret directly, and it measures native recovery (a reader succeeding through the system's own retrieval) and residual recovery (the same reader given surviving objects traced to annotated disclosures or evidence). Testing three reference deletion baselines across five memory designs and four LLMs, removing the explicit disclosures reduces native recovery far more than residual recovery, and **LLM-guided deletion of ten extra turns from twenty retrieval candidates still leaves 39-76% residual recovery**. Subset sweeps show that widening the candidate pool at a fixed deletion budget reduces residual recovery more than deleting all original candidates, pointing to candidate coverage as the bottleneck.

papers.title: Identifying Effective Strategies in Prompt Evolution for Stress and Emotion Prediction
papers.abstract: Early stress detection and risk prediction are crucial for timely mental health assessment and support. While large language models have recently shown promise for social media stress prediction, relying on accuracy can obscure false positives. Also, prompt revisions yield inconsistent gains across models and tasks, with unclear links to strategy combinations and instruction changes. By comparing six methods on social media stress and emotion data across two model sizes, we found that GEPA and its extension combining instructions from two prompts (GEPA+merge) improved prediction over initial prompts in several settings. We also identified five prompting strategies associated with development gains. These strategies included directing attention to emotional evidence, distinguishing current from past distress, illustrating indirect cues, requiring emotional context, and guiding label selection. Moreover, we documented four observations across tasks and evaluation settings. In a separate set of searches, binary stress prediction improved early, whereas multilabel emotion prediction initially declined and partly recovered. The other three concerned incorrect or conflicting instructions, gains on small comparison samples that did not hold on full development data, and changes in selected prompts' development and reported test rankings. These findings identify effective prompt evolution methods, strategy combinations associated with gains, and task and evaluation limits, providing guidance for applying prompt evolution methods to social media stress detection.
papers.summary: Large language models show promise for predicting stress and emotion from social media posts, but accuracy can mask false positives and prompt revisions produce inconsistent gains across models and tasks. The authors compare six prompt evolution methods on social media stress and emotion data across two model sizes and find that **`GEPA` and a `GEPA+merge` extension, which combines instructions from two prompts, improved prediction over initial prompts in several settings**. Five prompting strategies are associated with development gains: directing attention to emotional evidence, separating current from past distress, illustrating indirect cues, requiring emotional context, and guiding label selection. They also document that binary stress prediction improved early while multilabel emotion prediction first declined, that evolved prompts sometimes contained incorrect or conflicting instructions, and that gains on small comparison samples and development rankings did not reliably hold on full development data or test sets.

papers.title: Jev-LiteMAS: Separating Decisions from Generation in Multi-Agent Workflows
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems use generative models even for coordination steps that only need a bounded decision, such as picking the next expert or judging an artifact, and profiling three representative frameworks shows routing and review consume 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. Swapping those steps for a cheap decision model opens two interface gaps: planners also produce execution plans and handoff instructions, and reviewers produce actionable repair feedback. `Jev-LiteMAS` pairs the lightweight decision model `Jev` with generative execution, selecting experts dynamically from the task and accumulated prior outputs instead of a pre-generated trajectory, and screening intermediate artifacts so only flagged ones go to LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones it **cuts generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% relative to `LAS`** while staying within 1.34 accuracy points, lowers latency in seven of eight settings, and grounding routing in expert outputs avoids up to 18.0 points of accuracy loss.

papers.title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.
papers.summary: Agent harnesses call a large language model (LLM) at every step even though most steps end in a multiple-choice decision such as which tool to call next, which a cheaper decision model like `Jev` could answer directly. `AgentDecisionBench` evaluates decision models from isolated questions up to control of a running agent on public benchmarks and a new `DecisionGym` environment, and it shows that the model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, while delegating tool choices without a fitted confidence threshold cut success by 19.0 points. `JevAgentHarness` fits a per-choice confidence threshold on the agent's own trajectories and defers to the LLM below it, and `AgentDecision-4B`, an open 4B model, is trained on post-mistake states labeled with `Jev` answers. On out-of-distribution tasks the agent solved 91.5% with `AgentDecision-4B` versus 82.0% with `Jev`, and on in-distribution tasks these 4B models made agents **81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster** without losing 3 or more points of task success.
papers.highlight_summary:
Agent harnesses call a large LLM at every step, even though most of those calls just pick one option from a list, such as which tool to run next. The idea is to send these choices to a cheap decision model like `Jev` and use its answer only when its confidence clears a threshold fitted for each kind of choice on the agent's own trajectories; below that threshold the LLM decides as usual.

- `JevAgentHarness` turns eight kinds of choice (tool, arguments, stop, reflect, memory read and write, routing, and next action) into typed multiple-choice questions in five integration modes, and it fits each confidence threshold in a silent "shadow mode" run over 150 calibration tasks.
- `AgentDecisionBench` tests decision models on isolated questions, on recorded agent runs and in control of a live agent, and it shows that isolated scores misrank them: `StartLux-9B` was the most accurate on `BFCL` tool choice (**92.2%**) yet solved only **69.5%** of agent tasks, while step-level accuracy tracked task success closely (Kendall correlation 0.84).
- The fitted threshold is what protects success: letting `Jev` make every tool choice lost **19.0 points**, whereas the tool-choice cascade cut cost by **14.2%** without changing the outcome of any of 500 `DecisionGym` tasks.
- `AgentDecision-4B` is `Qwen3-4B` fine-tuned with LoRA on 15,694 states the agent actually visited, 30.9% of them following a mistake, using `Jev`'s probabilities as soft labels; supervised fine-tuning alone raised success on shifted tasks from **13.5% to 96.0%**, the follow-up `GRPO` stage added no measurable gain, and in the final comparison the agent solved **91.5%** of shifted tasks with `AgentDecision-4B` against **82.0%** with `Jev`.
- In deployment, trained 4B models made agents **81.1–89.0% cheaper** and up to **2.5× faster** without losing 3 or more points of success, but coding agents saved only 7.0–10.5%, an unseen task rule dropped success to 3.0% (against 88.0% for the LLM alone) until thresholds were refit or the model retrained, and results rest mostly on English tasks with `Gemini` agent LLMs.

papers.title: Learning to Forecast on Multiple Spatiotemporal Hierarchies
papers.abstract: Hierarchical forecasting exploits aggregation structures that expose multiple views of the same underlying spatiotemporal forecasting problem, while ensuring coherence among forecasts. Individual series provide fine-grained information, while progressively coarser aggregates reveal temporal and spatial patterns at different scales. In the associated deep learning architectures, the hierarchy determines which aggregate series are available and how they are processed together with individual series (e.g., through reconciliation or message-passing operators). Different hierarchies thus provide distinct learning signals and inductive biases for forecasting the same collection of time series. Nonetheless, existing architectures are typically trained on a single, often fixed, structure. In this work, we propose a graph deep learning framework that leverages variations across hierarchies as multi-task regularization. We show that jointly learning across these structures can reduce over-specialization to any single hierarchy and improve forecasting performance. Indeed, training across hierarchies provides an inductive bias toward representations that are useful across different structures, and as such, generalize better. Making forecasts coherent with the aggregation constraints for each sampled hierarchy is computationally expensive: to complement the framework, we propose a novel operator-based on a top-down approach-that produces coherent forecasts with linear time and space complexity w.r.t. the hierarchy size. Experiments show that our approach improves forecasting accuracy over training on a single structure and is competitive with current state-of-the-art methods.
papers.summary: Hierarchical forecasting exposes the same spatiotemporal time series at multiple aggregation levels, but existing deep architectures train on a single fixed hierarchy, so one aggregation structure acts as the sole inductive bias. The authors propose a graph deep learning framework that samples different hierarchies during training and treats the variation as multi-task regularization, encouraging representations that are useful across structures and less over-specialized to any one. Because enforcing coherence with each sampled hierarchy's aggregation constraints is expensive, they add a top-down reconciliation operator with **linear time and space complexity in the hierarchy size**. Experiments show gains over training on a single structure and competitiveness with current state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: What Does History Add? Calendar Controls and Information-Timing Audits for University Trajectory Forecasting
papers.abstract: We audit the predictive value of historical summaries in a rule-based university trajectory simulator. Seventeen ridge specifications and persistence separate current plans, past-state and past-plan summaries, and calendar-only history-length indicators. Across training, validation and two family-held-out evaluations, we reconstruct 16,750 routes and 804,000 monthly records. On the original 40-family set, six-month history lowers six-step normalized RMSE from 0.159234 to 0.151522, but its difference from a length-only control is -0.000895 (descriptive paired 95% interval [-0.001957,0.000248]). Fixed weights on 30 families unused in identified prior tasks reproduce this pattern: 0.156480 to 0.150074 versus current-state prediction, but -0.000558 [-0.001783,0.000728] versus the length control. These uncertain comparisons do not generalize to all-history summaries, which improve on their own calendar control. Exploratory decomposition finds clearer preparation-index and funds benefits, whereas fatigue dominates the six-month model's loss and has an uncertain length-controlled benefit. Moreover, 28.20% of its six-step fatigue predictions violate the simulator's [5,90] support. We document family dependence, prior exposure, strict temporal indexing, matched recursive references and independent numerical replay. The task conditions on recorded future plans; it does not evaluate real-student forecasts, causal action effects, autonomous planning or language-model memory. This is an evaluation audit, not a new memory architecture.
papers.summary: Whether historical summaries add predictive value beyond simply knowing how long a history exists is tested in a rule-based simulator of university student trajectories, comparing seventeen ridge regression specifications and persistence against calendar-only history-length controls over 16,750 reconstructed routes and 804,000 monthly records. Six-month history lowers six-step normalized RMSE from 0.159 to 0.152 relative to current-state prediction, but **its difference from a length-only control is only -0.000895 with a paired 95% interval spanning zero**, a pattern reproduced with fixed weights on 30 held-out families. All-history summaries do beat their calendar control, decomposition shows clearer benefits for preparation-index and funds variables, and 28.20% of six-step fatigue predictions fall outside the simulator's valid range. The authors stress that the task conditions on recorded future plans and does not evaluate real students, causal effects, autonomous planning, or language-model memory.

papers.title: Where, How, and When: Query-Guided Grounding for Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Understanding video content requires reasoning at multiple levels of granularity, from identifying objects to interpreting their interactions and localizing when specific actions occur. This thesis studies three query-guided grounding tasks that answer where key objects are (object-level grounding), how they interact (relationship-level grounding), and when specific moments occur (moment-level grounding). For object-level grounding, we present QDETRv, a query-guided extension of the Detection Transformer for one-shot localization of unseen objects in videos, which combines query-context fusion, a memory module for temporal consistency, and unsupervised pretraining on synthetic object trajectories. We further propose the Temporal Object-Aware Vision Transformer (TOViT) for few-shot video object detection, which builds on a language-aligned open-set vision encoder and propagates high-confidence object features across frames. For relationship-level grounding, we introduce few-shot referring relationships in videos: given a (subject, predicate, object) query and a few support videos sharing the predicate, the entities are localized by optimizing a T-partite random field using a meta-learned relation network with query-conditioned translational embeddings, Global Semantic Aggregation, Local Localization Aggregation, and belief-propagation-based message passing. For moment-level grounding, we propose the Moment Alignment Transformer (MATR) for video-to-video moment retrieval, which uses dual-stage Dynamic Time Warping for pre- and post-fusion alignment, learnable queries for boundary prediction, and self-supervised pretraining with temporal augmentations; MATR also extends to text-to-video moment retrieval with performance comparable to, or better than, the state of the art. These contributions advance query-guided video understanding across spatial, relational, and temporal grounding.
papers.summary: Understanding a video requires localizing objects, grounding their interactions, and pinpointing moments in time, each conditioned on a query, and the thesis contributes one method per level. For object-level grounding it presents `QDETRv`, a query-guided Detection Transformer for one-shot localization of unseen objects with query-context fusion, a temporal memory module, and unsupervised pretraining on synthetic trajectories, plus the Temporal Object-Aware Vision Transformer (`TOViT`) for few-shot video object detection built on a language-aligned open-set encoder. For relationship-level grounding it introduces few-shot referring relationships in videos, localizing the entities of a (subject, predicate, object) query by optimizing a T-partite random field with a meta-learned relation network and belief-propagation message passing. For moment-level grounding, the Moment Alignment Transformer (`MATR`) uses dual-stage Dynamic Time Warping, learnable boundary queries, and self-supervised temporal augmentation for video-to-video moment retrieval, and **extends to text-to-video moment retrieval with performance comparable to or better than the state of the art**.

papers.title: Do Agents Need a New Kind of Paper? SPRA: Structured Paper Representation for Agents
papers.abstract: Scientific agents must connect research problems, methods, and findings dispersed through narrative articles. We introduce SPRA (Structured Paper Representation for Agents), a paper-level representation of persistent research objects and typed relations. Its empirical-AI profile organizes Problems, Contributions, Components, ExperimentSetups, Measures, and Findings for querying, traversal, and reuse. Selected paper-level citation relations record dependencies, component use, and comparisons with prior work; source locations support verification. We instantiate SPRA across more than one million AI papers, with 19.95 million research units and 24.07 million internal relations. Evaluations access SPRA through Schema-RAG with task evidence fixed before inference. Across seven subfields, SPRA improves source-conditioned scientific QA by 0.381/5 over passage retrieval while remaining close to Full Compact (0.078/5 lower on average). In directed cross-paper reasoning, qualification improves by 0.184/5 over passage retrieval; Top-5 synthesis shows mixed quality effects. Across all paired RQ2 tasks, including Top-5, input+output tokens decrease by 28.5% relative to passage retrieval and 95.3% relative to Full Compact. In idea generation, a 0.067-point lower Overall score than Full Compact accompanies 93.7% fewer input+output tokens. Together, these results support SPRA as a usable representation of scientific content and a foundation for research workflows that connect, inspect, and reuse paper-level research objects. The SPRA resource is accessible through the SciVerse scholarly-data platform.
papers.summary: Scientific agents need to connect problems, methods, and findings that are scattered through narrative articles. Structured Paper Representation for Agents (`SPRA`) represents each paper as persistent research objects (Problems, Contributions, Components, ExperimentSetups, Measures, Findings) with typed relations, paper-level citation links for dependencies and comparisons, and source locations for verification, and the authors instantiate it over **more than one million AI papers with 19.95 million research units and 24.07 million relations**. Accessed through `Schema-RAG` with evidence fixed before inference, it improves source-conditioned scientific question answering by 0.381 out of 5 over passage retrieval across seven subfields, trailing the `Full Compact` paper-text baseline by only 0.078, and improves qualification in directed cross-paper reasoning by 0.184. Across paired tasks it uses 28.5% fewer tokens than passage retrieval and 95.3% fewer than `Full Compact`, and for idea generation it scores 0.067 points lower than full text while using 93.7% fewer tokens, with the resource available via the `SciVerse` platform.

papers.title: Learning from Interaction Experience via Localized Context Distillation
papers.abstract: Learning from interaction experience is essential for enabling large language models to continually improve during deployment. Context distillation offers a promising path: privileged information extracted from experience is provided to a teacher, whose behavior is then distilled into a student model that has no access to it. However, both existing forms of context distillation have limitations. Off-policy context distillation trains the student on teacher-generated trajectories and thus suffers from exposure bias; whereas on-policy context distillation trains on the student's own rollouts, whose states are often uninformative and fail to convey behaviors the student cannot yet produce. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Localized Context Distillation (LoCD). LoCD first localizes the critical spans of a student trajectory that require revision. The teacher then regenerates only these spans from the student's own prefix, and the student is trained on the regenerated segments. LoCD thereby concentrates learning on the most informative states while keeping exposure bias low. Extensive experiments across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks demonstrate that LoCD consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves more stable training with smaller and sparser parameter updates.
papers.summary: Context distillation lets a language model learn from deployment experience by giving a teacher privileged information and distilling its behavior into a student without that access, but off-policy variants trained on teacher trajectories suffer exposure bias while on-policy variants trained on student rollouts rarely reach states that reveal behaviors the student cannot yet produce. Localized Context Distillation (`LoCD`) first localizes the critical spans of a student trajectory that need revision, has the teacher regenerate only those spans from the student's own prefix, and trains the student on the regenerated segments, concentrating learning on informative states while keeping exposure bias low. **Across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks, `LoCD` consistently outperforms strong baselines** and yields more stable training with smaller and sparser parameter updates.

papers.title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space
papers.abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.
papers.summary: Diffusion models remain costly because of iterative denoising, and most acceleration work targets per-sample latency, where gains are saturating. `ManiFusion` instead raises throughput by fusing multiple samples into a shared representation before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward, with a geometric account of how fused samples retain enough information to guide their individual trajectories and a Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (`TFS`) rule that varies the fusion factor over sampling stages. The backbone-agnostic approach is demonstrated on U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces, composes with existing acceleration methods, and the authors claim it **reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation**.

papers.title: Policy-Aligned Predictive Verification for Adaptive VLA Action-Chunk Execution
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA's internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with pi_0 and pi_0.5 across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success-query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy's proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies emit chunks of actions to amortize inference, but how much of each chunk to execute is left to heuristics like generation stability or prediction agreement that do not test whether executing a prefix preserves the ability to finish the task. The policy-aligned predictive verifier (`PAV`) anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes within the VLA's own task-conditioned representation space and scores their compatibility with successful continuation, learning local judgments from terminal outcomes via trajectory-level survival supervision plus a localization prior that salvages useful behavior from failed rollouts. Validity scores then set the execution horizon, and evaluations with `pi_0` and `pi_0.5` on `LIBERO`, `RoboTwin 2.0`, and real-world manipulation show **improved success-versus-query trade-offs**, suggesting future prediction is better used to decide how far to trust proposed actions than to generate new ones.

papers.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which assigns depth to the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, executed on the device, and alternative branches to one SLM pass. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An {\epsilon}-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three Spec-Bench runs per system show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-{\epsilon}. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.
papers.summary: Device-cloud speculative decoding offloads drafting to a phone to save server compute, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) needs repeated passes on the mobile neural processing unit (NPU). `HyCo` splits the job: the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, run on the device from the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries the server returns, supplies draft depth, while one SLM pass supplies alternative branches, with quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fitting both drafters to the NPU and an epsilon-threshold rule that relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. On a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, **server GPU time per output token drops 38.6% on `Spec-Bench`** and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization relative to server-side MTP self-speculation, with 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. Judge scores differ from a cloud-plus-MTP baseline by +0.2 points with a confidence interval spanning zero, and without the relaxation the exact variant saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.

papers.title: Each Reward to Its Relevant Tokens: Reward-Specific Token-Level Credit Assignment for Multi-Reward RL
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly trained against several verifiable rewards at once, such as the correctness and the format of a tool call, or the individual constraints of a complex instruction. Reward-decoupled normalization (GDPO) normalizes each reward separately so that different reward combinations keep distinct advantages, but it still spreads every reward's advantage evenly over the whole response, although each verifier checks only a few positions. We propose MRTPO, which assigns the advantage of each reward to the tokens relevant to it, using the information its verifier checks, without auxiliary models or token-level annotations. For each reward, the policy replays its own response with and without that reward's verifier information, and the per-token Jensen-Shannon distance between the two next-token distributions measures each token's relevance and reassigns the advantage. On text-to-SQL, multi-constraint instruction following and tool calling, MRTPO converges faster and achieves better performance than the compared methods.
papers.summary: Training language models against several verifiable rewards at once, such as the correctness and format of a tool call, usually spreads each reward's advantage evenly across the whole response even though each verifier inspects only a few positions. Reward-decoupled normalization (`GDPO`) keeps the rewards distinct but still shares this uniform credit. `MRTPO` instead routes each reward's advantage only to the tokens its verifier actually inspects by replaying the policy's own response with and without that reward's verifier information and using the per-token Jensen-Shannon distance between the two next-token distributions as a relevance weight, with no auxiliary models or token-level annotations. **On text-to-SQL, multi-constraint instruction following, and tool calling, `MRTPO` converges faster and outperforms the compared methods.**

papers.title: SITAR: A Situational Distortion Metric for Automatic Speech Recognition Evaluation
papers.abstract: In automatic speech recognition (ASR), transcription errors with similar lexical or semantic discrepancies can have markedly different consequences for the situation conveyed by speech. Capturing these differences requires not merely contextual assessment, but an understanding of what the spoken discourse describes, establishes, or seeks to bring about. However, relying on LLM judges introduces computational cost and scoring variability. We introduce SITAR, a situational distortion metric for ASR, realized through a comprehensive end-to-end construction framework. Specifically, this framework aggregates situational severity and cumulative extent into a unified score via a bounded recursive formulation. Using targets derived from this formulation with limited offline LLM support, we train SITAR as a lightweight BERT-family regressor that scores reference-hypothesis pairs in a single forward pass, entirely free of any prohibitive runtime costs. Recognizing that introducing a new metric demands rigorous justification, we formalize a principled validation protocol spanning both extrinsic validity, assessed at macro and micro levels, and intrinsic scorer reliability. The former, evaluated across diverse datasets and models, demonstrates that SITAR reliably tracks broad capability scaling while providing orthogonal diagnostic utility, whereas the latter, examined on a purpose-built controlled benchmark, confirms the operational soundness of the scoring instrument itself. Through systematic validation, we demonstrate that SITAR holds strong potential as a practical, lightweight complement to existing ASR metrics. We will release the full recipes (code, model weights, dataset, etc.) after the internal review to support community research.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors with similar lexical or semantic distance can distort the described situation to very different degrees, and using LLM judges to capture this is costly and inconsistent. `SITAR` scores how much a transcription error distorts the situation the speech describes, built by aggregating situational severity and cumulative extent into a single score through a bounded recursive formulation, with targets derived using limited offline LLM support and then distilled into **a lightweight BERT-family regressor that scores reference-hypothesis pairs in one forward pass**. A validation protocol covering extrinsic validity at macro and micro levels and intrinsic scorer reliability on a purpose-built controlled benchmark shows the metric tracks broad capability scaling across datasets and models while offering diagnostic signal orthogonal to existing ASR metrics. Code, weights, and data are promised after internal review.

papers.title: V-SHARE: Provable Convergence Guarantees for Advantage-based Algorithms
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning, advantage-based value-learning methods, unlike standard Q-learning, share information across actions by decomposing the action-value function into a state-dependent value component and action-specific advantages. While this mechanism has proven effective in both tabular and deep reinforcement learning, its theoretical understanding remains incomplete. We introduce V-SHARE, an advantage-based value-learning algorithm that combines cross-action value sharing with an importance-weighted Bellman-residual correction. To our knowledge, we provide the first complete theoretical characterization of an advantage-based algorithm, including both asymptotic convergence and non-asymptotic finite-sample guarantees. We identify a regime in which V-SHARE mitigates the rare-action bottleneck of asynchronous Q-learning and uncover a contraction--variance tradeoff between stronger deterministic contraction and increased importance-weighting noise. Motivated by this tradeoff, we develop decreasing residual-preconditioning schedules that combine faster early contraction with lower asymptotic noise. We further develop a two-timescale analysis that removes the single-timescale residual-weight threshold while preserving convergence guarantees. Experiments on discrete Markov decision processes (MDPs) and deep reinforcement-learning benchmarks corroborate our results.
papers.summary: Advantage-based value learning decomposes the action-value function into a state value plus action-specific advantages so that information is shared across actions, but unlike Q-learning it has lacked a complete theoretical treatment. `V-SHARE` combines cross-action value sharing with an importance-weighted Bellman-residual correction, and the authors provide **both asymptotic convergence and non-asymptotic finite-sample guarantees**, identifying a regime where it mitigates the rare-action bottleneck of asynchronous Q-learning and exposing a contraction-variance tradeoff between stronger contraction and importance-weighting noise. Motivated by that tradeoff they propose decreasing residual-preconditioning schedules and a two-timescale analysis that drops the single-timescale residual-weight threshold while keeping convergence, with experiments on discrete Markov decision processes and deep reinforcement learning benchmarks reported as corroborating the theory.

papers.title: Incentivizing Tool-Use Reinforcement Learning for Post-Arrival Emergency Care Prediction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reason over both structured measurements and free-text records, which makes them attractive for emergency department (ED) prediction. However, most existing LLMs still fall short of conventional ML methods like trees on EHR-based prediction tasks. Our controlled analysis traces this gap to two weaknesses: LLMs do not select informative features, and they misjudge what numerical values imply for risk even when given the right features. We propose TIR-EC, a tool-integrated reinforcement learning framework that addresses both. TIR-EC exposes EHR feature groups as tools the LLM can call. It trains the LLM with rewards from a gradient-boosted tree teacher, which provides a reference set of informative tools and a graded risk target. TIR-EC also distills task-specific clinical skills into the model weights through a reverse curriculum that gradually removes the skills from the prompt during RL process. Evaluation on three clinical prediction tasks shows that our 4B agent achieves the highest macro F1 of all compared models, outperforms conventional ML baselines, and is competitive with much larger frontier LLMs. Further analysis shows that TIR-EC selects more useful evidence with fewer tool calls and combines measurements more effectively.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can read both structured measurements and free-text records, yet they still trail gradient-boosted trees on electronic health record (EHR) prediction, and a controlled analysis attributes the gap to poor feature selection and misjudging what numerical values imply for risk. `TIR-EC` exposes EHR feature groups as tools the model can call and trains it with reinforcement learning using rewards from a gradient-boosted tree teacher, which supplies a reference set of informative tools and a graded risk target, while a reverse curriculum gradually removes distilled clinical skills from the prompt so they end up in the weights. On three emergency department prediction tasks the resulting **4B agent achieves the highest macro F1 of all compared models**, beating conventional ML baselines and rivaling much larger frontier LLMs while selecting more useful evidence with fewer tool calls.

papers.title: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.
papers.summary: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are slow to query, and executing an entire predicted action chunk before replanning cuts inference from 195 to 42 ms per waypoint, but it pushes the policy into states that expert demonstrations never cover and never teach it when to stop, so on `OpenFly` test-seen no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. `X-Fly` is a staged training framework: Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state, then `Flow-GRPO` jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, **`X-Fly` reaches 74.18% success rate on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen**, versus 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for `DreamFly`.

papers.title: Full-Duplex Interaction with Speech, Expressions and Gestures
papers.abstract: Human face-to-face conversation requires coordinating speech, gestures and expressions across both speaking and listening. We present ELLSA 2, an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation. An autoregressive, chunk-wise synthesizer combines pretrained acoustic features with distinct listening and speaking hidden states from the dialogue backbone and speech synthesizer, enabling continuous non-verbal generation even when the model is verbally silent. To translate dialogue understanding into vivid semantic gestures, we introduce contextual semantic calls and template guidance, separating whether to invoke an available semantic gesture from how to realize it. We also establish a curated data and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation and investigate reference-based multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as automatic judges. Experiments show that ELLSA 2 remains highly competitive with open-source full-duplex speech interaction models and outperforms cascaded baselines across dialog-aware gesture and expression metrics. Semantic template guidance further significantly improves semantic gesture quality. Strong system-level correlations with human judgments support these reference-based scores as useful preliminary metrics for full-duplex and semantic gesture assessment. Together, these results advance dialogue modeling from spoken responses toward coordinated multimodal interaction.
papers.summary: Face-to-face conversation means coordinating speech, gestures and facial expressions while both speaking and listening, and most dialogue models handle only the spoken part. `ELLSA 2` is an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that trains speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation together. A chunk-wise autoregressive synthesizer draws on separate listening and speaking hidden states, so it keeps producing non-verbal behavior even while the model is silent. Contextual semantic calls and template guidance separate the choice of whether to use a meaningful gesture from how to perform it. The model stays competitive with open-source full-duplex speech systems and **outperforms cascaded baselines on dialog-aware gesture and expression metrics**, and judges built on reference-based multimodal large language models (MLLMs) correlate strongly with human ratings.

papers.title: Translation Circuit Discovery and Targeted Optimization for Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
papers.abstract: Recent multilingual large language models achieve strong translation performance, yet the internal mechanisms responsible for low-resource multilingual translation remain insufficiently understood. In this paper, we study translation circuits in multilingual decoder-only LLMs for Hindi-to-Urdu and Hindi-to-Sindhi (Devanagari). We propose TITAN, a mechanistic framework that combines causal intervention, sparse feature decomposition, and targeted preference optimization to identify and optimize crucial translation components in the transformer. Unlike conventional full-parameter fine-tuning, TITAN restricts optimization to sparse, causally important circuits, enabling scalable and parameter-efficient adaptation while updating fewer than 5% of model parameters. Experimental results show that TITAN achieves BLEU improvements of 33.75% on Hindi-to-Urdu and 45.86% on Hindi-to-Sindhi over the strongest multilingual baselines. Human expert evaluation further confirms substantial gains in adequacy and fluency across both language pairs. Additional analyses reveal that multilingual translation is implemented through sparse, structured circuits operating over a shared semantic subspace rather than through an English-centric pivot representation. Overall, our findings demonstrate that mechanistic circuit discovery can directly improve low-resource multilingual translation while providing interpretable insights into multilingual transformer behavior.
papers.summary: `TITAN` looks for the internal circuits that multilingual decoder-only LLMs use to translate between low-resource language pairs, here Hindi-to-Urdu and Hindi-to-Sindhi (Devanagari). It combines causal intervention and sparse feature decomposition to find the causally important components, then applies targeted preference optimization only to those circuits, updating fewer than 5% of the parameters. BLEU scores rise by **33.75% on Hindi-to-Urdu and 45.86% on Hindi-to-Sindhi** over the strongest multilingual baselines, and human experts confirm better adequacy and fluency. The analysis also suggests that translation runs through sparse circuits over a shared semantic subspace rather than pivoting through English.

papers.title: Can Visual Generation Expand What Unified Multimodal Models Know?
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) receive image-generation supervision that exposes them to visual information not fully documented in text. Can learning to generate images expand what pretrained models know? We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), a controlled protocol that supplies new knowledge through image-generation training and tests its accessibility through text-only question answering. Across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs, we observe direct but uneven transfer from visual supervision to language. Motivated by these observations, we successively introduce Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image--Text Alignment, which connect generation and answering through shared knowledge and interleaved responses, respectively. Guidance on selected entities can improve knowledge access on other entities without QA supervision, with additional gains from interleaved alignment. Further analysis shows that knowledge correctly reproduced in images is often more accessible through text, although substantial gaps remain between the two forms of access. These findings support visual generation as a source of knowledge beyond textual supervision, and motivate joint investigation of training data design and model architecture to make this knowledge more broadly accessible.
papers.summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) are trained to generate images, which exposes them to visual information that text may not fully describe. The question is whether that training adds knowledge the model can then use in language. `Knowledge Transfer Probing` (`KTP`) teaches new knowledge only through image-generation training and then tests it with text-only question answering, across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs. Knowledge does transfer **directly but unevenly** from visual supervision to text. Two techniques, `Textual Alignment` and `Interleaved Image-Text Alignment`, improve access to the knowledge, including for entities that received no question-answering supervision, though large gaps remain between what models can draw and what they can say.

papers.title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $\tau^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.
papers.summary: Tool-using LLM agents usually have one strong model generate every step, even though many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. In `SpecAgent`, a weak model drafts a run of steps and executes the read-only tool calls along the way, then stops before the first action that would change the environment. The strong model checks the whole drafted segment in a single parallel prefill pass, keeps the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. On `τ²-Bench` it comes **within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time**. It recovers 44-75% of the weak-strong quality gap on `AutomationBench` and `VitaBench`, and in an edge-cloud deployment on `MCP-Atlas` it closes 53-75% of the gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens.

papers.title: Ontology Refinement with Embeddings and LLMs: A Case Study on CASTON
papers.abstract: Ontologies are widely used to represent and organize complex knowledge in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare. However, constructing reliable ontologies remains challenging, as class hierarchies, whether manually or automatically constructed, may contain subtle subsumption errors that require careful refinement. We study this problem in CASTON, a casting-domain ontology, and present a lightweight but scalable refinement workflow that combines a fine-tuned ontology embedding model with Large Language Models (LLMs). The embedding model is used to extract a limited number of candidate axioms for refinement together with possible replacement candidates, and an LLM then returns repair suggestions. In a small expert evaluation, the default configuration using a CASTON-fine-tuned OnT embedding model and Qwen3-8B produced reliable high-confidence repairs: all six high-confidence replacements were accepted by both domain experts. The implementation is available at https://github.com/HuiYang1997/OntRefine.
papers.summary: Ontology class hierarchies, whether built by hand or automatically, can contain subtle subsumption errors (wrong "is-a" relationships) that need refinement. A lightweight workflow, tested on `CASTON`, an ontology for the metal-casting domain, uses a fine-tuned `OnT` ontology embedding model to pick a small set of suspect axioms and possible replacements, and an LLM then suggests repairs. In a small expert evaluation of the default setup with `Qwen3-8B`, **all six high-confidence replacements were accepted by both domain experts**.

papers.title: DuET: Note-Frame Dual Encoding for Piano Performance-to-Score Transcription
papers.abstract: Transcribing expressive piano performances into scores requires interpreting individual note timings within an underlying metrical structure. However, score attributes are associated with notes, whereas beats may occur without coincident note onsets. We introduce DuET, a Dual-Encoder Transformer that jointly learns note-level performance MIDI-to-score (PM2S) transcription and frame-level beat and downbeat tracking. Bidirectional cross-attention connects note and frame encoders, while an autoregressive decoder alternates between their representations to predict structured score attributes. We further introduce TimeRoPE and Time-Pitch Rotary Positional Encoding (TPRoPE) to establish a shared performance-time reference and explicitly encode relative temporal and pitch relationships. Evaluations on ASAP, a classical piano dataset, and our curated Gangqinpu dataset, which spans multiple genres with a focus on popular piano music, demonstrate improvements in score timing and notated duration. Compared with the strongest baseline on each dataset, DuET reduces MUSTER mean error from 6.56% to 3.64% on Gangqinpu and from 11.30% to 11.22% on ASAP. Ablations support the benefits of frame-level context, time-based positional encoding, and decoder-history masking. Code, weights, and demos are available at https://github.com/wei-zeng98/DuET.
papers.summary: Turning an expressive piano performance into a written score means reading individual note timings against an underlying meter, even though beats do not always line up with note onsets. `DuET`, a dual-encoder Transformer, jointly learns note-level performance-MIDI-to-score (PM2S) transcription and frame-level beat and downbeat tracking. Bidirectional cross-attention links the two encoders, and new positional encodings (`TimeRoPE` and `TPRoPE`) explicitly encode relative time and pitch. On the classical `ASAP` dataset and a new multi-genre `Gangqinpu` dataset, it improves score timing and note durations, cutting `MUSTER` mean error **from 6.56% to 3.64% on Gangqinpu**, with only a marginal gain on ASAP (11.30% to 11.22%).

papers.title: Can LLMs Tell Stories Out of Order? A Corpus and Benchmark for Nonlinear Narrative Generation
papers.abstract: Every story has two orders: the order in which its events happen and the order in which they are told. A story is nonlinear when the two differ. We introduce a benchmark of 83 published works that measures whether language models can tell nonlinear stories. For each work, we annotate one list of events in both orders, together with a story graph of causal dependencies, character knowledge, and the questions the telling raises and resolves. Given events in chronological order, all 19 models tell them, on average, more chronologically than the published works do; asked for a specific structure, they land within the human range about half the time. We then compare a model's stories of the same events under different conditions, using both an automated judge and 71 human readers. Both prefer the chronological story a model writes by default to the nonlinear one it writes on request, which readers find harder to follow in 81% of decisive judgments. Readers also prefer stories written from the story graph to stories constrained to the published telling order (72% of decisive judgments), a difference the judge does not detect. Our results suggest that following an instruction to reorder a story is not yet the same as telling it well out of order.
papers.summary: A story is nonlinear when the order in which events are told differs from the order in which they happen. A benchmark of 83 published works tests whether language models can tell stories this way, with each work annotated with its events in both orders and a story graph of causal dependencies, character knowledge, and the questions the narrative raises and resolves. All 19 models tested tell events more chronologically than the published works do, and when asked for a specific structure they fall within the human range only about half the time. In a study with 71 human readers, people found models' requested nonlinear stories **harder to follow than their default chronological ones in 81% of decisive judgments**. Readers also preferred stories written from the story graph, a difference the automated judge missed.

papers.title: Tool-Augmented Large Language Models for Reliable Medical Calculation from Patient Notes
papers.abstract: Medical calculators translate raw patient observations into clinically actionable values and scores. However, applying these calculators directly to free-form patient notes requires precise variable extraction combined with the exact execution of complex formulas, scoring rules, and output conventions. Relying solely on direct large language model (LLM) prompting is unreliable in this context, as rule recall, parameter extraction, arithmetic reasoning, and formatting become entangled within a single generative step. To address these limitations, we propose a tool-augmented LLM framework for reliable medical calculation from patient notes. The framework retrieves and structures calculator specifications, generates reusable executable tools, and uses a constrained extractor to map each patient note to calculator-ready inputs. The tools then perform deterministic calculation, separating clinical language understanding from rule execution and arithmetic. Evaluated on the MedCalc-Bench dataset, our method achieves 86.73% final-answer accuracy, outperforming the one-shot prompting and supervised fine tuning-only baselines by 24.0 and 17.27 percentage points. Ablation and error analyses show that these performance gains are primarily driven by rule-grounded tool synthesis and schema-constrained extraction, whereas remaining failures are concentrated in clinical-semantic extraction and benchmark-specific output contracts. By grounding calculator logic in executable tools, the proposed approach alleviates arithmetic hallucinations and improves the computational reliability of the final clinical outputs.
papers.summary: Applying medical calculators to free-form patient notes requires extracting the right variables and executing formulas exactly, and plain LLM prompting tangles rule recall, extraction, arithmetic and formatting into one unreliable step. A tool-augmented framework separates these tasks. It retrieves calculator specifications, generates reusable executable tools from them, and uses a schema-constrained extractor to map each note to tool inputs, leaving the calculation to deterministic code. On `MedCalc-Bench` it reaches **86.73% final-answer accuracy**, 24.0 and 17.27 percentage points above one-shot prompting and fine-tuning-only baselines. Ablations credit the gains mainly to rule-grounded tool synthesis and constrained extraction.

papers.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: Curse of Dimensionality and Structural Bias
papers.abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) have a dimension-independent approximation exponent when the target admits a sufficiently smooth representation by univariate edge functions. We ask whether this favorable scaling belongs to the architecture or to the assumed target class. For arbitrary-depth standard spline-KANs, we prove a worst-case lower bound on isotropic Sobolev balls: below a dimension-independent accuracy threshold, the required number of spline coefficients grows at least exponentially with input dimension. Existing composition-matched MLP results, by contrast, show that favorable exponents on low-arity targets are not exclusive to KANs. We also revisit empirical comparisons. On four scaling-law targets, spline-KAN approximants constructed from known decompositions transfer exactly to MLPs with the cubic ReLU activation $\sigma(x)=(\max\{0,x\})^3$, although their full dense parameter counts are larger. In controlled ridge-profile scans, KANs have a strong advantage when each nonlinear component depends on one input coordinate. When a component couples multiple input coordinates, this advantage may narrow sharply. At tight budgets, interacting targets often favor MLPs. In the random-label test on MNIST, ReLU-MLPs fit the randomized training labels more efficiently than spline-only KANs. Together, these results locate favorable scaling in target structure and a compatible inductive bias, not a general KAN-specific escape from the curse of dimensionality.
papers.summary: Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) are known to scale well regardless of input dimension when the target function decomposes into smooth one-variable pieces. The authors ask whether that advantage comes from the architecture or from the assumed class of targets. They prove that for spline-KANs of any depth, on general Sobolev targets, **the number of spline coefficients needed grows at least exponentially with input dimension** below a certain accuracy. Empirically, KAN solutions on standard scaling-law targets transfer exactly to MLPs with a cubic ReLU activation, and KANs keep a strong advantage only when each nonlinear component depends on a single input coordinate. When components couple multiple inputs, MLPs are often better at tight parameter budgets, and ReLU-MLPs fit random labels on `MNIST` more efficiently.

papers.title: AI-Driven Disaster Response and Displacement Monitoring
papers.abstract: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) has demonstrated its potential across a wide range of humanitarian tasks, offering scalable and data-driven solutions to some of the world's most pressing challenges. For instance, in addressing climate change, AI-powered models are being used for faster and more accurate global weather forecasting, control and design of renewable energy, and monitoring deforestation. Machine learning algorithms analyze satellite imagery and socioeconomic data to predict poverty and promote sustainable development. AI has also transformed disaster response and conflict monitoring, providing innovative solutions for assessing damage and urgent needs and tracking displacement.
papers.summary: The abstract gives an overview of humanitarian uses of AI, focusing on disaster response and displacement monitoring. It points to examples such as AI-based weather forecasting, renewable energy design and deforestation monitoring for climate change, and machine learning on satellite imagery and socioeconomic data to predict poverty. It also describes **AI for assessing damage and urgent needs and for tracking displacement** after disasters and conflicts.

papers.title: FlashAttention with Statistics: Low-Overhead Attention Features for Compact Hallucination Detectors
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent answers that the supplied context does not support. A compact frozen proxy model can detect such answers by reading the context and another model's response, even from a proprietary generator. Attention-based detectors use summary statistics of the proxy's attention weights, but standard pipelines materialize the attention matrix, whose memory grows quadratically with sequence length. We compute these statistics without materializing attention, by accumulation in the FlashAttention pass, sparse lookups after it, or a second tiled pass over the scores, and classify them by this path into nearly free and costlier ones. On an H100, the statistics of five published detectors add 16% to the latency of a Qwen3-8B forward at 2K tokens, falling to 1.4% at 35K, and store 22.5 KiB per response token. On three benchmarks, probes trained on frozen Qwen3 proxies of 0.6B to 8B parameters prove strong detectors: a 4B proxy outperforms the strongest of nine zero-shot 4-9B LLM judges in F1 on two of the three, the proxies match or outperform specialized grounding checkers of up to 7B parameters, probing each proxy beats prompting it as a judge, and adding attention features significantly improves F1 in half of the 12 benchmark-proxy pairs, never significantly lowering it.
papers.summary: A small frozen proxy model can detect hallucinated answers, meaning answers the supplied context does not support, even when another model (possibly a proprietary one) wrote them. Detectors that use attention statistics normally build the full attention matrix, whose memory grows quadratically with sequence length. Here the statistics are computed without building it, either by accumulating them inside the `FlashAttention` pass, through sparse lookups afterward, or through a second tiled pass. On an H100, the statistics for five published detectors add 16% latency to a `Qwen3-8B` forward pass at 2K tokens and only 1.4% at 35K. Probes on frozen `Qwen3` proxies of 0.6B to 8B parameters work well as detectors: **a 4B proxy beats the strongest of nine 4-9B zero-shot LLM judges in F1 on two of three benchmarks**, and attention features never significantly lower F1.

papers.title: MetaExp: Learning to Self-Improve through Experience via Verifiable Cross-Task Environment Scaling
papers.abstract: Language-model agents can accumulate interaction feedback, but reliably turning that feedback into reusable experience remains challenging. Existing methods either optimize external experience scaffolds or train experience-related behavior on specific task distributions, leaving open whether experience learning itself can become a transferable model capability. Training such a capability calls for supervision beyond isolated tasks, which mainly support in-episode problem solving rather than revealing what knowledge remains useful across episodes. In this work, we introduce MetaExp, a scalable framework that trains this capability through verifiable task families with controlled cross-task structure. Each family preserves a reusable factor while varying task-specific realizations, enabling transfer without direct solution reuse. We propose two complementary designs: Shared-Tool families keep black-box tools fixed across tasks to elicit operational experience, while Shared-Workflow families preserve latent procedures across changing realizations to elicit procedural experience. We scale environments under both designs, collect and filter sequential interaction trajectories, and fine-tune Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 4,956 trajectories from 1,000 task families. With parameters frozen during downstream evolution, MetaExp improves by +8.5 points on SpreadsheetBench, peaks at +2.3 on APEX-Agents, and improves by +14.8 on AutomationBench. The gains persist under domain-excluded training, supporting experience learning as a transferable capability for continued non-parametric improvement after deployment.
papers.summary: LLM agents collect feedback from their interactions, but turning it into experience they can reuse later is hard, and existing methods either depend on external scaffolds or train on narrow task distributions. `MetaExp` trains experience learning as a general capability using verifiable task families that share a reusable element across tasks. `Shared-Tool` families keep black-box tools fixed so the agent learns how they behave, and `Shared-Workflow` families keep a hidden procedure constant across variations. After fine-tuning `Qwen3.5-122B-A10B` on 4,956 trajectories from 1,000 families, the model keeps improving from experience after deployment with its parameters frozen, gaining **+14.8 points on `AutomationBench`**, +8.5 on `SpreadsheetBench`, and up to +2.3 on `APEX-Agents`. The gains hold even when the evaluation domains are excluded from training.

papers.title: Phase Kernel Lifts Capacity of Dense Associative Memory
papers.abstract: Dense associative memory underlies modern attention mechanisms; however, Modern Hopfield Networks (MHNs) with linear kernels yield overlapping attractor basins and spurious states under high memory load, limiting their theoretically exponential storage capacity in practice. We construct a class of nonlinear phase kernels that modify the energy landscape and retrieval dynamics, and prove that these kernels preserve exponential storage capacity and local fixed-point convergence under given conditions on kernel smoothness, memory separation, and memory distributions.
