The framework is instantiated by the Sigmoidal Phase Hopfield Network (S-Hop), which guarantees monotone energy descent and mitigates practical capacity loss. S-Hop has $8.3\times$ and $4\times$ gains in one-step noisy retrieval load over Uniform Hopfield Networks (U-Hop) on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet respectively, and reaches a $50\times$ gain in first-failure load for ImageNet. The results demonstrate that phase kernels provide a principled route to robust dense associative memory.
papers.summary: Modern Hopfield networks, the dense associative memories behind attention mechanisms, have exponential storage capacity in theory, but with linear kernels their attractor basins overlap and spurious states appear under heavy memory load. The authors construct a class of nonlinear phase kernels and prove that, under conditions on smoothness and memory separation, they keep exponential capacity and local convergence to fixed points. The `Sigmoidal Phase Hopfield Network` (`S-Hop`) instantiates the framework and guarantees that energy decreases monotonically. It handles 8.3x and 4x the one-step noisy retrieval load of the uniform `U-Hop` baseline on `CIFAR-10` and `TinyImageNet`, and **50x the load before first failure on `ImageNet`**.

papers.title: OPRD: On-Policy Reminder Distillation for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Reliable repository-level coding requires agents not only to generate correct code but also to preserve constraints and respond to tool feedback across long interactions. However, our diagnostic analysis shows that agents often fail to act on relevant information already available in context, while final Pass/Fail outcomes provide only sparse process supervision. We introduce On-Policy Reminder Distillation (OPRD), which combines Multi-Scope Reminder supervision with outcome-based routing on reminder-free student rollouts. Successful rollouts provide autoregressive self-imitation targets, whereas failed rollouts receive Reminder-conditioned reverse-KL supervision from a teacher that re-evaluates the same student-generated prefixes. A Global Reminder converts final-test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance, while Turn-local Reminders apply only to the next decision following the relevant environment observation. The teacher and student share a two-stage initialization from Coding SFT and Instruction-Following (IF) SFT. At inference, the student operates without Reminders. On SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Multilingual, OPRD improves the benchmark-averaged task resolution rate by 11.3 points over the open-source Qwen3.5-4B base model. Under the same diagnostic protocol, it reduces the aggregate error-event count from 446 to 222, a 50.2% reduction.
papers.summary: Coding agents working on whole repositories often ignore relevant information already in their context, and final pass/fail results give little supervision over the process. `On-Policy Reminder Distillation` (`OPRD`) trains on the student's own rollouts, which run without reminders. Successful rollouts become self-imitation targets, while failed ones get reverse-KL supervision from a teacher that re-scores the same steps with reminders added. These reminders are either a global one built from final-test diagnostics or turn-local ones tied to specific tool observations, and the student runs without any reminders at inference. Across `SWE-bench Verified`, `SWE-bench Pro` and `SWE-bench Multilingual`, OPRD raises the average resolution rate by **11.3 points over the `Qwen3.5-4B` base model** and cuts diagnosed error events by 50.2%.

papers.title: When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill
papers.abstract: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.
papers.summary: Long-context LLM serving reuses the attention KV cache across requests, often through a remote tier shared by all engines. A production study of `GLM-5.3`, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model, on 8xB300 nodes with prefill context parallelism found that enabling `LMCache` with a `Valkey` store raised 16k-token p99 time-to-first-token from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. A remote hit took longer than recomputing the prompt, and synchronous loading made the request queue unstable. A two-term cost model explains this: a hit only pays off above a bandwidth threshold, and a fixed per-hit cost means prompts under about 17k tokens can never beat recompute. Guided by the model, the authors shard the KV store across ranks, partition the remote tier per rank, add asynchronous loading and fix three client bugs, which **drops p99 from 83.32 s to 0.67 s** on a hit-heavy stream. All changes have been submitted upstream to LMCache.

papers.title: ISW-Agent: Integrating LLM-Driven Dialogue with n8n Workflow for Internal Solitary Wave Remote Sensing Image Processing
papers.abstract: Internal solitary wave (ISW) remote sensing requires task parameters and spatial information to be transferred across image acquisition, detection, stripe extraction, and propagation prediction. Here, we present ISW-Agent, which integrates large language model (LLM) interpretation with n8n workflows and independent scientific models through structured task constraints, geospatial transformations, and stage-specific output validation. In tests of 120 Chinese instructions per backend, GPT-5.6 Sol and DeepSeek both achieved a strict task-match rate of 94.2%, with all intents and execution decisions matching the reference. Sentinel-1 cases demonstrated continuous processing from dialogue requests to wavefront prediction for the specified scene. Of 50 timed scenes, 39 completed detection, extraction, and prediction with a median turnaround time of 48.04 s; 11 stopped after empty extraction. Across 3,408 controlled fault-injection runs, retries recovered 234 transient-failure conditions and output validation rejected 234 structural defects, while 61 provenance or completeness errors indicated the need for content-consistency checks. Overall, ISW-Agent thus connects natural-language requests to traceable spatial processing chains for multimodel ISW analysis.
papers.summary: `ISW-Agent` connects natural-language requests to a multi-stage pipeline for internal solitary wave (ISW) remote sensing, covering image acquisition, detection, stripe extraction and propagation prediction. It combines LLM interpretation with `n8n` workflows and separate scientific models through structured task constraints, geospatial transformations and validation of each stage's output. On 120 Chinese instructions, both `GPT-5.6 Sol` and `DeepSeek` reach **94.2% strict task-match rates**. Of 50 timed Sentinel-1 scenes, 39 ran end to end with a median turnaround of 48.04 s, and fault-injection tests show that retries and output validation catch many failures but not every provenance error.

papers.title: Decomposing Brain-LLM Alignment with Interpretable Semantic Representations
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) predict neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension, but the linguistic information underlying this brain alignment remains difficult to interpret. We use SCRIBE, an interpretable contextual semantic representation spanning 65 neurocognitively grounded semantic properties, as a lens for decomposing the brain alignment of one LLM, LLaMA2-7B. Using variance partitioning between LLaMA2-7B and SCRIBE on naturalistic fMRI data from seven participants listening to narrative stories (Moth Radio Hour), we separate brain-predictive variance shared between the two representations from variance unique to each. We find that shared variance is the dominant component across the whole brain and language-related regions, while both representations also retain significant unique contributions. We then examine whether the concreteness of individual semantic properties relates to shared and SCRIBE-unique brain-predictive variance. Concrete properties show greater shared variance with LLaMA2-7B than abstract properties across the whole brain and most examined regions, whereas abstract properties do not show greater SCRIBE-unique variance. Finally, property ablations reveal that semantic contributions extend across multiple dimensions, with cumulative effects on both shared and SCRIBE-unique variance. Together, these results show that, for LLaMA2-7B on this dataset, a substantial portion of brain-LLM alignment is associated with interpretable semantic information, while revealing complementary brain-predictive semantic information beyond the LLaMA2-7B representation.
papers.summary: LLMs can predict brain activity during natural language comprehension, but it is unclear which linguistic information drives this alignment. The authors use `SCRIBE`, an interpretable representation covering 65 semantic properties grounded in neuroscience, and run variance partitioning against `LLaMA2-7B` on fMRI data from seven people listening to `Moth Radio Hour` stories. **Variance shared between the two representations is the dominant component** across the whole brain and language regions, though each also explains some unique variance. Concrete semantic properties overlap more with the LLM than abstract ones, and ablations show that semantic contributions are spread across many dimensions.

papers.title: QREF: Improving DeepSearch Agents by Aligning Search with Reasoning via Query Refinement and Evidence Filtering
papers.abstract: DeepSearch agents achieve strong performance on complex information-seeking tasks through iterative search and reasoning. However, they often issue intent-misaligned, under-constrained, or redundant search queries, resulting in poor evidence coverage and accumulating retrieval noise. To mitigate these limitations, we propose QREF, a plug-and-play Query Refiner and Evidence Filter. Specifically, the Query Refiner rewrites search queries according to the current reasoning intent while ensuring complementary coverage across each search batch. The Evidence Filter retains evidence relevant to both the current search batch and the reasoning objective, reducing distracting retrieval results. We initialize the Query Refiner with supervised fine-tuning and optimize it through reinforcement learning based on interactions with a real-world web search environment, reducing ineffective queries. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach improves the performance of DeepSearch agents across four challenging benchmarks, achieving average relative Pass@1 improvements of 33.55% on WebSailor and 11.04% on TongyiDeepResearch without modifying architectures or retraining their reasoning policies. Compared with the original DeepSearch backbone without QREF, the RL-trained refiner reduces the fraction of query batches that lack discriminative retrieval anchors by 95%. Compared with the SFT-trained refiner, it also lowers the filter-based ineffective query ratio.
papers.summary: DeepSearch agents answer complex questions through repeated rounds of search and reasoning, but they often issue queries that are off-intent, under-constrained or redundant, which piles up retrieval noise. `QREF` is a plug-in that pairs a Query Refiner, which rewrites queries to match the current reasoning goal and to cover complementary ground across a batch, with an Evidence Filter that drops irrelevant results. The refiner starts from supervised fine-tuning and is then trained with reinforcement learning against a real web search environment. Without changing or retraining the agents, QREF delivers **average relative Pass@1 gains of 33.55% for `WebSailor`** and 11.04% for `TongyiDeepResearch` across four benchmarks, and cuts query batches lacking discriminative retrieval anchors by 95%.

papers.title: Poison Valleys: Diagnosing Path-Dependent Failure in LLM Code Repair
papers.abstract: When code-repair agents fail, final tests reveal that a patch is wrong but not which earlier commitment caused it or which software obligation failed. Poison Valleys traces this path in 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases: PersistQueue adds atomic batch claiming to a disk-backed queue, while Dijkstra adds source-sensitive filtering to shortest-path search. We define plausible but incorrect software mechanisms, place each in a model's hypothesis, implementation plan, or both, and evaluate the generated code with an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates. Moving the misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failure by 32.2% in PersistQueue and 28.9% in Dijkstra after matching the experimental mix. Different misconceptions produced distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated obligations, although several could converge on the same behavior. This creates a measured connection from upstream misconception to code mechanism and failure form. Code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org.
papers.summary: When a code-repair agent fails, the tests show that the patch is wrong but not which earlier decision caused it or which requirement it broke. `Poison Valleys` traces this across 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python tasks: atomic batch claiming in a disk-backed queue, and source-sensitive filtering in Dijkstra's shortest-path search. Plausible but incorrect mechanisms are planted in the model's hypothesis, its implementation plan or both, and the resulting code is checked with an oracle and targeted diagnostics. **Moving the misconception from the hypothesis to the plan increased failure by 32.2% and 28.9%** on the two tasks, and different misconceptions broke different requirements in ways that varied by model.

papers.title: SCRIBE: Scalable Contextual Representations of Interpretable Brain-Grounded Semantics
papers.abstract: Understanding how the human brain constructs meaning from real-world language remains a fundamental challenge, as semantics depend on context that varies in natural settings. To enable the study of real-world linguistic meaning in the brain, we introduce SCRIBE, a framework grounded in a neuroscience-informed semantic space that leverages an ensemble of open-source large language models to generate interpretable, word-level semantic representations of arbitrary text. In a behavioral study with 921 participants, we show that human semantic feature judgments vary systematically with context, and that SCRIBE captures these shifts, reaching 75-81% of the estimated human noise ceiling. Using brain activity recorded while participants listen to naturalistic stories, we further demonstrate that SCRIBE predicts neural responses in language-selective brain regions, significantly outperforming non-contextual semantic representations. Variance partitioning reveals that SCRIBE explains unique brain-predictive information beyond syntactic features, suggesting that its representations capture aspects of linguistic meaning not accounted for by the measured syntactic features. Together, these findings establish SCRIBE as a scalable and interpretable foundation for studying natural language semantics in the brain.
papers.summary: `SCRIBE` uses an ensemble of open-source LLMs to produce interpretable, word-level semantic representations of any text, grounded in a semantic space informed by neuroscience. The goal is to study how the brain builds meaning from natural language, where meaning depends on context. In a behavioral study with 921 participants, human judgments of semantic features shifted with context, and SCRIBE tracked those shifts, reaching **75-81% of the estimated human noise ceiling**. On fMRI data recorded during story listening, it predicts activity in language-selective brain regions significantly better than non-contextual semantic representations and explains variance that syntactic features do not.

papers.title: Hierarchical Interpretable Multitask Audio Representation Learning: An Analysis of Event-Scene Relationships through the Information Bottleneck
papers.abstract: Joint Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) and Audio Tagging (AT) models traditionally rely on unconstrained multihead architectures. However, this design ignores the natural hierarchical dependency between sounds and acoustic scenes. In this work, we investigate a hierarchical (sequential) conditioning paradigm that predicts scene categories directly from intermediate event probabilities. Through a large-scale empirical benchmark with 66 full training runs across three state-of-the-art backbones (PaSST, PANNs, and BEATs) and different loss-weighting settings (beta in [0.0, 1.0]), we show that hierarchical conditioning achieves competitive classification performance while altering multitask optimization dynamics. Unlike multihead baselines, which sequentially solve the easier ASC task before optimizing AT, the hierarchical architecture enables synchronized dual-task learning for specific loss-weighting settings (beta in [0.6, 0.9]). Furthermore, we propose a multi-perspective interpretability framework that combines an analysis of the information bottleneck, manifold geometry, and Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) on a Term-Frequency Inverse-Document-Frequency (TF-IDF) event representation, providing complementary insights into event-scene relationships. Our findings reveal that hierarchical conditioning systematically yields lower conditional entropy, higher mutual information, and superior latent cluster separability (higher Silhouette scores), establishing a more structured and semantically faithful intermediate feature space.
papers.summary: Models that jointly perform Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) and Audio Tagging (AT) usually put independent output heads on a shared backbone, which ignores the fact that sound events help define scenes. The authors test a hierarchical design that predicts the scene directly from intermediate event probabilities, running 66 training runs across the `PaSST`, `PANNs`, and `BEATs` backbones at different loss weightings. The hierarchical design classifies about as well as multihead baselines. It also changes how training unfolds: **at loss weights between 0.6 and 0.9 it learns both tasks in sync**, whereas multihead models solve ASC first. An interpretability analysis based on the information bottleneck, manifold geometry, and Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) finds lower conditional entropy, higher mutual information, and better-separated latent clusters under hierarchical conditioning.

papers.title: CriticaLLM: Using LLMs as Autonomous Game Master for Tabletop Role-Playing Games
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across many tasks, including processing large amounts of text, following instructions, and generating ideas. This allows the use of such models in various contexts, including games and Tabletop Role-Playing Games (TTRPGs), such as Dungeons & Dragons. However, these games include many complex components, from crafting interesting stories to adhering to rules, while allowing some freedom in players' actions. In this work, we first highlight key components that LLMs should exhibit in the context of TTRPGs. Then, we introduce our framework, CriticaLLM, a fully automated Game Master that can run entire TTRPG games, from creating diverse and interesting stories to managing exploration and combat phases. We evaluate our framework with actual TTRPG players and examine the diversity of generated plots and antagonists across four LLMs of varying sizes. Overall, our framework appears to be a promising option for running entire TTRPG games.
papers.summary: Tabletop Role-Playing Games (TTRPGs) such as Dungeons & Dragons ask a game master to tell compelling stories, enforce rules, and still give players freedom, which is hard for large language models (LLMs) to manage together. The authors first set out the capabilities an LLM game master needs, then present `CriticaLLM`, a **fully automated game master that runs entire sessions**, from story creation through exploration and combat. Real TTRPG players evaluated it, and the authors measured how diverse the generated plots and antagonists were across four LLMs of different sizes.

papers.title: Activation-Adjacent Layer Normalization: Effects on Approximation Power
papers.abstract: Layer normalization (LN) and root mean square normalization (RMSNorm) depend on their inputs and remain nonlinear at inference. Inserting either next to an activation may therefore change the function a network represents. We study when shallow activation-normalized (AN) and preactivation-normalized (PN) networks can approximate a prescribed width-$N$ one-hidden-layer MLP. Viewing RMSNorm as input-dependent scaling, we use width augmentation to locally linearize normalization on compact feature sets. For AN networks, an unbounded activation range allows width $N+1$, while every continuous nonconstant activation admits width $N+r$ with error $O_f(r^{-1})$. For PN networks, affine parameters or, without them, degree-one positive homogeneity recover width $N+1$; general continuous activations admit width $N+r$ with error tending to zero. The corresponding LN constructions use centered coordinate pairs, yielding widths $N+2$ and $N+2r$, respectively. We prove that $N+1$ for RMSNorm and $N+2$ for LN are also the worst-case bound for approximations, and show that applicable universal-approximation theorems for ordinary MLPs transfer to these normalized architectures. Numerical experiments recover the predicted approximation rates for both normalizations across all five settings and illustrate the shifted-ReLU finite-width obstruction.
papers.summary: Layer normalization (LN) and `RMSNorm` stay nonlinear at inference, so placing them next to an activation can change what functions a network can represent. Treating `RMSNorm` as input-dependent scaling, the authors prove width bounds for when shallow activation-normalized and preactivation-normalized networks can approximate a width-N one-hidden-layer MLP. In many settings width N+1 suffices for `RMSNorm` and N+2 for LN, and the authors show these are **tight worst-case bounds**; with general activations the extra width grows and the error shrinks as it does. They also show that universal-approximation theorems for ordinary MLPs carry over to the normalized architectures, and numerical experiments reproduce the predicted rates.

papers.title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.
papers.summary: Continual learning in large language models (LLMs) suffers from catastrophic forgetting, where training on new data erases earlier skills. Using gradient-attribution profiling, the authors find functional subnetworks tied to different cognitive skills that overlap very little. They then propose `CiMEO` (Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization), which routes each training example to its matching subnetwork and restricts parameter updates and optimizer state to that region. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, `CiMEO` achieves **the highest average performance among compared methods on five benchmarks** covering programming, exam-style tasks, and math while reducing forgetting. Subspace analyses indicate that the localized updates preserve pre-trained representations.

papers.title: Agent Status Protocol (ASP): A Lightweight Specification for State Reporting in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: The Agent Status Protocol (ASP) defines a lightweight way for heterogeneous AI agents to report their operational state to a status server, and for observers such as dashboards to receive that state as soon as it changes. Agents push small JSON events over HTTP POST; the server exposes the aggregated state to observers over Server-Sent Events (SSE). Because an agent that has crashed, hung or been compromised cannot be trusted to report its own failure, ASP does not rely on self-reports alone: the server infers liveness from missed heartbeats, can detect agents that are alive but no longer making progress, and accepts observations from supervisors, guardrails, operators and peers, some of which take precedence over what the agent says about itself while others are shown alongside it. ASP models state along independent dimensions (lifecycle, health, task, floor, governance), so that an agent can be, for example, online, degraded, working on a task and waiting for the floor at the same time. It reuses existing vocabularies: task states from the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, floor states from the Open Floor Protocol (OFP), and attribute conventions from the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. This paper presents version 0.1 of ASP as a proposal, not as an approved standard. It is a working draft intended to open a discussion, and the authors invite comments, alternative proposals and independent implementations from the community.
papers.summary: The `Agent Status Protocol` (`ASP`) is a draft specification for how heterogeneous AI agents report their operational state to a status server. Agents push small JSON events over HTTP POST, and dashboards receive aggregated state over Server-Sent Events (SSE). Because a crashed, hung, or compromised agent cannot be trusted to report its own failure, **the server infers liveness from missed heartbeats, detects agents that are alive but stuck**, and accepts observations from supervisors, guardrails, and peers, some of which override the agent's self-report. State is tracked along independent dimensions (lifecycle, health, task, floor, governance), reusing vocabularies from `A2A`, the Open Floor Protocol, and the `OpenTelemetry` GenAI conventions. Version 0.1 is offered as a proposal for community discussion, not an approved standard.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning-driven Diffusion Models: Language, Vision, and Beyond
papers.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have steadily demonstrated outstanding performance in high-fidelity, controllable generation across diverse scenarios, following the "pretraining-finetuning" paradigm established in LLMs. Despite these advances, conventional DMs still face critical limitations in sophisticated reasoning, autonomous exploration of generation pathways, and adaptability to complex, human-aligned objectives. Inspired by RLHF's success in LLMs, RL has recently emerged as a pivotal post-training mechanism to iteratively refine DMs through reward-driven trajectory optimization. This paper presents the first comprehensive review of RL-driven DMs and an empirical analysis of how RL reshapes the diffusion process towards experience-centric, goal-directed generation. We propose a novel technical panorama elucidating RL's multifaceted roles in diffusion-based language, multimodal, robotic, and scientific models, with a granular focus on diffusion trajectory optimization and reward engineering. Through extensive experiments on multiple task-specific benchmarks, we systematically evaluate representative methods to intuitively highlight the advantages of different RL post-training strategies. Furthermore, we reveal and dissect three crucial bottlenecks that currently hinder the real-world deployment of RL-driven DMs: reward design fragility, exploration-exploitation trade-off in high-dimensional generation spaces, and training instability under sparse rewards. Based on these perspectives, we provide a principled roadmap for the integration of RL into DMs and outline promising future research directions for robust, interpretable RL-diffusion systems. We also construct a public repository to continuously track the latest developments in this rapidly evolving field: https://github.com/MAIR-Lab-HUST/Awesome-RL-for-Diffusion-Models.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a key post-training tool for diffusion models (DMs), much as RLHF is for language models, and this survey reviews how RL is applied to diffusion-based language, multimodal, robotic, and scientific models. The review focuses on diffusion trajectory optimization and reward engineering, and the authors run experiments on task-specific benchmarks to compare representative RL post-training strategies. They identify **three bottlenecks to real-world deployment: fragile reward design, the exploration-exploitation trade-off in high-dimensional generation spaces, and training instability under sparse rewards**. The survey closes with a roadmap for future work and a public repository that tracks new papers in the area.

papers.title: Federated Art Chase: Privacy Leakage and Data Poisoning in Federated Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used to adapt a pretrained, centrally fine-tuned model to data that remain on user devices, beyond training a model from scratch. In this report, prepared for the 4th Federated Machine Learning International Summer School, we study the privacy and integrity of this approach with a reproducible pipeline. An ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV4-Conv-Small model is fine-tuned centrally on ten Quick, Draw! classes (97.50% test accuracy) and then adapted with head-only FedAvg over ten non-IID clients, which raises client training accuracy from 90.34% to 91.49% while preserving global accuracy. We evaluate four adversarial scenarios. First, from a single one-step client update, an honest-but-curious server recovers the complete private label set, but its reconstructions follow class prototypes rather than the private drawings (mean SSIM 0.130). Second, from a one-round FedAvg aggregate, label-count recovery falls from 87.5% with one client to 75.0% with five and ten clients, below the 80.0% of an uninformed uniform guess. Third, under FedAvg, a backdoor injected by 30%, 50%, and 100% of the clients reaches an attack success rate (ASR) of 21.9%, 31.3%, and 54.7% at a cost of at most 0.8 percentage points of clean accuracy, whereas label flipping is effective only when most of the source-class data are relabeled. Fourth, FLTrust with a root set retained from centralized fine-tuning lowers the backdoor ASR to 1.8% and 4.0% at 30% and 50% malicious clients and the label-flipping ASR from 12.6% to 0.8% without measurable clean-accuracy loss, but provides no protection when every client is malicious. The report closes with a live session in which participants draw, fine-tune, and poison the model through Indigma's FedMaestro orchestrator. Code and executed notebooks, runnable on Google Colab, are at https://github.com/Indigma-Innovations/fl-summer-school.
papers.summary: Written as a summer-school report, this reproducible pipeline studies privacy and integrity risks when federated learning (FL) adapts a centrally fine-tuned `MobileNetV4-Conv-Small` on `Quick, Draw!` classes using head-only `FedAvg` across ten non-IID clients. A curious server can recover a client's full label set from a single update, but its image reconstructions resemble class prototypes rather than the private drawings. Label-count recovery from aggregated updates falls below a uniform guess once five or more clients participate. Backdoors reach up to 54.7% attack success at almost no cost to clean accuracy, while **`FLTrust` cuts backdoor success to 1.8–4.0%** at 30–50% malicious clients but offers no protection when every client is malicious. Code and executed Colab notebooks accompany the report.

papers.title: Finite-Time Guarantees for Constrained Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: We study reinforcement learning in constrained partially observable Markov decision processes (CPOMDPs), where an agent maximizes reward subject to a cost constraint using only incomplete information about the underlying state. The lack of state observability may require optimal policies to depend on arbitrarily long observation-action histories, making planning and learning challenging. We leverage recent advances in finite-memory approximations of POMDPs and represent finite history windows as states of a constrained MDP. We then develop a primal--dual algorithm that provides the first non-asymptotic guarantees that jointly bound average reward suboptimality and constraint violation in the original CPOMDP. A key challenge is that this finite-window approximation affects both reward values and the set of feasible policies. Under a filter-stability assumption, we derive bounds relating optimality and feasibility in the finite-state model to those in the original CPOMDP, with approximation errors that decay geometrically with the window length. Experiments in partially observable gridworlds demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
papers.summary: In constrained partially observable Markov decision processes (CPOMDPs), an agent must maximize reward under a cost constraint while seeing only part of the underlying state, so optimal policies may depend on arbitrarily long histories. The authors treat finite windows of recent observations and actions as states of a constrained MDP and solve it with a primal-dual algorithm. This yields **the first non-asymptotic guarantees that jointly bound reward suboptimality and constraint violation** in the original problem. Under a filter-stability assumption, the approximation error shrinks geometrically with window length, and experiments in partially observable gridworlds support the approach.

papers.title: When Is Muon Optimal? Radial Fragility and Minimax Geometry
papers.abstract: Muon replaces a matrix gradient by an approximate polar factor and has shown strong empirical performance in neural-network training. The Isotropic Curvature Model (ICM) provides a curvature-based explanation for this update by asking when gradient orthogonalization minimizes a one-step local-loss surrogate. We investigate the stability of this explanation when the fixed input radius of the ICM is replaced by a general radial law. We introduce the Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model (RR-ICM) and the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set, which encodes exact scaled-polar optimality as a geometric condition on the positive polar factor of the gradient. We derive an exact characterization of this set for arbitrary radial laws and show that all nonscalar admissible responses arise from radial atoms aligned with curvature kinks. Consequently, every atomless radial law exhibits zero-capacity rigidity: exact scaled-polar optimality is possible only when the gradient is already a scaled column isometry. To connect the curvature-based framework with the established spectral geometry of Muon, we introduce the Minimax RR-ICM by replacing directional averaging with worst-case optimization over probability laws on the sphere. We prove that every nonzero global minimizer lies on the polar ray of the gradient, while its scale is determined by a one-dimensional convex problem. The corresponding admissibility geometry is a positive-semidefinite trace slab, in sharp contrast to the spherical-zonoid geometry of the RR-ICM. Together, these results expose the radial fragility of average-curvature explanations and provide a new minimax variational characterization of Muon's polar direction.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer replaces a matrix gradient with its approximate polar factor, and the Isotropic Curvature Model (`ICM`) explains this as minimizing a one-step loss surrogate under a fixed input radius. The authors generalize the model to random radii (`RR-ICM`) and find the explanation is fragile: **for any atomless radial law, exact polar optimality holds only when the gradient is already a scaled column isometry**. They then introduce a minimax variant that optimizes against the worst-case direction distribution instead of averaging, and prove that every nonzero minimizer of this variant lies along the gradient's polar direction. This gives a new variational characterization of `Muon`'s update.

papers.title: Rethinking Classifier-Free Guidance for TI2I Flow Matching
papers.abstract: We study Text-and-Image-to-Image (TI2I) flow matching methods for controllable image editing. In a broader generative modeling context, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is established as a key component responsible for high quality outputs. However, we argue that its role in TI2I modeling is poorly understood. Specifically, we make the surprising observation that the CFG mechanism is implicitly harmful for editing in the noisy phase of flow modeling, hindering instruction following and controllability. We propose a simple correction in the early flow steps, enabling a richer alignment-preservation tradeoff at no extra cost. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated on both pixel-space and latent TI2I flows.
papers.summary: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is widely used to improve output quality in generative models, but its role in Text-and-Image-to-Image (TI2I) flow matching for image editing has not been well understood. The authors observe that **CFG actually hurts instruction following and controllability during the early, noisy steps of the flow**. They propose a simple correction for those early steps that improves the trade-off between following the edit and preserving the source image at no extra cost, and show it works for both pixel-space and latent TI2I flows.

papers.title: Writability and the Pathway: A Controlled Study of Knowledge Injection into Addressed Memory
papers.abstract: Addressed conditional memory provides a local surface for post-hoc knowledge injection, but a successful write need not transfer to a new question or preserve untargeted behavior. This study combines a controlled GPT-2 comparison with production-memory experiments on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Newly initialized modules attached to frozen GPT-2 are tested in a 2 x 2 design: row-only versus row-plus-projection updates, each with or without fixed module-residual anchoring. All arms reproduce 50 trained completions in each of three sampling seeds. Natural-question target-string hits average 5.3% for both row-only arms, 28.7% for unanchored projection updates, and 22.0% with anchoring, while strict answer scores remain zero. Anchoring lowers measured drift; lexical hits do not establish entity-specific retrieval. In the archived Qwen experiments, gradient writes make the designated first answer token top-ranked for 132 independently reset targets, comprising 93 new promotions and 39 already top-ranked targets. A separate matched 24-target comparison gives 13 new promotions with Adam versus two with SPSA at equal iteration counts but unequal computational procedures. An 80-row case includes saved continuations and a replay record, while reformulations bound its scope. Six DeepSeek zero-order cases yield one new target-token promotion and one regression. These results support bounded writing feasibility and separate trained expression, question-form behavior, and preservation; first-token rankings do not establish complete-answer success or universal conditions for writable memory.
papers.summary: Addressed conditional memory modules offer a local place to inject new knowledge into a language model after training, but a successful write does not guarantee the knowledge transfers to new questions or that other behavior stays intact. In a controlled `GPT-2` study, every update variant reproduced its trained completions. On natural questions, projection updates reached target-string hits of 22–29%, versus 5.3% for row-only updates, but **strict answer scores stayed at zero**; residual anchoring reduced drift. Experiments on `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8` and `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` show that gradient writes can make the target's first answer token top-ranked, and Adam outperformed the zeroth-order optimizer SPSA, though the authors caution that first-token rankings do not show complete-answer success.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification in Pairwise Difference Learning for Classification
papers.abstract: Instead of learning a mapping from instances to outcomes in the standard way, the key idea of pairwise difference learning (PDL) is to learn a function that takes two instances as input and predicts the difference between the respective outcomes. Given a function of this kind, predictions for a query instance are derived from every training example and then averaged. We propose a version of PDL for the task of classification and propose a suitable meta-learning technique for this purpose. Moreover, we address the problem of uncertainty quantification, i.e., of representing and quantifying the uncertainty of a PDL classifier's predictions in a faithful manner. Building on recent work on the decomposition of total uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, we propose different ways of extending corresponding measures to the setting of PDL, depending on how and to what extent uncertainty is represented by the underlying base learner. In large-scale empirical studies, we analyze both the predictive accuracy and the uncertainty awareness of our PDL classifier.
papers.summary: Pairwise difference learning (PDL) trains a function that predicts the difference in outcomes between two instances, then averages predictions for a query over all training examples. The authors adapt PDL to classification, add a suitable meta-learning technique, and extend recent methods that split total uncertainty into aleatoric (data noise) and epistemic (model knowledge) components to the PDL setting. **Several uncertainty measures are proposed, depending on how much uncertainty the base learner itself represents**, and large-scale empirical studies evaluate both accuracy and uncertainty awareness.

papers.title: When Does Muon Actually Win? A Paired Data-, Time-, and Tuning-Budget Benchmark
papers.abstract: Muon's gains in data efficiency motivate evaluating its performance under explicit data, time, and tuning budgets. On a single A100 GPU, we compare a reference single-device Muon implementation with AdamW across 17.7M- and 33.6M-parameter causal language models and 2.70M-parameter vision transformers. A common 23-candidate development budget selects configurations evaluated with five matched seeds, full validation trajectories, optimizer-step timing, and a frozen one-shot test. Muon reduces validation-loss area under the curve by 3.25--22.44\% at equal data and lowers test loss in all 20 primary pairs. In this configuration, Muon improves time-normalized loss area} by 19.68--22.31\% on vision, while AdamW is better by 3.38--6.96\% on language. The full Muon optimizer call, including auxiliary AdamW updates, consumes 56.1--69.6\% of training time, compared with 6.1--9.1\% for the AdamW baseline. Muon also has higher expected regret under restricted access to these candidate pools. These results characterize small models with reference kernels; their wall-clock ordering does not establish a ranking for larger models or optimized implementations.
papers.summary: This benchmark compares the `Muon` optimizer against `AdamW` on a single A100 GPU, using small causal language models (17.7M and 33.6M parameters) and vision transformers under matched data, time, and tuning budgets with five seeds each. At equal data, `Muon` reduces validation-loss area under the curve by 3.25–22.44% and lowers test loss in all 20 primary comparisons. Measured by wall-clock time, however, `Muon` wins by about 20% on vision while **`AdamW` is 3.38–6.96% better on language**, because the reference `Muon` implementation takes 56–70% of training time. The authors note that these results apply to small models with reference kernels and may not hold for larger models or optimized implementations.

papers.title: Reducing the Cost of Qudit State Preparation by Learning a Sparse Structure for SNAP Gates
papers.abstract: Preparing quantum states in bosonic qudits with SNAP--Displacement sequences requires both optimizing the gate parameters and deciding which Fock levels should be controlled by each SNAP gate. A fully parameterized ansatz assigns an independent phase to every Fock level in every gate, leading to a number of phases that grows steeply. This constitutes a problem for short to medium term systems as controlling many phases requires complex control pulses which are subject to increased control errors. Previous work reduced this cost by restricting the trainable phases to predefined sparse patterns, such as a diagonal or a grid, which however may not be optimal for a specific target state. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing a method that learns which phases are needed together with their values, using a differentiable mask. A sparsity penalty encourages the removal of unnecessary phases, while temperature annealing gradually turns the masks into binary decisions. We compare the proposed method with fully parameterized and predefined sparse ansatzes on Fourier and Haar-random target states. The evaluation considers both the minimum number of phases required to reach different infidelity thresholds and the overall trade-off between fidelity and phases required, measured through Pareto frontiers and hypervolume. The results show that learning the location of the phases together with their values provides competitive or improved fidelity--resource trade-offs, although the advantage depends on the target state and qudit dimension.
papers.summary: Preparing quantum states in bosonic qudits with SNAP–Displacement gate sequences becomes costly because a fully parameterized ansatz assigns a phase to every Fock level in every gate, and controlling many phases increases control errors. Earlier work restricted phases to fixed sparse patterns, which may not suit a given target state. The authors instead **learn which phases to keep together with their values**, using a differentiable mask with a sparsity penalty and temperature annealing. On Fourier and Haar-random target states, the learned structure matches or improves the fidelity-versus-phase-count trade-off, though the advantage depends on the target state and qudit dimension.

papers.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under the MIT license at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.
papers.summary: Conversational agents built on large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent, factually plausible replies while drifting from the process they are meant to follow, a failure the authors call procedural hallucination. They introduce `DialFork`, a benchmark of 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains, built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turns and injecting one of four hallucination types, with construction validated by 30 human annotators. Three tasks measure deviation at the level of a dialogue set, a single dialogue, and the first turn where a dialogue goes off track. Two new flow-aware metrics, `FlowKL` and `FlowScore`, compare how dialogues unfold rather than what they say, and **`FlowScore` significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders**, showing that semantic similarity does not capture procedural similarity.

papers.title: A Quantum Machine Learning Approach to Content-Based Media Recommendation
papers.abstract:
We use quantum machine learning techniques to develop a content-based media recommender system and evaluate its performance on TV programmes using textual descriptions from one week of BBC iPlayer data. Grounded in the Quantum Natural Language Processing framework (QNLP), programme synopses are mapped to variational quantum circuits using their semantic structure. The parameters of these circuits are trained via a supervised pairwise similarity learning task.
  We benchmark the quantum recommender against a classical BiLSTM baseline trained on the same dataset and objective. While both models achieve comparable performance on the similarity learning task, the quantum model requires significantly fewer parameters (47k vs. 17.8M). When the BiLSTM is constrained to a matching parameter budget, its performance degrades substantially (by 3.63 percentage points in Mean Average Precision (MAP)), indicating that the structured quantum representation provides a highly parameter-efficient alternative in this setting. We demonstrate the feasibility of executing the trained models on quantum hardware by deploying the circuits on Quantinuum's System Model H2 (and accompanying emulator) using a SWAP-test-based protocol. The results confirm that the similarity signal is preserved under realistic, noisy conditions. Taken together, these findings highlight the potential of variational quantum circuits for recommendation tasks and represent a practical step toward their real-world deployment.
papers.summary: Using the Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) framework, the authors build a content-based TV recommender by mapping BBC iPlayer programme synopses to variational quantum circuits and training them on pairwise similarity. The quantum model matches a classical `BiLSTM` baseline while using **47k parameters versus 17.8M**, and a `BiLSTM` restricted to the same parameter budget loses 3.63 points of mean average precision. The trained circuits were also run on Quantinuum's `System Model H2` hardware using a SWAP-test protocol, where the similarity signal survived realistic noise.

papers.title: BiShield-TEE: On the (In-)Security of Unilateral Weight Obfuscation in On-Device TEE-Shielded LLM Partition
papers.abstract: On-device deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly adopted due to latency and privacy requirements, but exposes proprietary models to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-enforced isolation for on-device inference, yet most TEE-based parameter obfuscation relies on unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only output side. We identify a vulnerability in this design, termed the \emph{Solution Determinacy Property (SDP)}: the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key and enabling attackers to break the protection. Under our attacks, representative methods \textsc{GroupCover} and \textsc{ArrowCloak} are reduced to negligible protection, with attack accuracy reaching over $2.4\times$ the full-shielding black-box baseline and recovering near-complete model functionality.To address this vulnerability, we propose \textsc{BiShield-TEE}, a bilateral framework that induces \emph{Ambiguous Solutions} through joint obfuscation of input and output dimensions, hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates. Experiments across diverse models and datasets show that \textsc{BiShield-TEE} confines attack accuracy to the full-shielding black-box baseline, while achieving higher inference efficiency than prior methods on real hardware.Our code is available at https://github.com/laduiw/BiShield-TEE.
papers.summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on-device exposes proprietary weights to theft, and Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) defenses often obfuscate weights with transformations applied only on the output side. The authors show that this design has a Solution Determinacy Property: the secret key is uniquely determined, so attackers can recover it. Under their attacks, **`GroupCover` and `ArrowCloak` provide negligible protection, with attack accuracy over 2.4× the full-shielding black-box baseline**. Their fix, `BiShield-TEE`, obfuscates both input and output dimensions so the true key hides among many equally valid candidates, keeping attack accuracy at the black-box baseline while running inference faster than prior methods on real hardware.

papers.title: Sharp and Stable Label-Free Calibration Certificates from Logical Coherence
papers.abstract: Query-conditioned probabilistic predictors answer logically related questions one at a time, and labels to check their calibration are often missing. For each restriction on what a bettor's stakes may use, a minimax theorem identifies, for finitely supported laws of the answers, the sharp label-free lower bound on the corresponding calibration residual. On bundles of different events its mean, marginal and joint stages can separate strictly, and a bundle's bound cannot be attributed to one question without assumptions on the others. The sharp marginal bound is discontinuous in the answers, and no label-free lower bound continuous in the Wasserstein distance stays within a constant factor of it. Lipschitz stakes give a stable bound, sharp for a smooth calibration residual and, for every positive Lipschitz constant, positive exactly when the sharp marginal bound is. On i.i.d. streams, projected online gradient ascent at fixed nodes gives fixed-horizon certificates whose shortfall is bounded by grid, learning and statistical terms, and predictable betting gives anytime-valid ones. In a preregistered study of four predictors on two data sets, all seven confirmatory certificates were positive (the eighth pair did not pass the pilot). A certificate shows only that calibration is at least this bad; zero means "not refuted".
papers.summary: Probabilistic predictors often answer logically related questions one at a time, and the labels needed to check their calibration are frequently unavailable. Using a minimax theorem, the authors derive sharp label-free lower bounds on calibration error from the logical coherence of a predictor's answers alone. They show the sharp bound is discontinuous, so they propose a stable Lipschitz variant, and give fixed-horizon and anytime-valid certificates for streaming data. In a preregistered study of four predictors on two datasets, **all seven confirmatory certificates were positive**. A positive certificate shows that calibration is at least that bad; a zero means only that miscalibration was not detected.

papers.title: From Perception to Prediction and Intervention: Benchmarking Proactive Video Assistants in Real-Life Scenarios
papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.
papers.summary: Video benchmarks for multimodal language models mostly test whether a model understands what it has seen, not whether it can anticipate what help a user needs and decide when to offer it. `P³IBench` evaluates proactive assistance in real-life streaming video across three capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction, and intervention. Across 12 open-source and proprietary video-language models, **current systems struggle to make well-calibrated decisions about when to respond**. A model trained on additional proactive data, `P³I-Assistant-4B`, improves on several tasks, though gains are uneven across capabilities.

papers.title: Independent Data-Integrity Verification for LLM-Driven Functional Coverage Closure in Hardware Design
papers.abstract: LLM agents can write directed tests that close functional coverage, but coverage only shows that a state was reached, not that the data on the way there was correct. This is a long-known point in verification and we do not claim it as new. We describe a small coverage-closure agent that applies it to an LLM loop: coverage is read from the report that the simulation itself exports (cocotb-coverage YAML) and never taken from the model's account, and data integrity is checked by scoreboards that are separate from the model. On three architecturally distinct RTL designs (an asynchronous FIFO, a UART transmitter and an AHB2APB bridge) the agent raised coverage from 91.7%, 88.9% and 67.4% to 100% within its 8-iteration budget in every logged run, using one design-agnostic agent. A reactive scoreboard monitor attached to the FIFO's base testbench also found a clock-domain-crossing bug in the author's own stimulus code. The monitor is not yet attached to the LLM-generated tests, so their data integrity is not independently checked; one manual check on a single FIFO test is reported as preliminary. We list the weaknesses of this evidence: three designs, no baseline, no ablation, and logged runs that come from several agent checkpoints.
papers.summary: LLM agents can write directed tests that close functional coverage in hardware verification, but reaching a coverage point does not prove the data along the way was correct. The author builds a small coverage-closure agent that reads coverage only from the simulator's exported `cocotb-coverage` report, never from the model's own account, and checks data integrity with separate scoreboards. On an asynchronous FIFO, a UART transmitter, and an `AHB2APB` bridge, **one design-agnostic agent reached 100% coverage within 8 iterations in every logged run**, and a scoreboard monitor found a clock-domain-crossing bug in the author's own stimulus code. The author lists the limits of the evidence: only three designs, no baseline or ablation, and scoreboards not yet attached to the LLM-generated tests.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents that call external tools over multiple turns sometimes use tool graph memory, which records past experience as transitions between tools and uses them to suggest the next tool. Across nine models and two benchmarks, this memory seldom beats baselines by a significant margin, and where it helps it costs more than twice the LLM calls. The memory's suggestions are often wrong, and random or no guidance keeps most of the gain, so **the benefit comes from extra computation rather than from the memory itself**. Storing the same experience as textual insights works better with almost no extra calls, which suggests memory is more useful as a soft prior than as a prescription for the next tool.

papers.title: Learning to Search for Executable Patternmaking from Certified Programs
papers.abstract: Recent models generate sewing patterns from images or text, and program-based representations make these patterns executable. These systems produce a finished pattern and do not model how a patternmaker turns one pattern into another. In practice a new style is made by editing an existing pattern: lengthening the bodice, moving a dart, swapping a sleeve. Pattern archives record the results of such edits and none of the steps. We observe that the steps can be recovered by searching over editing actions until one pattern becomes the other. A deterministic compiler makes the recovered steps checkable. To this end, we present SemDraft, the first framework that learns to search for executable patternmaking programs from paired before-and-after sewing patterns without recorded editing steps. Specifically, a bounded search recovers a program of editing actions and certifies it only after three checks: it recompiles from scratch, every pair of its actions is classified as ordered or interchangeable, and an independent replay reaches the same pattern. The certified programs then train a model that ranks candidate actions inside the same search. On two frozen draws of 80 order-sensitive cases, with every other search component fixed, the learned ranker certifies 63 and 64 cases within 1,000 search executions, against at most 53 and 52 for non-learned rankers.
papers.summary: Pattern archives store sewing patterns before and after a patternmaker's edits but not the editing steps themselves. `SemDraft` recovers those steps by searching over editing actions until one pattern becomes the other. A recovered program is certified only if it recompiles from scratch, each pair of its actions is classified as ordered or interchangeable, and an independent replay reaches the same pattern. The certified programs then train a ranker that guides the same search, and on two sets of 80 order-sensitive cases it certifies **63 and 64 cases within 1,000 search executions**, against at most 53 and 52 for non-learned rankers.

papers.title: ClaimScope: Label-Blind Witness Verification for Mathematical Claim Auditing
papers.abstract: Mathematical agents are commonly evaluated by answer accuracy or proof acceptance. We introduce ClaimScope, a 72-task benchmark for auditing proposed claims through a verdict, scope, counterexample, and repair. Tasks cover optimizer-state transport, finite-horizon affine recurrences, and exact $2\times2$ linear algebra. We evaluate Qwen3-8B with direct generation and four matched two-pass conditions, each starting from the same draft. A witness checker evaluates only the model's submitted state, without consulting reference verdicts or supplying a replacement witness. Its feedback still conveys information about validity: a verified refutation establishes that the claim is false, and rejection reasons can suggest structural fixes. In this evaluation, verifier feedback yields $23/39$ accepted counterexamples on invalid claims and $25/72$ safe completions, compared with $15/39$ and $20/72$ for checker-free generic feedback. Strict completion remains $17/72$; verdict accuracy changes from $47/72$ to $46/72$. The claim-grouped safe-completion difference is $.094$, with a bootstrap 95\% interval of $[.000,.198]$. All seven task-level gains follow horizon/input-length diagnostics. A post-hoc schema-only correction of the direct outputs reaches the same 25 safe tasks without another model call. These results separate claim classification from executable evidence, while locating the observed gains in witness-structure correction rather than demonstrating broader reasoning improvement.
papers.summary: `ClaimScope` is a 72-task benchmark that tests mathematical agents on auditing a proposed claim, which means giving a verdict, a scope, a counterexample, and a repair, rather than only on answer accuracy. Using `Qwen3-8B`, the authors compare a witness checker that looks only at the model's submitted evidence, without reference labels, against generic feedback that uses no checker. Checker feedback raises accepted counterexamples on invalid claims from 15/39 to **23/39**, while verdict accuracy barely moves. A schema-only correction applied after the fact matches the same gains without any extra model call, so the improvement comes from fixing the structure of the evidence rather than from better reasoning.

papers.title: Transfer Learning in Bandits from Unknown Adaptive Policies: Problem-Dependent Lower and Upper Bounds
papers.abstract:
Transfer learning in stochastic multi-armed bandits is typically studied assuming that prior data forms a fixed offline dataset or is generated by a known source. In practice, historical observations come from a previous adaptive decision process whose policy is unknown. We study this setting for bounded rewards in $[0,1]$.
  Before the online game starts, the learner receives, for each arm $k$, $N'_k$ observations drawn i.i.d.\ from an unknown distribution $\nu'_k$, collected by an arbitrary and possibly data-dependent strategy, so the sample sizes $N'_k$ may be random. Source and target means satisfy $|\mu_k-\mu'_k|<L_k$ for known constants $(L_k)_k$.
  We derive an asymptotic problem-dependent lower bound and propose KL-UCB-Transfer, which combines online and historical data and achieves logarithmic regret with an improved leading constant whenever $\mu'_a<\mu_1-L_a$, and recovers the classical KL-UCB guarantee otherwise. Since bounding the source-target discrepancy is often unrealistic, we relax the assumption to the one-sided condition $\mu_k-\mu'_k<L_k$ and show that logarithmic regret can survive under misspecification, characterizing three regimes ranging from improvement to a degraded logarithmic bound to a loss of guarantee. Simulations illustrate the practical benefits of exploiting process-generated historical data.
papers.summary: This work studies transfer learning in stochastic multi-armed bandits where the historical data comes from an earlier adaptive process whose policy is unknown, so the number of samples per arm may itself be random. Assuming the source and target means of each arm differ by less than a known bound, the authors derive an asymptotic problem-dependent lower bound and propose `KL-UCB-Transfer`. The algorithm achieves **logarithmic regret with an improved leading constant** when the historical data rules an arm out, and recovers the standard `KL-UCB` guarantee otherwise. Under a weaker one-sided assumption, the analysis identifies three regimes, ranging from improvement to a degraded logarithmic bound to a loss of the guarantee.

papers.title: AVALON: Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation with Human-Seeded Topological Memory
papers.abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.
papers.summary: `AVALON` targets indoor service robots entering buildings they have never traversed but whose layout their users already know. Starting from only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial alignment, the robot navigates using a topological memory seeded by humans. It re-anchors its position at verified node arrivals instead of building a global SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping) map, and humans and robot update the memory together, with field evidence gating each change. On a `Unitree Go2`, `AVALON` with `X-NavDP` completed a 12.81 m mission in 46.4 s in 5 of 5 runs, **40.9% less robot time** than `DimOS-Go2`, while the navigation policy alone timed out in every run.

papers.title: LOADBench: A Large Open Analog Dataset and Benchmark for Machine Learning in IC Design
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) for analog IC design is constrained by limited open data and the absence of standardized evaluation: results reported in different papers are typically obtained on bespoke, often closed, datasets and with ad-hoc metrics, leaving comparisons across methods unreliable. We address both gaps with a large opensource dataset and a suite of standardized benchmarks. The dataset contains more than 100 operational amplifier (opamp) topologies (1-, 2-, and 3-stage) in the SkyWater130 PDK, each shipped with structural and functional annotations, topology-specific sizing constraints (symmetry and sizing rules), an Ngspice testbench, and a multi-objective NSGA-II sizing run producing around 103 Pareto-optimal and 106 intermediate sizing-performance pairs per topology. On top of this data we define six benchmark tasks with precise protocols: inverse sizing, topology selection, sub-circuit classification, structural circuit generation, Pareto-membership prediction, and multi-objective optimization. Thus, the data presented here constitutes the most comprehensive dataset for ML development in over four decades of analog IC design automation. The dataset, ground-truth annotations, and reference implementations of the metric-defining routines are released under an open license, enabling reproducible and directly comparable evaluation across heterogeneous analog design automation methods.
papers.summary: Machine learning for analog integrated circuit (IC) design has lacked open data and standardized evaluation, so results reported in different papers are hard to compare. `LOADBench` releases **more than 100 operational amplifier topologies** in the `SkyWater130` process design kit, each with structural and functional annotations, sizing constraints, an `Ngspice` testbench, and a multi-objective `NSGA-II` sizing run that yields many Pareto-optimal and intermediate sizing-performance pairs. On top of this data it defines six benchmark tasks with precise protocols, including inverse sizing, topology selection, sub-circuit classification, structural circuit generation, Pareto-membership prediction, and multi-objective optimization.

papers.title: LoopAhead: Speculating Ahead for Faster Decoding in Looped Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. However, generating each token still involves sequential computation and repeated access to model weights, leading to high decoding latency. Recent pipelined self-speculative decoding methods reduce this delay by drafting tokens from early-loop predictions and asynchronously advancing tokens at different recurrent depths in the same batch, but they do not fully exploit early-loop features for longer lookahead and still spend computation verifying incorrect speculative branches. We introduce \method, a speculative decoding framework for looped transformers that enables earlier drafting of future tokens and assigns complementary roles to different recurrent depths. A lightweight lookahead drafter (LAD) predicts multiple future tokens with early-loop states, and deeper-loop feedback helps decide which draft branches to continue and which to pause, while the full-depth model makes the final token decisions. LoopAhead achieves up to 7.82x decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers save parameters by applying the same layers repeatedly, but decoding stays slow because every token still requires sequential computation. `LoopAhead` is a speculative decoding framework in which a lightweight lookahead drafter uses early-loop states to predict several future tokens. Feedback from deeper loops then decides which draft branches to continue or pause, and the full-depth model makes the final token decisions. The method reaches **up to 7.82x decoding speedup** over standard autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution.

papers.title: Decoding What iOS Location Services Send to Apple: An LLM Is an Unreliable Analyst but a Useful Toolmaker
papers.abstract: Reverse engineering the data formats used by mobile software is skilled and slow, and using AI to assist with it is attractive. We evaluate this for the protobuf messages that an iPhone sends to Apple's location services. Working from Apple's binaries, we use two frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Codex GPT Sol 5.6) to reconstruct the schemas of protobufs observed in network traffic. The great majority of the schemas contain substantial errors, and these are hard to detect because the schemas are internally consistent. Direct AI use is therefore unsuitable for forensic and privacy analysis. AI can, however, write reliable analysis tools when their output can be validated. We use Claude to write a Python tool, Extractor, that reliably recovers protobuf schemas from Apple binaries. We validate it against binaries compiled from schemas with known answers, previously published schemas, and network measurements. We demonstrate the use of Extractor to decode and analyse the location services network traffic of a jailbroken iPhone 8 (iOS 16.7.11).
papers.summary: Working from Apple's binaries, the authors tested whether frontier models (`Claude Opus 4.8` and `Codex GPT Sol 5.6`) can reconstruct the schemas of protobuf messages an iPhone sends to Apple's location services. **The great majority of model-reconstructed schemas contained substantial errors**, and these errors were hard to spot because the schemas were internally consistent, which makes direct AI use unsuitable for forensic and privacy analysis. Claude was, however, able to write a Python tool, `Extractor`, that reliably recovers the schemas and was validated against binaries compiled from known schemas, previously published schemas, and network measurements. The authors then use `Extractor` to decode the location services traffic of a jailbroken iPhone 8.

papers.title: Waypoint-OPD: Transferring RL-Induced Policy Shifts via Gated On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Policy-shift distillation reuses the difference between a teacher's log probabilities before and after reinforcement learning (RL) as supervision on student-generated trajectories.
