Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.
papers.summary: Training models to do autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) is hard because each experiment's result depends on many earlier decisions and long runs contain many costly experiments. `MLExpert` is a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model trained with a pipeline that has four parts: a `Kaggle-MLE Factory` that builds executable tasks; hierarchical agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT) guided by outcomes; Windowed Interaction RL (`WIRL`), which gives all decisions between two consecutive experiment results a shared outcome-based reward; and asynchronous collection that allows policy updates before a trajectory ends. On `MLE-Bench Lite` it **raises the base model's average medal rate from 37.9% to 72.7%**, comparable to larger frontier models such as `Kimi-K3` and `GLM-5.3`. It also improves on `NatureBench Lite`, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization.
papers.highlight_summary:
Long-horizon machine learning engineering is hard to train for because each costly experiment returns feedback that reflects many earlier decisions, and full runs last for hours. `MLExpert` is a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agent post-trained to run its own experiments: it learns from outcome-filtered teacher trajectories, then from reinforcement learning applied to "execution windows," the stretch of decisions between consecutive experiment results.

- The `Kaggle-MLE Factory` uses a multi-agent pipeline to turn historical Kaggle competitions into **154** executable tasks with hidden test splits, and a ReAct-style harness lets the model itself branch, backtrack, and invalidate candidate solutions in an experiment tree.
- Training starts from `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` with two-stage SFT, first on general tool-use data and then on `GLM-5.2` and `Qwen3.8-Max` teacher trajectories trimmed after their peak score, followed by `WIRL`, which gives each window a shared medal-tiered reward plus a ±0.2 local-trend bonus and uses token-level policy correction so asynchronous updates can happen mid-trajectory.
- On the 22-task `MLE-Bench Lite`, the medal rate rises from **37.9% to 72.7%**, matching `Kimi-K3` and `GLM-5.3` in the authors' harness, with gold rising from 22.7% to 50.0%; inside `Claude Code` it reaches **69.7%** versus the base model's 42.4%.
- Ablations show each stage adds to the score (47.0% after general SFT, 62.1% after MLE SFT, 72.7% with `WIRL`), while trajectory-level `GRPO` (56.1%) and PPO-style training (60.6%) both end up *below* the SFT starting point.
- The gains carry over to other tasks: Surpass-SOTA on `NatureBench Lite` goes from 0% to 50%, held-out accuracy of an AIME scaffold built for `GPT-4.1-nano` goes from 23.3% to 43.7%, and mean `MLS-Bench-Lite` reward goes from 0.322 to 0.425; however, the benchmarks are small (22 and 10 tasks), frontier baselines were run only once with some numbers taken from prior work, and under `Claude Code` the model still trails `GLM-5.3` (77.3%).

papers.title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
papers.abstract: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.
papers.summary: Agent benchmarks usually provide well-specified tasks, while real customer delivery requires forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) to clarify vague requirements, work in live systems, and discover constraints nobody stated. `FDE-Gym` contains 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, adapted by industry experts from real projects. Agents work with scripted stakeholders and production-like systems, and each delivery is scored by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, with penalties for messages, trial runs, and waiting time. Across 13 model configurations from seven providers, **the best configuration resolves only 14 of 95 tasks** in the realistic setting, with a mean score of 0.56. Discovering unstated constraints is the main bottleneck, but even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtained every key fact, it delivered strong results on only 10.

papers.title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.
papers.summary: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models commonly combine fine-grained expert segmentation, which enlarges the space of possible expert combinations, with shared experts that are active for every token. The authors identify a conflict between the two: shared experts reduce the variability of token representations, which makes routing less exploratory just when the larger routing space needs more exploration, so fine-grained segmentation may not deliver its full expressiveness. `MirrorMoE` resolves this by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts, and **it consistently improves performance across model scales**.

papers.title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling
papers.abstract: Generative visual verifiers play a crucial role in advancing multimodal intelligence. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique signal. Our experiments further demonstrate that these structured and interpretable outputs improve the verifier's generalization to out-of-domain multimodal critic tasks. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring at the global level. Under a general reinforcement learning framework, we first empirically demonstrate that the proposed pointwise graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in traditional text-to-image scenarios. We then extend our investigation to rule-governed generative world modeling where generative models are leveraged for world simulation and world reasoning under explicit rules. From a theoretical standpoint, we further show that a pairwise verification paradigm yields more accurate critiques than the pointwise formulation when ground-truth images are available, with empirical results on diverse structured world-modeling tasks such as Maze and Sudoku further validating the effectiveness of our approach. Overall, our findings suggest a key insight: the transition from generative models to structured world-modeling agents critically hinges on the availability of accurate pairwise graded visual verifiers.
papers.summary: Binary visual verifiers that output only true or false give a weak critique signal for prompts with many compositional requirements. `OmniVerifier-C1` instead breaks complex prompts or environment rules into fine-grained components and scores each one. It is trained with a decoupled reinforcement learning strategy that jointly optimizes binary judgments on each sub-question and an overall alignment score. This **graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in text-to-image settings** and generalizes better to out-of-domain critique tasks. For rule-governed world modeling tasks such as `Maze` and `Sudoku`, the authors show theoretically and empirically that pairwise verification against ground-truth images yields more accurate critiques than scoring each image on its own.

papers.title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.
papers.summary: Most leading time series foundation models predict marginal quantiles at each future step and leave the dependence between steps unspecified. That gap matters for quantities that depend on the whole trajectory, such as cumulative demand, peak load and event timing. `PathFM` uses flow matching to generate complete future paths, and it is distilled to one or two sampling steps with a history attention cache shared across draws, so it can produce many paths in **roughly the time a quantile model needs for one query**. It matches competing models on marginal accuracy on `fev-bench` and `TIME`, beats all external baselines on aggregate path score on the new `fps-bench` (which adds energy, variogram and downstream metrics), and keeps long-run variability on chaotic systems where strong baselines collapse.

papers.title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies
papers.abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.
papers.summary: Generative simulation can build robot training environments automatically, but an environment that is physically valid is not necessarily useful for fixing a given policy's weaknesses. `CoDA` makes a simulation data engine and an action policy evolve together through a shared memory of environment construction, policy failures and learning progress. The memory turns diagnoses from a vision-language critic into programs that recreate the difficulties and programs that train the policy to overcome them. A companion method, `Text2potential`, converts those diagnoses into staged potentials that give dense reward for action-chunk value learning without changing the optimal policy. Across four manipulation task families, out-of-distribution success rises from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to **27.6%**, and on `LIBERO-Pro` 15 rounds lift success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

papers.title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
papers.abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
papers.summary: Robot world models have to account for environmental factors that cannot be observed directly, such as friction, mass or human-defined rules. `T2-Z` conditions a world model on a compact learnable environment latent, trained without any labels for which factors exist. Training alternates between learning shared action-conditioned dynamics with the latents fixed and optimizing the latents with the model frozen. At test time a fresh latent is optimized from one or more interactions to adapt to an unseen environment. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-robot tasks, object prediction error falls from 15.20 to 7.00 and **action success rises from 33.73% to 72.96%**, and ablations show a single test-time trajectory can be enough to infer the latent.

papers.title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
papers.abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.
papers.summary: Practical quantum advantage depends on efficient circuits for a small set of computational primitives, which are hard to optimize because quantum computation must be reversible. The authors run an evolutionary loop in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them, and they apply it to eight tasks across numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation and number theory. In **seven of the eight tasks the discovered circuits reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts below the state of the art**. In the eighth, the search found a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion that makes the classical `divsteps` algorithm workable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off.

papers.title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.
papers.summary: Household robots need to respect user preferences, but personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) has had no controlled benchmark that separates finishing a task from satisfying a preference. `LIBERO-PeRM` builds on `LIBERO` with a taxonomy of language-expressible preferences covering motion, skill and user-profile choices, plus a procedural pipeline that generates paired demonstrations with and without each preference. The result is five task suites totaling 312 tasks, used to test zero-shot preference following, learning from demonstrations, sample efficiency, generalization, and composition and conflicts between preferences. **Current vision-language-action (VLA) policies struggle with zero-shot personalization**, while supervised fine-tuning makes preferences learnable. Mixed training keeps no-preference performance better than sequential adaptation but can weaken motion-preference learning, and generalization, decomposition and conflict handling remain unsolved.
